title: Special Topics in American Studies
special: Classical Music and American Mass Culture Between the World Wars
course-description: This course is designed primarily to allow faculty to develop focused interdisciplinary courses which address specific issues, themes, or problems in American society. Topics vary from semester to semester. Students should consult the department's webpage for current offerings before the start of the semester.
class-description: Classical music was big business in the United States in the years preceding the First World War, but not for American composers. As audiences flocked to performances of music by European composers, the most famous work of "American" classical music was not American at all: Czech composer Antonín Dvořák's New World Symphony. But all that would soon change. Over the course of the 1920s and 30s, a new wave of composers redefined what American classical music could be by responding to the distinctly American experiences of their time. Black composers like Florence Price and William Grant Still blended symphonic forms with blues and spirituals. “Ultra-modern” composers like Ruth Crawford Seeger and (UC Berkeley alum) Henry Cowell wrote radical music to match their increasingly radical politics. And Aaron Copland crafted what would become known as a quintessentially American sound, but only after drawing inspiration from the folk-music-infused works of Mexican composer Carlos Chávez.

title: Examining U.S. Cultures in Place
special: Wilderness and Civilization: Nature, Culture, and the American Zoo
course-description: This course examines how U.S. cultures are constructed, reinforced, and changed--particularly in reference to place and material culture. Qualitative and quantitative methods of analysis drawn from several disciplines will help students develop skills in cultural interpretation. Case studies may focus on a neighborhood, a city, or a region. Topics will vary from semester to semester.
class-description: This course will explore the history, culture, and significance of zoos and other sites of animal display in the United States. Both before and after the formation of the first zoological park in Philadelphia in 1874, Americans have collected and displayed animals for sport, amusement, education, and research. As growing numbers of Americans moved from rural areas to large urban centers in the late nineteenth century, the zoo offered a connection to the natural world—a taste of wilderness amidst the civilization of the city. But nature and culture were never as binary as this story might suggest. Zoos and other sites of animal encounters—such as menageries, circuses, world’s fairs, aquariums, drive-through safari parks, and the roadside zoos made famous by Tiger King in 2020—have both shaped and been shaped by changing ideas about the relationship between American culture and what Frederick Jackson Turner called “the western wilderness” in 1893. This class will therefore take an interdisciplinary approach to understand the significance of the American zoo as we consider what zoos can teach us about science, popular culture, race, gender, colonization, popular entertainment, the environment, media, and power in the United States. The course will also include multiple field trips to local zoos, museums, and animal sanctuaries (at no cost to the students); potential field trip locations include the Oakland Zoo, California Academy of Sciences, Tilden Little Farm, and Marine Mammal Center. This class fulfills the American Cultures requirement.

title: Ancient Greek Political Thought
course-description: In this course we will investigate the political thought of ancient Greece by discussing some of its most important and influential texts.  All texts are to be read in translation.

title: Greek Philosophy
course-description: Introduction to the philosophies of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle.

title: Greek and Roman Myths
course-description: The society, culture, values and outlook on life of the ancient Greeks as expressed in their mythology; their views on life, birth, marriage, death, sex and sexuality; on culture and civilization, the origin and meaning of the world. Their use of myth to think about, and give order to human experience. The course includes some of the most important works of Western literature in English translation (the 'Odyssey', the 'Theogony', twelve plays by leading Greek dramatists (Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides), along with their historical and religious context, as well as drawing on material evidence (vase paintings, sculpture, archaeological sites).
class-description: Telling stories is one of the most common ways that humans make sense of the world and their lives in it. For the ancient Greeks and Romans, these stories were very often in the form of tales of the adventures, triumphs and sufferings of gods and heroes – what we call classical myths. This class examines many of these myths, what they meant to Greeks and Romans, and what they still mean for us. We will cover major myths (including myths of creation, myths of nature and the stars, the Trojan war myths, the story of the house of Oedipus, the exploits of Hercules and Theseus, the career of Aeneas, and the myths of the early Roman kings) and the various media that record them (including ancient literature in translation and visual representations). This serves as an excellent introduction to ancient Mediterranean culture and society: through the myths we can learn more about ancient religion, politics and art. We will also discuss post-ancient and global responses to the classical myths, from medieval revulsion to modern poetry to spectacular Hollywood renditions.

title: Senior Honors Thesis Seminar
course-description: This is a required course for students wishing to graduate with honors in American studies. Entails writing a bachelor's thesis pertaining to the student's individual area of concentration within the American studies major. The completed thesis will be read by the thesis supervisor and one other faculty member.

title: Freshman Seminar
course-description: The Freshman Seminar Program has been designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. Freshman seminars are offered in all campus departments, and topics may vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to 15 freshmen.
class-description: Everyone's people built with earth at one time or another. As we are finding our way towards sustainable building practices, the use of one technology might hold some clues to saving energy, emitting less carbon, and potentially returning our structures to the earth with less damage once we are gone. We will make adobes, build with them, and explore how they intersect with food, architecture, and cultures around the world.

title: Reading and Composition in Anthropology
special: Re/writing Culture: Feminist Interventions in Anthropology
course-description: Reading and composition courses based on the anthropological literature. These courses provide an introduction to issues distinctive of anthropological texts and introduce students to distinctive forms of anthropological writing, such as ethnography and anthropological prehistory. Readings will be chosen from a variety of texts by authors whose works span the discipline, from bioanthropology to archaeology and sociocultural anthropology. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: In this reading and composition course, students will explore key issues, themes, and debates in feminist anthropology through text and visual mediums. We will examine how ethnography, as a method and a mode of writing, is approached from a feminist perspective to understand how categories and hierarchies of sex and gender are constructed through culture and intersect with other axes of difference, such as race, nationality, disability and class. In conversation with scholarship from Black Studies, Trans Studies, Disability Studies students will engage with the following questions: How do notions of gender and sex shift across different geographical, political, and temporal contexts? And to what extent does ethnographic methods in feminist anthropology extend beyond scholarly texts to encompass visual, sonic, and other expressive forms?
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Reading and Composition in Anthropology
course-description: Reading and composition courses based on the anthropological literature. These courses provide an introduction to issues distinctive of anthropological texts and introduce students to distinctive forms of anthropological writing, such as ethnography and anthropological prehistory. Readings will be chosen from a variety of texts by authors whose works span the discipline, from bioanthropology to archaeology and sociocultural anthropology. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Reading and Composition in Anthropology
special: Landscapes of Knowledge: Environmental Archaeology in Latin America
course-description: Reading and composition courses based on the anthropological literature. These courses provide an introduction to issues distinctive of anthropological texts and introduce students to distinctive forms of anthropological writing, such as ethnography and anthropological prehistory. Readings will be chosen from a variety of texts by authors whose works span the discipline, from bioanthropology to archaeology and sociocultural anthropology. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: This course explores long-term relationships between humans and their environments through the lens of archaeology. Centering on Latin American case studies, it examines how societies have shaped, and been shaped by, the landscapes they inhabit. Key themes include historical ecology, traditional ecological knowledge, and collaborative, community-based approaches to research that bridge archaeology, ethnography, and environmental studies.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Reading and Composition in Anthropology
course-description: Reading and composition courses based on the anthropological literature. These courses provide an introduction to issues distinctive of anthropological texts and introduce students to distinctive forms of anthropological writing, such as ethnography and anthropological prehistory. Readings will be chosen from a variety of texts by authors whose works span the discipline, from bioanthropology to archaeology and sociocultural anthropology. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Reading and Composition in Anthropology
course-description: Reading and composition courses based on the anthropological literature. These courses provide an introduction to issues distinctive of anthropological texts and introduce students to distinctive forms of anthropological writing, such as ethnography and anthropological prehistory. Readings will be chosen from a variety of texts by authors whose works span the discipline, from bioanthropology to archaeology and sociocultural anthropology. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: Attempts to grapple with the “future of work” appear more pressing than ever. Yet, while an array of factors seem unique to this moment—for example, the proliferation of AI technologies, significant shifts in workplace norms in the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic, and intensifying ecological crises—efforts to describe and evaluate the changing landscape of work have been a longstanding, recurring feature of policy discourse and academic debates. In this course, we will examine how a central claim, namely, that the nature of work is fundamentally changing, has been asserted in times both historical and contemporary, situated in the United States and elsewhere globally. Why is the language of dramatic, epochal change so often invoked when a wide range of actors discuss issues of labor and work? Who benefits from this rhetoric? What have been its effects? In the latter half of the course, in particular, we will ask how workers have used such language to alter public perception and advocate for labor rights.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Introduction to Social/Cultural Anthropology (American Cultures)
course-description: The structure and dynamics of human cultures and social institutions from a comparative perspective with special attention to American cultures and their roots. Case studies will illustrate the principles presented in the course. It fulfills the requirements for 3.

title: World of Ancient Maya
course-description: A survey of the history of development of Maya society and culture in Central American prior to Eurpean contact in the 16th century AD.
class-description: The evidence of ancient Maya history permeates our world; from archaeological infrastructures and cities in the Petén, to its influence in contemporary art, to the current Indigenous Maya Land movement in Belize; understanding the ancient Maya past can also help us understand our present and our future. This course is a survey of the history of ancient Maya society and culture in Central America. We will cover the history of political structures and governance, the material culture of regional polities, and understand the specific histories that cities and people had within themselves and to each other. To do this, we will learn to unpack the basic components of the layered and embedded systems of Maya imagery and writing, and trace the history of Maya decipherment and archaeological work. While this course mostly focuses on Maya history up until the 16th century, we will also discuss in tandem how Maya people today are fighting for access to ancestral sites and land, and learn how ancient Maya material culture came to be extracted and dispersed to some of the most renowned global museums today.

title: Introduction to Medical Anthropology
course-description: Cultural, psychological, and biological aspects of the definitions, causes, symptoms, and treatment of illness. Comparative study of medical systems, practitioners, and patients.

title: History of Anthropological Thought
course-description: This course will present a history of anthropological thought from the mid-19th century to the present, and will draw upon the major subdisciplines of anthropology. It will focus both upon the integration of the anthropological subdisciplines and upon the relationships between these and other disciplines outside anthropology.

title: The Palaeopathological Perspective
course-description: An exploration of the record and human experience of health and disease with specific focus on bioarchaeology, the study of human remains from ancient and recent archaeological contexts, using a biocultural approach. Evaluates how morbidity, prevalence, and mortality in the past are identified using a biocultural lens to analyze and interpret the etiology of disease in the past. Discusses how evolution and adaptation plays a central role in disease emergence and prevalence; how humans are agents in the co-evolution of infectious agents in food webs and ecosystems; and how people define and experience disease, illness, wellness and suffering in different cultural contexts.

title: Special Topics in Biological Anthropology
course-description: Varying topics covering current discoveries, research, theories, fieldwork, etc., in biological anthropology. Topics vary with instructor.
class-description: Using an interdisciplinary framework, this course seeks to center diversity and variation in the study of the human brain. Our goal will be to understand how the brain works and how it has come to work in the ways that it does, while at the same time challenging the normative conception of a typical or average ("the") human brain.

title: Psychoneuroendocrinology: Stress, Disease, and Health Inequalities
course-description: This course explores the sophisticated and complex interactions between the brain, hormones, and behavior and their relevance to human development and health – a growing scientific field known as psychoneuroendocrinology. Topics include the multiple psychological and biological systems that make up psychoneuroendocrinological processes; evolutionary and developmental perspectives on the emergence and function of these mechanisms; the social experiences of stress, trauma, nurturance, and support; the psychoneuroendocrinology of physical, mental, and psychosomatic disease; and how historical, societal, and political dynamics of power structure the patterns of intersectional health inequities.
class-description: How do psychological, social, and physical experiences become incorporated into the body and shape human health? Understandings of the mind and body have historically been split since the time of Descartes (early 1600s), when he asserted a dualistic divide between the immaterial mind and the body. Since then, mind-body dualistic perspectives have persisted across the development of “modern” (Western) scientific thought, leading to perpetual distinctions between human biology and psychological experience. Recent scientific developments have illuminated previously underappreciated physiological, molecular, and more recently, neurobiological processes that show the interconnectedness and singularity of the mind and body. This course explores the sophisticated and complex interactions between the brain, hormones, and behavior and its relevance to human development and health – a growing scientific field known as psychoneuroendocrinology.

title: Sophomore Seminar
special: Race, Gender, and Social Life in Colonial Honduras: Reading Over the Shoulder of People in the Past
course-description: Sophomore seminars are small interactive courses offered by faculty members in departments all across the campus. Sophomore seminars offer opportunity for close, regular intellectual contact between faculty members and students in the crucial second year. The topics vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to 15 sophomores.
class-description: How de we learn about people's everyday lives in the past? One source is documents, which collectively form archives. Scholars learn to read old handwriting, explore why documents were produced, and expand from them to understanding people's lives. This seminar introduces students to this process of research with original documents from the Spanish colonial period in Central America. Working with digital copies of documents from the colonial Spanish archives in Spain, Guatemala, and Honduras, we will "read over the shoulder" of the writers whose words form one of our most immediate links to Spanish colonial Honduran life. Students will learn how to locate archival documents online; how to read colonial handwriting; and how we can begin to understand more about society from even brief documents. Working together, we will discuss several longer documents about the lives of native Americans who were obliged to work for Spanish citizens and petitioned for relief, about free black residents of a military fort, and about a variety of women and men who shaped colonial life.

title: Introduction to Archaeology
course-description: Prehistory and cultural growth. Introduction to the methods, goals, and theoretical concepts of archaeology with attention to the impact archaeology has had on the construction of the histories of diverse communities - Native Americans, Hispanics, and Euro-Americans. It fulfills the requirements for 2.
class-description: This is an introduction to how an explicitly Americanist archaeology is used to tell stories about the past, especially those parts of the human past which are hidden by the limitations or objectives of written histories. Readings, lectures, section discussions and activities, and out-of-class exercises explore the practical and social dimensions of archaeology as practiced in the United States. We begin with a basic orientation, seeing how archaeology developed here, and the contrast between popular images of archaeology and its real social and political context with consequences for communities today. We then explore how archaeologists work--how they gather data and how they reconstruct social behavior and cultural meaning from material remains, with particular attention to architecture, domestic artifacts, mortuary practices, foodways, and trash disposal in contexts unique to different American communities. Next we examine how these methods are used to study fundamental aspects of society and culture, including human ecology and subsistence; social relations and identities; production and exchange; symbolism and ideology; and the relationship between power, social inequality and the state. While the course materials (e.g. Deetz) present a variety of North American pre-contact, colonial, and post-colonial contexts, we will use additional case studies and guest lectures from a range of practicing Americanist archaeologists to explore the consequences of archaeological practice for diverse American communities including those with heritages from Native America, Latin America, Asia, Europe, and Africa. We also discuss some of the professional and ethical problems affecting the practice of archaeology today and the conservation, protection, and control of our nation’s cultural resources. Students selected to work as American Cultures Engaged Scholars will have additional opportunities to partner on community-accountable projects in lieu of some coursework, but will be graded by community partners (details TBA in class).

title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology
course-description: An introduction to an evolutionary and biocultural perspective on evolutionary theory and basic human genetics; evolutionary and comparative biology of humans and our closest living relatives the nonhuman primates; origins of early humans and uniquely human anatomical and cultural development; and modern human variation, health, and adaptation.

title: Teaching Interdisciplinary American Studies
course-description: This course will introduce graduate students to a number of techniques and theories used in teaching at the university level. In particular, it will focus on the challenges of teaching interdisciplinary American studies courses that rely on a range of materials and methodological approaches drawn from multiple disciplines and that address students who come from a variety of disciplinary backgrounds.

title: Special Topics in Archaeology/Area
course-description: Special topics in archaeology which meet the area requirement for the anthropology major.
class-description: This course is designed to provide an introduction to the archaeology of the U.S. Southwest. People have lived in the Greater Southwest for at least 12,000 years.  This course provides an archaeological overview of Indigenous societies in the Southwest from the earliest occupation through the colonial period, including where, when, and how they lived. One of the major goals of the course is to understand the great diversity of societies that occupied the Southwest, and how and why they differed from each other. Another major goal is to understand changing adaptations of Southwestern peoples over the 12,000 years of occupation. In addition to looking at current interpretations of the history of past Southwestern peoples, we will also look at how archaeologists piece together information from field and laboratory work, the intersection of archaeological and Indigenous oral histories and traditions, and the relevance and uses of archaeology for contemporary communities.

title: Forms of Folklore
course-description: A world-wide survey of the major and minor forms of folklore with special emphasis upon proverbs, riddles, superstitions, games, songs, and narratives.
class-description: Challenging nationalistic constructions of folklore, this course explores how racial, class, gender, sexual, (dis)ability, and national hierarchies shape identities and how people create notions of difference through folklore. It features research by Black, Latinx, Native American, and Asian American and Pacific Islander scholars.

title: Anthropology of the Environment
course-description: Surveys anthropological perspectives on the environment and examines differing cultural constructions of nature. Coverage includes theory, method, and case materials extending from third world agrarian contexts to urban North America. Topics may include cultural ecology, political ecology, cultural politics of nature, and environmental imaginaries.

title: Mobile City Chronicles
special: Mobile City Chronicles: Data and Design for Civic Engagement
course-description: Information and data technologies are remaking human society.  If left to corporate and state remodeling, de-democratization and polarization seem likely outcomes in this new world of algorithmic life.  Are there alternatives?  In this course, students learn to develop other possibilities that generate more civically engaged, transparent, and sovereign data streams.  This is a lab-based course. Projects will address how data could operate in civic spaces to increase direct democratic agency in local lives. Lab work includes building apps that implement story concepts, game dynamics, and collaborative development strategies. No course prerequisites or software competences. Experience with digital art and/or JavaScript and Python desirable.

title: Introduction to Museum Methods
course-description: This course will introduce participants to the fundamentals of contemporary museum practices. It is intended for two groups of students: individuals who may be thinking of conducting research in museums, and may benefit from an understanding of the way these institutions work; and individuals who may be thinking of museum work as a post-graduate career. The course will include both discussion of museum concepts and practical application of these concepts through real-world exercises. While the course fulfills the method requirement, it covers practices of art, natural history, and science museums as well.

title: Analysis of the Archaeological Record
course-description: Guidance in the preparation of excavated materials for publication, including sampling and analysis strategy, drawing, photography and write-up.
class-description: Learn modern archaeological survey methods commonly used in the United States. ANTHRO 134 is designed to introduce students to common practices used by entry-level archaeologists in the cultural resource management (CRM) industry. Through a series of hands-on exercises, including outdoors activities, students will learn how to identify artifacts, conduct a pedestrian survey, how to date historical buildings, and how to describe an archaeological site.

title: Special Topics in Archaeology
special: Critical Heritage Studies in Archaeology: Land, Law, and Labor
class-description: What does it mean to own and own up to the past? Archaeology as a discipline emerged in tandem with imperialism and dispossession. Conceptualizations of ownership, cultural property, stewardship, museological display, and the science of archaeology itself have antecedents in entangled colonial histories. How do we locate these historical threads in the discipline of archaeology? How have territorial jurisdictions, legal precedent, and labor patterns influenced the way that we read the material record? And what current work is challenging, remaking, and creating new futures for the way that we understand the past? This seminar explores both the historiographic emergence of cultural heritage studies within archaeology, and interrogates the very heritage of archaeology as a discipline.

title: Archaeological Research Strategies: Research Design
course-description: Required for all first and second year graduate students in archaeology. Three hours of seminar discussion of major issues in the history and theory of archaeological research and practice (229A), and of the research strategies and design for various kinds of archaeological problems (229B). To be offered alternate semesters.

title: Undergraduate Seminar
course-description: Seminar for the advanced study of the subject matter of a previously given upper division course, emphasizing reading and discussion.
class-description: This course is an introduction to Indigenous Archaeologies, sometimes defined as archaeology "with, by, and for" Indigenous peoples (Nicholas and Andrews 1997). These approaches are distinctive in that they often combine the study of the past with contemporary social justice concerns. At their core, they advocate an archaeology that is more inclusive of and responsive to the needs of Indigenous peoples. This acknowledgement of the relationship between knowledge production and human interests is fundamental to doing better science. This course covers a broad range of topics including the history of anthropological archaeology, Indigenous knowledge and science, decolonizing methodologies, representational sovereignty, repatriation, National Museum of the American Indian, and Indigenous futures. Specific cases studies from the Southwestern, Western, Northeastern, and Northwestern regions of the US are highlighted.

title: Undergraduate Seminar
course-description: Seminar for the advanced study of the subject matter of a previously given upper division course, emphasizing reading and discussion.
class-description: Persons have lived and worlds have been sustained outside of the fixity of gender assigned at birth for thousands at years, but at universities in Texas in 2025 professors are being fired for acknowledging this reality.  How might we enter into rigorous discussion, as anthropologists and within the range of our gendered being and experience, in this time? How might we think beyond the United States, for example in India where transgender is not being attacked by the religious right but on the contrary is being made into a vehicle of religious nationalism?  How might we address the ways trans and other spaces of gendered life on the social margin are brought together into assemblages with other forms and politics of human difference?

title: Undergraduate Seminar
course-description: Seminar for the advanced study of the subject matter of a previously given upper division course, emphasizing reading and discussion.
class-description: This seminar will analyze the period and process of “post-communism” (aka “post-socialism”) and will focus on Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union, and Central Asia. We will investigate the ongoing social, cultural, political, economic, moral, and personal transformation that has taken place in the former communist world since its “collapse” in the late 1980s-early 1990s. These processes have been optimistic and liberating, and at the same time, traumatic and brutal. They created new freedoms and forms of cultural effervescence, but also new unfreedoms, dispossession, and disillusionment. They led to the development of democratic reforms and nationalist movements, left-wing critique and right-wing opposition, peace, prosperity, and violent wars. Special attention will be paid to the causes and conditions of the current war in Ukraine, the brutal invasion, the rise of a new authoritarianism in Russia and responses of the Russian and Ukrainian societies to the war, the new Putinist discourse of “new civilizationism” that has emerged since the invasion and that is also becoming dominant in some other parts of the world. The course will draw on material from anthropology, history, political philosophy, literature, media, and art. The course will include videos and documentaries.

title: Undergraduate Seminar
special: Anthropological Explorations of Reading, Knowing, and Resistance
course-description: Seminar for the advanced study of the subject matter of a previously given upper division course, emphasizing reading and discussion.
class-description: This is a course on reading and knowing in the broadest sense. It investigates the relationship between reading, knowing, and liberation. Reading may seem a simple act, one most of us do unthinkingly in the course of our day. However the expansion of mass literacy, and a personal and public culture of reading, is an epochal transition in the history of humanity.

title: Special Topics in Social/Cultural Anthropology
special: Collecting, Collaborating, and Coming Home: Museum Anthropology and Indigenous Museums
course-description: Various topics covering current research theory, method; issues of social and cultural concern; culture change, conflict, and adaptation. May combine more than one subdiscipline of Anthropology.
class-description: Indigenous museums worldwide empower communities to represent their own cultures and participate directly in the creation and dissemination of knowledge on their own terms. This raises critical questions: How can museums exhibit objects responsibly, address their colonial histories, invite meaningful community participation, and collaborate with Tribes, Nations, and communities whose cultural belongings they hold?

title: South Asia
course-description: Cultural traditions, social organization, and social change, with an emphasis on India and Pakistan.
class-description: The countries of the region called South-Asia (India, Pakistan, Nepal, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Afghanistan, Burma, Bhutan) collectively comprise almost 2 billion people, making it the most densely populated region of the world. It is home to hundreds of languages, all the world’s major religions, and encompasses enormous cultural, social, and ecological diversity. This course will introduce students to the study of South Asia, with a focus on what anthropologists term ‘life cycle’ events. Life cycle events are major moments that mark the stages and phases of the life of people and societies. Life cycle events——birth, puberty, youth, marriage, childbirth, old age, death—these are moments of heightened social significance where personal experience intersects with broader social and political processes, norms, and structures. We learn a great deal about what a society is, what it values, how it is changing, sites of conflict and transformation by attending to such moments.

title: Japan
course-description: This course offers an introductory survey of Japan from a four-field anthropological perspective.  It is open without prerequisite to anyone with a curiosity about what is arguably the most important non-Western society of the last 100 years, and to anyone concerned about the diverse conditions of modern life.  We will range over many aspects of contemporary Japan, and draw on scholarship in history, literature, religion, and the various social sciences.

title: China
course-description: Chinese culture and society with an emphasis on the village level.
class-description: This class takes up "China" as an object of knowledge and focuses on its Cultural aspect of a long historical duration. Today's world is different from what it used to be, witnessed by ChatGPT and other digital technologies, and yet China has remained an Other for us in terms of its cultural logic and logographic language—two essential features of a fundamental Difference. This class aims at an anthropological understanding of the Chinese world as an essential part of a Self-understanding for ourselves, and as an anthropology class we will focus on the Chinese way of thinking and being, i.e. rather than on China's geopolitical significance or its fast material growth, in order for us to understand today's world in a more intelligent manner.

title: Research Theory and Methods in Socio-Cultural Anthropology
course-description: Introduction to research problems and research design techniques. Will involve local field research on the collection, analysis, and presentation of data. This course requires 15 hours of work per week including class time, outside work and preparation. One section meeting per week will be required.
class-description: This course will introduce students to a range of methodologies, theories, practical strategies, and ethical considerations for conducting ethnographic research today.  Through a combination of in-class activities, readings, lectures, and practical assignments, you will learn how to design, conduct, and present/write up ethnographic research. This course includes two lectures and one section meeting per week. If you intend to write a senior thesis, this will be a good opportunity to start designing your research plan.

title: Topical Areas in Archaeology: Archaeology of Hunter-Gatherers
course-description: Course will provide an overview of hunter-gatherer archaeology, focusing on the history of hunter-gatherer archaeology in North America and Britian; long-term changes in hunter-gatherer subsistence, settlement, mortuary/ceremonial practices and crafts/trade; social archaeology of hunter-gatherers including studies of gender, cognition, and cultural landscapes; and discussions of the relevance of hunter-gatherer studies in the context of world archaeology.
class-description: Modern Humans evolved over three hundred thousand years ago, and during the vast majority of those intervening years we have lived by hunting, gathering, and fishing.  For that reason alone, it is worthwhile and important to study the archaeology of hunter-gatherer societies.  But in addition to that, both the analyses and the assumptions underlying hunter-gatherer archaeology have played an outsized (and not always positive) role in the assessment of human history and the understanding of human nature more broadly.  In this course we will examine hunter-gatherer archaeology in the context of both its unique and fascinating history and the development of the science of archaeology more generally.  We will consider various approaches taken to understand hunting, gathering, and fishing peoples throughout prehistory and modern times, and we will critique those approaches in light of current archaeological thinking and perspectives, including indigenous perspectives and the perspective of gender.  We will link those discussions to issues of today, such as the origins of social inequality and climate change.  At all times we will seek to bear in mind issues of epistemology, how we as archaeologists come to understand the past, the knowledge that archaeology alone can offer, and the limits to that knowledge.  The geographic scope of the course will be worldwide, including studies from Asia, Africa, and the Americas.

title: Fundamentals of Anthropological Theory
course-description: Anthropological theory and practice--following the rest of the world--have been undergoing important restructuring in the past decade. The course is organized to reflect this fact. We will begin by looking at recent debates about the nature and purpose of anthropology. This will provide a starting point for reading a series of classic ethnographies in new ways as well as examining some dimensions of the current research agenda in cultural anthropology.

title: Advanced Arabic
course-description: Intensive reading and analysis of texts of different genres. Guest lectures, films, documentaries, oral presentations, research papers. Formal and informal styles of writing and correspondence. Extensive vocabulary building.

title: Intermediate Arabic
course-description:
This course is the second semester of the intermediate level of Modern Standard Arabic. The course
further teaches skills in speaking, reading, listening and writing in Arabic and builds vocabulary,
expressions and grammar that allow students to discuss topics in detail and develop and support
opinions. Using task-based and proficiency-oriented approaches to foreign language instruction, the
course includes regular discussion in Arabic and prepares students to communicate in a variety of
contexts and for various purposes. The course engages students with authentic materials and features
of Arab cultures and deepens students’ knowledge of Arabic syntax and its rich morphological system.

title: Elementary Arabic
course-description: This course is the second semester of elementary Modern Standard Arabic. It focuses on developing skills in speaking, reading, listening, and writing, while expanding vocabulary, idiomatic expressions, and grammar. Students will learn to communicate effectively on topics such as self, family, surroundings, daily routines, past events, and future plans. The course uses task-based and proficiency-oriented methods to enhance language learning and incorporates an exploration of Arabic cultures. Additionally, it covers basic syntax and introduces the fundamentals of the Arabic morphological system.

title: Architectural Design IV
course-description: Students work on individual and/or group design projects that build on topics from previous studios with additional integration of conditions pertinent to architectural production that may include architectural precedents, context, landscape and urban issues, envelope, structure, and tectonics in the design of buildings. It may also include relevent and pertinent social, cultural, and technological issues facing architecture and design.

title: Fundamentals of Architectural Design
course-description: Introductory courses in the design of buildings. Problems emphasize conceptual strategies of form and space, site relationships and social, technological and environmental determinants.   100B stresses tectonics, materials, and energy considerations. Studio work is supplemented by lectures, discussions, readings and field trips.

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

title: Sophomore Seminar
instructor: Renee Y Chow, Thomas R Chastain
course-description: Sophomore seminars are small interactive courses offered by faculty members in departments all across the campus. Sophomore seminars offer opportunity for close, regular intellectual contact between faculty members and students in the crucial second year. The topics vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to 15 sophomores.
class-description: Home building is city building. The design of housing is inextricably linked to urban form - to patterns of settlement. Housing is both individual and collective, which highlights the challenges in housing design to balance the varied ways people have of dwelling and the current means of housing production organized around repetitive units. In this, design competence includes an understanding of use, dimensions, the capacity of forms, and their relationship to a multiplicity of systems that make and support it. Dwelling is about being at home in the world, in a room, in the shared space between things, in a town, and in the landscape. We have lost our way with the practice to the detriment of both housing and cities. So, what to do? Where do we begin?

title: Introduction to Design
course-description: Introduction to design concepts and conventions of graphic representation and model building as related to the study of architecture, landscape architecture, urban design, and city planning. Students draw in plan, section, elevation, axonometric, and perspective and are introduced to digital media. Design projects address concepts of order, site analysis, scale, structure, rhythm, detail, culture, and landscape.

title: Arabic Historical and Geographical Texts
course-description: Readings from the classical historians and geographers and from contemporary scholarship. Development of historiography.

title: Elementary Arabic
course-description: This course is the second semester of elementary Modern Standard Arabic. It focuses on developing skills in speaking, reading, listening, and writing, while expanding vocabulary, idiomatic expressions, and grammar. Students will learn to communicate effectively on topics such as self, family, surroundings, daily routines, past events, and future plans. The course uses task-based and proficiency-oriented methods to enhance language learning and incorporates an exploration of Arabic cultures. Additionally, it covers basic syntax and introduces the fundamentals of the Arabic morphological system.

title: Elementary Arabic
course-description: Elementary Arabic introduces students to Modern Standard Arabic and is designed for those with little to no prior knowledge of the language, including its alphabet and sounds. The course is suitable for individuals familiar with Arabic colloquial speech but without formal training in Modern Standard Arabic. The course develops foundational skills in speaking, reading, listening, and writing while building vocabulary, idiomatic expressions, and grammar. Students will learn to communicate and engage in discussions on topics such as self, family, and surroundings. The course uses task-based and proficiency-oriented methods to enhance language learning and incorporates an exploration of Arabic cultures.

title: Professional Development in Anthropological Archaeology
course-description: Required each term of all registered graduate students in Anthropology specializing in archaeology prior to their advancement to Ph.D. candidacy.

title: Survey of Anthropological Research
course-description: Required each term of all registered graduate students prior to their advancement to Ph.D. candidacy.

title: Seminars in Linguistic Anthropology: Fundamentals of Language in Context
course-description: Intensive introduction to the study of language as a cultural system and speech as socially embedded communicative practice. This is the core course for students wishing to take further coursework in linguistic anthropology.

title: Theories of Traditionality and Modernity
course-description: This seminar explores the emergence of notions of tradition and modernity and their reproduction in Eurocentric epistemologies and political formations. It uses work by such authors as Anderson, Butler, Chakrabarty, Clifford, Derrida, Foucault, Latour, Mignolo, Pateman, and Poovey to critically reread foundational works published between the 17th century and the present--along with philosophical texts with which they are in dialogue--in terms of how they are imbricated within and help produce traditionalities and modernities.

title: Seminars in Social and Cultural Anthropology: Special Topics
special: Afterlives of Communism: War and Peace
class-description: This seminar will analyze the period of “post-communism” (aka “post-socialism”) and will focus on Eastern Europe, the former Soviet Union, and Central Asia. We will investigate the ongoing social, cultural, political, economic, moral, and personal transformation that has taken place in the former communist world since its “collapse” in the late 1980s and 1990s. These processes have been optimistic and liberating and, at the same time, traumatic and brutal. They created new freedoms and forms of cultural effervescence but also new unfreedoms, dispossession, and disillusionment. They led to the development of democratic reforms and nationalist movements, left-wing critique and right-wing opposition, peace, prosperity, and violent wars. We revisit the “really existing socialism” of the past and will consider the intense nostalgias and “memory wars” that the end of socialism engendered. We will also analyze some roots and ideologies of the current political turn to the right in many former socialist places and of Putin’s imperialist war in Ukraine. The course will draw on readings from anthropology, history, political philosophy, literature, media, and art. It will include a few videos and documentaries.

title: Seminars in Social and Cultural Anthropology: Special Topics
class-description: This course explores what it means to conduct field research on politics and to write an ethnographic account of it.  This exploration entails developing an understanding both of ethnography and of politics as entangled subjects of inquiry.  Some anthropologists identify a subfield, political anthropology, as the domain of this inquiry.  But many anthropologists throughout the discipline claim to “work on politics.”  Do they?  In what sense?  By what means of form?  We will begin with a classic in “political anthropology” from the era of tribal studies that has been re-evaluated and reconfigured in contemporary terms.  Then we will move to current works, some of which address classic concerns and some of which attempt to establish new ethnographic terrains of the political.  We will focus on analyzing how each reading constructs its ethnography as a narrative form, its politics as a subject form, and its anthropology as a disciplinary form.

title: Special Topics in Architectural Design
course-description: Selected topics in the theories and concepts of architectural design. For current offerings, see department website.
class-description: Replicas, copies, editions, duplicates, and substitutes abound in architectural work(s). Historically, reconstruction has been reserved for pre-modern buildings — acts of preservation that aspire to fix form and meaning in time. However, through contemporary art practices such as Thomas Demand’s photo–model–photo process, the logic of replication acknowledges how images circulate, how absence and mediation construct history, and how making itself becomes a mode of inquiry. This seminar examines the replica not as a fixed 1:1 copy but as an instrument that moves between model, drawing, photograph, and text, by approaching the CED archive as a staging site—a place where architectural and institutional knowledge is produced through acts of replication, reconstruction, and re-presentation. Between the archive and its supporting structures is a field of architectural work(s): logistics of display, material thresholds, labor, specifications, and systems of notation. By engaging archival models through drawings, notes, and specifications, students will reinterpret, restage, and reconstruct them not as faithful replicas but as critical re-presentations.

title: California Architecture
course-description:
Many California architects came from other places: Maybeck from New York via the
Ecole des Beaux Arts; Schindler and Neutra from Vienna; Frank Gehry from Chicago.
But, once they arrived, their encounters with the Golden State produced new and original
forms of architecture. This seminar will examine the qualities of the state’s environment,
culture, economy, and population that have produced unique buildings and landscapes
during the 20th century. It will look at both Northern and Southern California architecture,
starting with canonical designers then moving beyond them to consider lesser-known
regional architects whose work embodies local characteristics.
class-description: This course looks at a broad range of buildings and landscapes that self-consciously reflect their California locations. From Maybeck to Frank Gehry, from Schindler to Google, we will examine buildings as a reflection of different facets of California culture. Multiple field trips allow students to directly experience as many of these buildings as possible.

title: Studio One, Spring
course-description: This course is the second semester of a one-year, post-professional studio intended for those students who have a professional architecture degree and wish to explore current design issues in a stimulating, rigorous, and highly experimental studio setting.

title: Thesis Studio
course-description: Focused design research as the capstone project for graduate students.

title: Graduate Option Studio
course-description: Focused design and research for graduate students.

title: Introduction to Architecture Studio 2
course-description: Introductory course in architectural design and theories for graduate students. Problems emphasize the major format, spatial, material, tectonic, social, technological, and environmental determinants of building form. Studio work is supplemented by lectures, discussions, readings, and field trips.

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

title: Special Topics in the History of Architecture
special: Design Radicals: Spaces of Bay Area Counterculture
course-description: Special topics in Architectural History. For current section offerings, see departmental announcement.
class-description: During the "long-'60s," a collection of intersectional countercultures emerged in the Bay Area. Parallel ventures in the collective remaking of society brought together projects of cultural transformation advanced by ecofreaks, cyberfreaks, and ‘outlaw builders’; Black, Chicano, and Native American activists; feminists, lesbians, and gay men; disabled people and their advocates; children and ‘free school’ educators. Our seminar relies primarily upon readings from Design Radicals: Spaces of Bay Area Counterculture (Univ. of Minnesota Press, forthcoming) to evaluate a moment in local history devoted to the creation of "liberated territories" and to consider their contemporary potential as a "usable past."

title: An Historical Survey of Architecture and Urbanism
course-description: The first part of this sequence studies the ancient and medieval periods; the second part studies the period since 1400; the aim is to look at architecture and urbanism in their social and historical context.

title: Special Topics in Construction Materials
special: Earthen Material Practices in Contemporary Art and Architecture
course-description: For current offerings, see department website.

title: Special Topics in Construction Materials
course-description: For current offerings, see department website.
class-description: This seminar format course focuses on the generation and development of creative design processes through exploratory drawing, modelmaking and prototyping. This semester we will continue to explore timber construction methods as an issue for design exploration at multiple scales from framing layouts to connection details. Our medium for design exploration shall be in physical making in materials and in drawing processes with timber construction as our primary subject area. Students will develop individual or small group drawing and fabrication studies as creative works in themselves and as vehicles for expanding and exploring knowledge and practice skills in design of timber architecture.

title: Special Topics in Construction Materials
course-description: For current offerings, see department website.
class-description: Contemporary buildings are inherently heterogeneous; more often than not, they are assemblages of different materials, programs, and subjects. Although homogenous finish layers may construct an image of purity, anyone that has looked closely at a contemporary wall section can attest to its many parallel technical layers. The twin tendencies within contemporary architecture towards both functional and aesthetic purism subvert the potency of difference as the basis of architectural production. While elaborations of both formal and programmatic heterogeneity are now well established, material heterogeneity is less theorized. Building codes, specification systems, the division of labor, materials science, and structural theories and pedagogies, are bodies of knowledge that privilege and reinforce the classification of material systems into discrete categories. While there are advantages to understanding each material system in isolation, there is an alternative methodology that considers materials in strategic combination.

title: Special Topics in Construction Materials
special: (Im)material Matters: Matters, Environments and their Techniques
course-description: For current offerings, see department website.
class-description: While the term ‘immaterial ’is defined as ‘not consisting of matter’ its recalibration as ‘(im)material’ emphasizes the inseparability between material and seemingly immaterial ‘matters of concern’ such as processes, energies, and invisible materialities. Closely examining the technical processes of making and operating buildings beyond the episteme of sustainability, students are expected to challenge architecture's role in shaping future relationships between people, construction, and climate within our urban and natural worlds. The seminar will engage discursive, textual, representational and material exercises. Students will be expected to develop research projects that foreground the invisible, energetic, and process-based materialities involved in the production of architecture.

title: Introduction to Construction
course-description: This introduction to the materials and processes of construction takes architecture from design to realization. The course will cover four material groups commonly used in two areas of the building assembly (structure and envelope): wood, concrete, steel, and glass. You will understand choices available and how materials are conventionally used. By observing construction, you'll see how our decisions affect the size of materials, connections, and where they are assembled. Architects must understand not only conventions, but also the potential in materials, so we will also study unusual and new developments.

title: Special Topics in Building Structures
course-description: Special topics such as experimental structures and architural preservation. For current offerings, see department website.
class-description: This research seminar examines the material and structural systems that make up residential buildings in the US from a carbon perspective. We investigate the environmental impact and embodied carbon of different materials and how they are used in construction. We compare different structural systems, facades, and foundations, with case studies from on-site framing to robotically prefabricated modular construction. Through computational and architectural analysis of structural elements we will create new visions for scalable low-carbon housing construction.

title: Special Topics in Energy and Environment
special: Artificial Intelligence and Generative Design Methods for Sustainable Buildings
course-description: Special topics include climatic design, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning systems, lighting, and acoustics. For current offerings, see department website.
class-description: The class introduces students to technical tools and background that is needed to apply artificial intelligence (AI) and generative design in a building context. We will investigate how we can use tools from computer science and data visualization in a design context. We will combine generative geometric methods with building performance simulations (energy, daylight, carbon) to explore how AI can be used to create more sustainable buildings.

title: Energy and Environment
course-description: This course provides undergraduates and graduates with an introduction to issues of physical building performance including building thermodynamics, daylighting, and solar control. The course presents the fundamentals of building science while recongnizing the evolving nature of building technologies, energy efficiency, ecology, and responsible design. The course begins with a detailed explication of the thermal properties of materials, heat transfer through building assemblies, balance point temperature, solar geometry, and shading analysis. Students apply these principles later in the course to a design project. The latter part of the course also provides a survey of broader building science topics including mechanical system design, microclimate, and current developments in energy-efficient design.

title: Special Topics in the Social and Cultural Basis of Design
course-description: Selected topics in the social and cultural basis of design. For current offerings, see departmental website.
class-description: Housing was a focus of architectural innovation and creativity during the early and mid-20th century. However, after the perceived failures of the Modern Movement, it took a back seat in the architectural profession and was mostly limited to infill proposals. As a result, housing programs in architecture schools became rare. Towards the end of the last century, they weren't considered suitable for the digital formal explorations that dominated studio production until about two decades ago.

special: Design Radicals: Spaces of Bay Area Counterculture
course-description: Selected topics in the history of architecture. For current offerings, see department website.

title: Robotic Fabrication and Construction
course-description: The emergence of robotics in creative sectors such as architecture and design has sparked an entirely new movement of collective making that is inextricably open and future-oriented. Challenged by increasingly complex technological and environmental problems, architects, designers, and engineers are seeking novel practices of collaboration that go far beyond traditional disciplinary boundaries.

title: Introduction to Structures
course-description:
This class focuses on the fundamental principles that affect the structural behavior of buildings. Through digital and hands-on exercises, students will learn analytical techniques for measuring and evaluating the flow of forces through structural systems. Students will also learn to consider the structural behavior of buildings as a fundamental factor in the design of architectural proposals. The goal of the class is to gain a fundamental understanding of the forces, moments, and stresses in typical building elements such as columns, beams,
frames and walls and to make better informed decisions when designing resource- and environmentally-friendly buildings with lightweight and material-efficient structural systems.

title: Special Topics in the Physical Environment in Buildings
special: User-Centric Design and Virtual Presence in Immersive Environments
class-description: The course addresses theoretical approaches as well as technical implementations and human subject experiments related to Human-Centric Design and Virtual Presence in Immersive Environments. Based on ongoing or recent research topics developed at the XR Lab, the class will discuss the potential of immersive technologies such as Virtual, Augmented and Mixed Reality to improved accessibility and equity across different constituents and population groups. Topics addressed may include:

title: Special Topics in the Physical Environment in Buildings
special: Artificial Intelligence and Generative Design Methods for Sustainable Buildings
class-description: The class introduces students to technical tools and background that is needed to apply artificial intelligence (AI) and generative design in a building context. We will investigate how we can use tools from computer science and data visualization in a design context. We will combine generative geometric methods with building performance simulations (energy, daylight, carbon) to explore how AI can be used to create more sustainable buildings.

title: Advanced Study of Energy and Environment
course-description: Minimizing energy use is a cornerstone of designing and operating sustainable buildings, and attention to energy issues can often lead to greatly improved indoor environmental quality. For designers, using computer-based energy analysis tools are important not only to qualify for sustainability ratings and meet energy codes, but also to develop intuition about what makes buildings perform well. This course will present quantitative and qualitative methods for assessing energy performance during design of both residential and commercial buildings. Students will get hands-on experience with state-of-the-art software -- ranging from simple to complex -- to assess the performance of building components and whole-building designs.

title: Advanced Architectural Design Theory and Criticism
course-description: Seminar in the analysis and discussion of contemporary and historical issues in architectural design theory and criticism.

title: Technologies of Representation 4: Computation & Generative Design
course-description: As a part of this larger sequence on the technologies of architectural representation, this course examines computational methods for architectural design, including parametric modeling and generative design techniques. Students develop an understanding of rule-based strategies that enable responsive and data-informed design solutions. Through structured explorations, the course provides a foundation in scripting and visual programming, allowing students to engage with emergent design methodologies that extend beyond conventional modeling approaches.

title: Technologies of Representation 3: Documentation & Coordination
course-description: As a part of this larger sequence on the technologies of architectural representation, this course introduces students to the structuring, coordination, and documentation of architectural projects through information modeling. Emphasizing the integration of design data with technical documentation, students learn to organize spatial, material, and performance-related information within models that support iterative design processes. Through hands-on projects, students gain insight into workflows that enhance collaboration, efficiency, and accuracy in design communication and project delivery.

title: Special Topics in the Social and Cultural Basis of Design
course-description: Topics include the sociology of taste, personal and societal values in design, participatory design, semantic ethnography, environments for special popultions such as the elderly, and building types such as housing, hospitals, schools, offices, and urban parks. For current offerings, see departmental website.
