class-description: In memoir, a writer shares a meaningful and “true” narrative about their life.  This entails, or can entail: making sense of what happened; selecting and shaping facts and memories; sharing a vision or furthering a cause; promoting values (or sometimes promoting yourself); building community; building bridges; providing a historical perspective, and more. In any case, the “truth” of the story is arrived at and constructed, versus simply transcribed. In this class, we’ll stand on this premise to analyze memoir from various critical perspectives. Over the course of the semester, you’ll further your analytical reading skills and undertake the hard and stimulating work of close reading, brainstorming, note-taking, critiquing, discussing, and revising (there will be a lot of revising), to produce writing you can be proud of. In and through this work you will also develop a critical awareness about writing for different audiences and in different genres.

class-description: This course investigates bold visions of community in our modern era. We’ll look at solidarity in crisis, ecological kinship, speculative futures, and collective actions that challenge power. We’ll ask how writers imagine the way that collaboration emerges amid digital overload, climate breakdown, and social fracture. class-description: From self-driving cars, to automated facial recognition software, to chatbots that have literally been trained to mimic us, technological change is reshaping our lives more than ever, raising urgent questions about what it means to be human in an age defined by our connection to machines. In this course, we will examine our evolving and increasingly fraught relationship with technology, artificial intelligence, and the digital lives we live through science fiction and speculative literature, nonfiction, and visual media. Students will develop critical thinking, reading, and writing skills around topics such as automation and surveillance, cybernetic assimilation and transhumanism, and the ethical dilemmas posed by unchecked technological advancement. Through close readings, classroom discussions, and writing essays, we will explore how stories of imagined futures can help us understand–and respond to–the concerns of the present.

class-description: What does it mean to belong somewhere — to a society or culture, a community or subculture, or to be a member of a small classroom community like this one? R1A: Belonging & Uprooting is meant to be an engaging exploration of different possible answers to these questions, both personal and theoretical. We'll use cultural theory, nonfiction essays, a novel (or two?) and poetry to examine how a sense of belonging is shaped, looking at its intersections with individual and communal identity, geography, and ancestry; how it's constructed through abstract "imagined communities" (in the words of Benedict Anderson, writing about the emergence of the modern nation-state); or the ways it reinvents itself out of the ashes of its own absence in diaspora cultures. We’ll also explore those absences, reading arguments against assimilation and in praise of outsidership and working-class, first-gen identities via the feminist theorist bell hooks (who uses her own experience as a working-class Black woman in academia as a lens to discuss & refute assimilation), personal essay by the novelist Daniel Peña (writing on social strata through the story of a formerly undocumented metalhead friend now returned to Mexico City), the short film Hey Man (which follows an early-transition rideshare driver as they navigate the public/private presentations of self) and several other texts. Via these as well as the the love story / refugee novel Exit West by Mohsin Hamid and the Pulitzer-winning poetry collection by Brandon Som, Tripas, about Chinese-Chicano belonging, we'll learn new strategies for close reading and analysis of literary texts.

class-description: This course theme invites students to examine the beliefs and attitudes we hold about our own and others’ language use and their relationship to systems of power. Through scholarly, journalistic, and literary texts, we will explore such questions such as: What is “standard” English? Who decides what counts as “correct”or “appropriate” usage? Is language regulation necessary to protect communities? When can it become a form of censorship that overly restricts free expression? What is linguistic prejudice and how does it contribute to social inequality? Students will reflect on the intersection of language and power in their own experiences, in educational settings, and in broader society. To enrich our exploration, we will also engage with film and other forms of media. Students will read and write in a variety of genres that facilitate reflection on their own experiences and put readings in conversation with one another.

class-description: A hallmark of humanity is our extraordinary creativity, born and nurtured within the natural world. Yet human industry and development have caused the alarming loss of nature and climate change. What obligations do we have to other species, ecosystems, each other, and coming generations? How can wild nature be conserved and restored? What can we learn from cultures, past and present, whose vision and values have embraced earth’s wonders? These are some of the questions we will pursue through reading a variety of writers—scientists, activists, journalists, poets, and others—and through films and art. During the term, you will have the opportunity to develop your perspectives in writing and lively discussion. This section is reserved for multilingual speakers.

class-description: Death is universal. For as long as human beings have been self-aware, we have faced the challenge of living with the knowledge that we will one day die. The subject of death can be heavy, but this class posits that reflecting on our shared mortality can be empowering, uplifting, and generative. We will analyze a number of works—fiction, drama, poetry, nonfiction, and film—that grapple with the relationship between death and living a meaningful life. We will examine attitudes toward death across cultures, the psychology behind how death has been personified in film and media, critiques of the American funeral industry, and speculations about whether new technologies can extend life or even abolish death altogether. In the process, we will learn to craft essays that analyze, inform, and persuade, with an emphasis on creativity, clarity, rigor, and organization.

title: Reading, Composition, and Research
special: Communicating with Expertise in Any Field
course-description: A lecture/seminar satisfying the second half of the Reading & Composition requirement, R4B offers structured and sustained practice in the processes used in reading, critical analysis, and writing. Students engage with thematically-related materials from a range of genres and media. In response, they craft short pieces leading to longer expository and/or argumentative essays. Students develop a research question, draft a research essay, gather, evaluate, and synthesize information from various sources. Elements of the research process--a proposal, an annotated bibliography, an abstract, a works cited list, etc.--are submitted with the final report in a research portfolio. Students write a minimum of 32 pages of prose.
class-description: Success in any profession—especially STEM-related fields—depends on the ability to read critically, analyze information accurately, and communicate ideas in ways that are valued by the target audience. This course helps students develop these skills by exploring how experts research, write, and share knowledge in different academic and professional settings. Students will work with real-world materials, practice strategies for understanding and producing complex texts, and complete a research-based project connected to their professional interests and goals. By strengthening their ability to read, write, and think critically, students will be better prepared for their upper-division coursework, internships, and careers.

class-description: Differences, disagreements, and conflict are inevitable in daily life. Though often stressful, these disagreements can also provide opportunity for reflection and growth, especially when they are relatively minor.  But, what happens when our differences get politicized, and we no longer see the humanity in our fellow citizens? class-description: Monsters used to represent fear of the unknown: unmapped regions in the medieval period were marked by dragons; imperialists in the 19th century bringing the "light" of civilization into the dark continent of Africa feared cannibals. Given the scientific basis of the modern period, would it not be accurate to say that we no longer believe in monsters, that they survive in the modern period if only so that they can serve as the very sign of an unenlightened, and superstitious past? No. Monsters have not been banished to the regions of superstition; they have not been relegated entirely to the past. Once we get over the fear that they might pop out from under our beds, we run to the cinema to delight in observing their contemporary manifestations: as mad scientists, bestial men and women, re-animated corpses, and cyborgs. In the modern period, monsters remain as figures not simply of fear and fascination but of real use. Monsters persist as an emblem of anxiety about a past that is too rapidly disintegrating so as to compromise the very structures of society; or alternatively as a mode of protest against the modernity of the modern period with its new forms of regulation and social control; or then again as the sign of a compromised future wherein the representation of the monster serves to question the "progress of progress," and direct suspicion onto the modern projects of science, industry, and technology. Two analytical papers; one research paper. Literature and film focus.

Students engage with thematically-related materials from a range of genres and media. In response, they craft short pieces leading to longer expository and/or argumentative essays. class-description: So often knowledge and learning are presented as something to be tested on, something to be “acquired,” or something others know that you don’t yet. Such learning is usually the basis of a lot of classes, both K-12 and in college. Of course, this knowledge is vitally important to having a strong foundation in any field, and there’s a comfort in being able to get the answers “right.” However, the most inventive research happens when we wander into the unknown, when we are inspired by wonder and awe. Getting into that “unknown,” though, is tricky. It’s often uncomfortable because we’ve been taught to memorize and only show what we know. But many of our most famous thinkers are not only comfortable with the “unknown,” they thrive on it. For example, physicist Richard Feynman kept notebooks called “Things I Don’t Know.” It’s in the unknown that we can find mystery and wonder. For this class, we’ll focus on how to get more comfortable with exploring the unknown, sometimes even “unlearning” what things we think we do know, and exploring the things we find awesome, in the real sense of that word. While we’ll approach the unknown in many fields, this class is particularly well suited for those in the sciences. We’ll start with common readings and then you’ll develop your own research projects, ideally projects that both add to established knowledge and point in directions for more research into what we don’t know, at least not yet.

class-description: From the first days when workers chanted and sang to today’s genre-spanning variety of protest songs, music has long been used as a soundtrack to social movements. From Civil Rights to the labor movement, from the fight for LGBTQ equality to feminism, every social movement, including global ones, has been accompanied by songs.  This makes music and social movements a natural topic for writing arguments and research. In this section of CWR4B, we will learn the nuts and bolts of writing persuasive and research essays,  as well as learning our way around  the UC Berkeley libraries and databases, building a research portfolio, presenting your research to a live audience and more.  There will be two short essays leading up to a capstone research essay at the end of the semester. Expect a lot of collaborative peer work, as well as daily presentations, workshops and discussions to help build your toolkit of writing and research skills to prepare you for writing across the disciples and beyond Berkeley.

title: Reading in and about U.S. Education Institutions
course-description: In this course, we will read, discuss, and write about the expectations of the American educational system, especially within a multicultural context. The goal is to deepen the understanding of the history and diversity of American educational institutions, while strengthening reading and seminar participation skills through critique and analysis of communication patterns. This course is intended for international students.
class-description: In this seminar, we will read, discuss, and write about the American educational system, especially within a multicultural context. The goal is to deepen the understanding of the history, diversity, and values of American educational institutions, while strengthening reading and seminar participation skills through synthesis, critique and analysis. All course texts will be available via bCourses or the UC Berkeley Library. This course is partially intended to introduce international students to U.S. educational policy, debates, and history, but all students are welcome. The best class is one that allows for dialogue between internationally- and U.S.-educated students from diverse backgrounds.

title: Berkeley Changemaker: Public Speaking
course-description: Emphasizing the Berkeley Changemaker pillars of critical thinking and communication, this variable unit (1 or 2) practicum is designed to help students refine their academic speaking skills. Students will learn the techniques of effective public speaking, practice their skills, and develop confidence in oral communication. Online, asynchronous class sessions will be complemented by “live” opportunities that enable students to practice course content in front of an instructor and audience and receive feedback.

title: Advanced Public Speaking
course-description: This is an advanced course that presumes introductory training in public speaking. Emphasis will be on real-world speaking situations. The course combines both theory and practice: it incorporates extensive speaking performance and individualized critiques from instructor and students, as well as analysis of advanced speaking models, and it explores theories, speech genres, and rhetorical processes beyond those in the introductory course. The intent of the course is to advance students' ability to deliver polished and informed public speeches adapted to a wide range of audiences and speaking situations.

title: Introduction to Public Speaking
course-description: This is a strictly introductory course. It presumes no formal training of any kind on the part of the students. Emphasis will be on organization and delivery with goals of improving control over speaking habits and enunciation. Part of the intent of the course is to introduce students to the rudiments of the rhetorical theory which lies behind the practice of public speaking.
class-description: This introductory course is designed to help you become a more confident, effective public speaker in a variety of real-world settings. Through a supportive and engaging classroom environment, students will learn the fundamentals of oral communication—including both speaking and listening—while gaining experience delivering speeches tailored to different audiences and occasions.

Students engage with thematically-related materials from a range of genres and media. In response, they craft short pieces leading to longer expository and/or argumentative essays. special: The Meme & the Human (& AI): Digital Literacies

Students engage with thematically-related materials from a range of genres and media. In response, they craft short pieces leading to longer expository and/or argumentative essays. class-description: Together we reflect on, read about, and discuss technological change, including AI. We also consider the existential devastation of our sacred earth, and other worldwide crises. With all of these paradigm shifts in mind, we ask, What does it mean to be human? We also analyze motivations for communicating in memes, their links to human identity, and their polysemous nature inviting diverse audiences to interpret them differently. Becoming more savvy digital citizens, we look at memes’ techno-social features, genres, (unwritten) rules of meme-related conduct, and whether the connections memes create are more important than their content. We explore best research practices and the myriad ways that Berkeley’s libraries and librarians empower these. You focus on a key issue, topic, or question of your choice and engage in process-based research to build an articulate, sound digital portfolio of inquiry that includes a proposal, abstract, research essay, works cited, annotated bibliography, and research presentation with slide deck, plus other assignments.

class-description: This course focuses on the burgeoning field of evolutionary psychology, which argues that humans vary little across time and space, and that our behavior is rooted in the choices of our ancestors. These arguments are compelling but also ripe with controversy. We will analyze these arguments from various perspectives – sociology, economics, politics, computer science, and more – and hopefully become better readers, writers, and researchers as we do. Here are some questions you will explore in this class: Is beauty truly in the eye of the beholder? Why are we drawn to certain types of food, people, landscapes, and art? Are people really that different from one culture or era to the next? How much free will do we really have? How are recent technological and economic developments impacting impulses that developed over millions of years? Is society to blame for gender differences, or are these differences a natural part of life?

title: Episodes in Literary Cultures: Literature and Philosophy
special: Catastrophe Now: The Jewish Tragic Mode, from Antiquity to Contemporary Culture
course-description: An introductory level exploration of a specific author, work, theme or literary movement in an international context. Emphasis on the ways in which literature has played (and continues to play) a crucial role in the relationship between different cultures, traditions, and languages. Readings and topics to vary from semester to semester.
class-description: We live in times of extreme uncertainty, but one thing is undeniable: we are living through catastrophe. From the ongoing wars in Gaza and Ukraine to environmental collapse, global pandemic, political upheaval, and the rise of authoritarian regimes, rupture has become a defining feature of our moment. What can Jewish history teach us about the emergence, experience, and consequences of catastrophe? And what is catastrophe to begin with?

title: English Composition in Connection with the Reading of World Literature
special: (Un)relatable Characters: Examples and Identity in Literature and Film
course-description: Expository writing based on analysis of selected masterpieces of ancient and modern literature. R1A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R1B satisfies the second half.
class-description: “Relatability” is a controversial metric of literary value. Some readers desire to relate to characters or plots, basing their interest in a fictional work on their ability to see themselves in it. Literary critics, in contrast, have sometimes pointed to the relatability of certain popular works as a sign of their low quality, or as the symptom of a self-obsessed culture at large. When do we read stories about other people for what they can show us about ourselves? And when do we read about people different from us because they’re different from us? Can we do both at the same time?
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: English Composition in Connection with the Reading of World Literature
course-description: Expository writing based on analysis of selected masterpieces of ancient and modern literature. R1A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R1B satisfies the second half.
class-description: Literature, and art in general, is often said to be “useless”. Sometimes this is meant as a badge of aesthetic autonomy; perhaps more often, it is a criticism from a scientific or simply more practical point of view. Yet, for most of the history of literature, fiction was supposed to “teach and delight”, that is, to be “useful” or “profitable” as well as entertaining or pleasurable. And this “utility” was primarily moral, or ethical: literature was supposed to help people become better and their lives happier. In this course, we will investigate how morals and happiness were conceived in different periods and places of western literary history and how literary authors sought to shape their readers’ behavior and/or improve their lives. In other words, we will consider our works as making ethical arguments, and students will make their own ethical arguments about them in their own close readings of these texts. Texts will range from ancient to modern, but there will be a formal focus on narrative fiction and a geographic focus on England and France.

title: English Composition in Connection with the Reading of World Literature
course-description: Expository writing based on analysis of selected masterpieces of ancient and modern literature. R1A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R1B satisfies the second half.
class-description: Windows. They’re everywhere we are, it doesn’t matter where. But what is a window? Inside, we peek through it to peer outside; outside, others peer through it to peek inside. Sure it separates inside from outside, but where does the window sit: inside or out? Perhaps it’s a facile question: we can’t divide space—it’s all one. Or perhaps a window marks a limit, a threshold even, the hypothetical point in any edifice where every neat spatial distinction collapses and emerges, if only briefly, to reveal this sublime contradiction. Though we may not overcome, we may nevertheless look through it as we do a window. Whether we choose to dismiss these unifying ruptures as sophistic babble, the liminal space they claim to inhabit will serve as our guide this semester as we grapple with an assortment of texts spanning from the ancient world of Hesiod and Heraclitus to the chimerical cityscapes of surrealism.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

class-description: Do you need to be at least a little crazy to be a great writer? Is going insane just a natural reaction to the world around us? To what extent should mental health crises be medicalized, and to what extent should they be accommodated as uncomfortable parts of most people's life experiences? These are just some of the questions that we will explore together over the course of the semester.

class-description: Mystical experience has traditionally been understood through the lens of religion. Yet as thinkers such as Max Weber and Charles Taylor argue, we inhabit an age of disenchantment, one in which spirituality no longer serves as a shared axis of meaning. This course examines the possibility of mystical experience within a secular world: What social, affective, and imaginative conditions allow the mystical to appear once its religious framework has receded?

class-description: Can we travel in time? What happens when time travel is no longer a speculative thought experiment, but a vivid “reality” made possible through wild literary imaginations? This course examines a wide range of works across historical periods and cultural contexts that mobilize time travel as a central narrative mystique. From premodern China to fin-de-siècle Europe to postwar America, we trace how authors imagine time travel to interrogate historical violence, modernity’s ruptures, political catastrophe, and irredeemable loss – while illuminating the worlds that produced them.

course-description: Expository writing based on analysis of selected masterpieces of ancient and modern literature. R1A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R1B satisfies the second half.
class-description: For this class, we consider the unique way that literary works challenge social categories. Students hone the skill of close reading, which examines how a work of literature makes its meaning through its style (e.g., its tone, narrative perspective, figurative language, and so on). The texts we read for class render strange that which might otherwise be taken for “normal”; they confront and change ideological constructs and social codes that might otherwise be taken for granted. Toni Morrison’s “Recitatif” (a short story from which the title of this course is taken) is an intriguing literary “experiment” or Rorschach test. Franz Kafka’s The Metamorphosis (1915) offers tragi-comic investigation into the limits of humanity. Interior Chinatown (2020) asks what it means to be Asian-American and probes the assumptions that might be lying beneath the question itself.

Law produces its own form of logic and truth, yet we seem to need stories to make sense of it.

class-description: What is love? Is it inherently complicated? How do a variety of literary traditions and genres represent love? To explore this topic we will read a wide array of literature (including novels, short stories, poetry, and autofiction), religious writings, and philosophical texts. Some of these will include Plato’s Symposium, selections from Dante and Mechthild of Magdeburg, and stories or novels by Robert Musil, James Joyce, Marguerite Duras, and Toni Morrison. As a class that counts towards R&C requirements, this is a writing intensive course. Writing workshops will be integrated into class sessions to practice close reading, structuring arguments, and other key skills for effective college-level writing.

class-description: How does representation respond to historical and present sites of violence? What is at stake in what we might consider to be “unrepresentable?” With an eye on the contemporary disasters of genocide, fascism, pandemic, and ecological collapse, we will work towards an understanding of how aesthetic form “informs” resistance- and/or the politics of what resists representation. We will work with varied texts in translation (from Spanish, Arabic, English, and French literary contexts) to collectively develop a repertoire of writing and critical skills with which to conceptualize the chronic disasters of our own present.
requirements: the Reading and Composition A requirement

title: English Composition in Connection with the Reading of World Literature
special: The Unlikely Protagonist: Stories about Translators and Their Work
course-description: Expository writing based on analysis of selected masterpieces of ancient and modern literature. R1A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R1B satisfies the second half.
class-description: We often rely on translation to learn about literature from other cultures and traditions, and we know that people have been doing so at least since Antiquity. Translation has also been a fundamental tool for such varied activities as conducting business, ruling empires, transmitting international news, receiving instructions for a new phone, and assembling IKEA furniture. However, we tend not to think about the role that translation plays in these activities. After all, what matters is that we can read about Achilles’s deeds, that enchanting garden from Dream of the Red Chamber, or Borges’s Library of Babel. Business has been conducted, empires have expanded, and more often than not, we have been able to assemble our new nightstand. But could there be particular ways in which translation shapes these activities? And what about the fact that we actually need a mediator, and sometimes more than one, to have something translated? What effort, research, negotiation, courage, danger, creativity, or hidden agenda go into the act of translation? In turn, as we drift between cultures, live with different languages, and get caught in intergenerational silence, do we see ourselves pick up a translator’s pen?

title: Studies in the Relations Between Literature and the Other Arts
special: Japanese Cinema, Visual Cultures and Media Theory
course-description: Comparative study of the historical and systematic relations between literature and other arts such as the visual arts, music, and film.
class-description: This course will delve into political and aesthetic theories underpinning artistic movements in the transforming media environments of the 20th century. Readings in the original Japanese will be supplemented by critical articles, books, and visits by emergent and established scholars in the field. Because many of these writings engage directly with international debates, we will consider the transnational contexts within which these theories are written and how they transform the terms and stakes of existing debates. Some writers (TBD) may include Nakai Masakazu, Murayama Tomoyoshi, Hanada Kiyoteru, Matsumoto Toshio, Tōno Yoshiaki, Lee U-fan, Nakahira Takuma, Yoshimoto Ryumei, Hasumi Shigehiko, Nakahara Yūsuke, and others writing on moving image media (cinema, animation, documentary and avant-gardes, video art, TV), contemporary visual arts (sculpture, painting, photography), mass culture and problems of mediation, as well as issues of leftist politics, cultural violence and memory.

title: Aesthetics as Critique
course-description: A close reading and discussion of the major texts of modern aesthetics, from the 18th century to the present, with emphasis on the Continental tradition of Kant, Adorno, and Derrida.
class-description: In his anticolonial classic “Por un cine imperfecto” (For An Imperfect Cinema), Cuban director Julio García Espinosa polemicized that “a perfect cinema…is almost always a reactionary cinema.” Taking inspiration from this work, we can say today that a perfect media in the 21st century has most often meant a reactionary media: maximizing economic gains and informational efficiency by ignoring ecological exploitation, universal design, and bias of all kinds. This course investigates the potential of imperfect media at the intersection of disability studies, anticolonial media theory, and media arts of all kinds. How might we respond to the particular problems of 21st century technologies that are presented to us as solutions: the scalar logic of LLMs and their server farms; the lasting paradigm of planned obsolescence; the capitalization of attention; the corporatization of piracy? What can we learn from the centrality of disability in the histories of smart phones and the mp3? How can we make media work differently through a focus on repair? How do prosthetic experiences, glitch art, hacktivism, and other social, medical, and aesthetic interventions create alternatives to the dominant modes of digital life.

title: Approaches to Comparative Literature
course-description: Lectures on literary theory, on the study of criticism, and on the methods of comparative literary theory.
class-description: This course introduces students to current conversations in the field of Comparative Literature. Topics include the politics of translation, debates regarding “world literature,” modalities of close reading, and the relevance of the posthuman to conceptions of fictional character.  Readings will be drawn from the work of Walter Benjamin, Rosi Braidotti, Judith Butler, Sharon Cameron, Barbara Johnson, Karl Marx, Fred Moten, William Pietz, Haun Saussy, and Eve Sedgwick.

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate. Course may be repeated for credit.

title: Senior Seminar in Comparative Literature
course-description: Seminar-style treatment of a major topic in Comparative Literature. Substantial paper required.
class-description: A chance to explore the “vegetal turn” in the environmental humanities, this senior seminar is devoted not just to literature about plants but to the close relation between human practices of mimicry, artifice, reading and writing (inscription and decryption) and plants as writers of light, image-makers, keepers of time, and figures transience and passing. We will read a number of literary and philosophical texts on the question of what differentiates plants from other living beings and what is specific to their ways of being in the world: their languages and morphologies, their modes of communication and sign-making, community, temporality, mobility, subsistence, and reproduction. Even as we read texts that try to enact and render the modes of agency specific to plants, we will try to resist the tendency –specific to the Western scientific tradition—of abstracting plants from their relations to other living beings. We will attend to plants’ entanglement with human practices of subsistence and cultivation, bearing in mind the sharp differences between plantation-like industrial monocultures and smaller-scale polycultures.

title: Senior Seminar in Comparative Literature
course-description: Seminar-style treatment of a major topic in Comparative Literature. Substantial paper required.
class-description: In the first part of this seminar, we will read and discuss a few short works of 19th-century crime fiction, along with a selection of theoretical/critical texts that will help us to understand the particular interest of these works in relation to questions of literary genre and narrative form.  We will also examine how these works position themselves with respect to the categories of otherness that have typically structured representations of colonized populations.  For the rest of the semester, we will try to answer the question of why so many authors of postcolonial literature have written novels that engage with different sub-genres within the field of crime fiction, including the “hardboiled” detective novel, the roman noir, and the serial killer novel.  What might account for this literary turn toward the dystopian, toward texts constructed around mysteries and often marked by shocking descriptions of extreme violence?  In what ways do the genres of crime fiction allow writers to tell stories that engage with long and complex colonial and post-colonial histories?  To what extent is storytelling itself implicated in these narratives of crime?  In what ways do writers push the generic boundaries of crime fiction, and to what ends?  Over the course of the seminar, we will consider these questions and others through close readings of several novels whose narratives emerge out of different historical, cultural, and geographic contexts. Authors considered will likely include Edgar Allan Poe, Ousmane Sembène, Driss Chraïbi, Patrick Chamoiseau, Didier Daeninckx, Yasmina Khadra, and Alain Mabanckou.

title: Topics in Modern Greek Literature
special: Creation, Creativity, and Origin Stories in Modern Greek Literature and Film
course-description: This course frames methodologically selected topics in Modern Greek Literature and places them in their historical, social or cultural context.
class-description: What is the potential of creation in a world characterized by catastrophe? Creation is the process of bringing something into existence, such as a work of art or a world. From experimental film to the recycling of myth to forge a distinctly modern poetic style, we will delve into case studies of literary and cinematic creation that intervene in forms of historical violence. The works that we will study critique the conditions of destruction out of which they emerge in the twentieth- and twenty-first centuries, including the project of the nation-state, colonization, the Balkan Wars, World War I, the Greco-Turkish War, the Population Exchange, the lasting effects of the National Schism, the Occupation of Greece during WWII, the Greek Civil War, and dictatorship. Creation involves the question of origins. Turning to philosophy, psychoanalysis, theology, anthropology, myth, and literary theory, we will grapple with competing accounts of creation and origin. What functions do origin myths serve? In this class we will try to understand how creation can become an aesthetic and ethical act of resistance.

title: The Modern Period
course-description: Literature of the 19th and 20th centuries.
class-description: In this course we will read imaginative works from Russia-Eurasia which foreground the magical, the marvelous, and the supernatural. We will begin by sampling the fables, fairytales, and epic poetry of the Slavic folk tradition, and then turn to a range of literary texts from Russia-Eurasia which have adapted myth, folklore, and fantasy to rapidly changing times. Attributing new meanings to religious myth, supernatural agency, and folk beliefs, this properly modern literary phenomenon began in the early nineteenth century and continues uninterrupted to this day. From the Romantic era we will be reading Alexander Pushkin’s Ruslan and Ludmila and Gogol’s bedevilled Ukrainian tales. From the Modernist era we will be sampling the stories of Alexei Remizov, lit by the fires of peasant revolution and the horrors lurking in Russia’s farflung provinces, and Nadezhda Teffi, whose émigré writings evoke a lost world of nature spirits and religious pilgrimage. From the Soviet era we will be reading the Communist wonder-tales of Pavel Bazhov, Evgeny Zamyatin’s dystopian “Fairy Tales for Grown-Up Children,” Mikhail Bulgakov’s masterpiece The Master and Margarita, a lively satire of Soviet society under Stalin which blends the story of Jesus Christ, a visit by Satan to contemporary Moscow, and a Faustian tale about an ostracized writer and his indomitable girlfriend, Evgeny Shvarts’ allegorical fable about modern-day tyranny The Dragon, and Yuri Rytkheu’s late-Soviet novella When the Whales Leave, an origin story and ecological parable rooted in the archetypal imaginary and historical experience of the Chukchi, an Indigenous people from the Arctic North. We will end the semester by reading a series of short stories by Victor Pelevin and Liudmilla Petrushevskaya, major contemporary authors who sift through the debris of post-Soviet society in search of the macabre and the miraculous. In sum, if traditional folklore viewed the supernatural as natural, a force permeating all of creation, then modern literature ascribes to magic a meaning we might call allegorical. What then are the allegorical uses of magic? How does enchantment enter history and alter the everyday? These are some of the questions we will explore over the course of the semester.

title: The Modern Period
special: Contesting the State in Modern Arabic Literature
course-description: Literature of the 19th and 20th centuries.
class-description: From Louis Bonaparte’s 1798 conquest of Egypt to the Algerian War of Independence (1954-1962), colonialism has been a determining force in the shaping of Arab modernity. For almost two centuries, the Arab region has undergone a major restructuring along the nation-state model after the dismantling of the Ottoman empire and the peripheral integration into global capitalism. In the postcolonial period, the region witnessed the rise of various forms of territorial nationalisms, socialist pan-Arab experiments, rentier state models, regional conflicts, neoliberal economic transformations, and popular uprisings. The literary discourses of the region responded to the pressures of the political with sophisticated engagements.

title: The Modern Period
special: MIND-BLOWING MODERN POETRY: CÉSAR VALLEJO & HIS LEGACIES
course-description: Literature of the 19th and 20th centuries.
class-description: César Vallejo wants us to know: When poetry's really being poetry, it's mind-blowing.

title: The Ancient Mediterranean World
course-description: The literature of Greece, Rome, the Biblical lands, and other ancient civilizations of the Mediterranean basin.
class-description: This course will study sexuality and gender in two very different historical periods--ancient Greece and 19th-century Europe. Sexuality will be defined as including sexual acts (e.g., sodomy, pederasty, masturbation); sexual identities (e.g., erastes and eromenos); and sexual systems (e.g., kinship structures, subcultures, political hierarchies). Readings and lectures will focus on situating queer sexualities relative to dominant organizations of sex and gender. Topics will include Greek democracy and male homosexuality; the biology of sexual difference; the politics of sodomy; “romantic” friendship between women and men; and the emergence of strictly defined homosexual and heterosexual identities. We will read literary texts along with historical documents and critical essays to constitute a comparative analysis of ancient Greek and 19th-century European systems of gender and sexuality.

title: Introduction to Comparative Literature:  Literature and Philosophy
course-description: An introduction to problems of the comparative study of literatures of the world in international and cross-cultural perspective along with philosophical texts and approaches. Emphasis on principles of comparative methods and analysis with focus on issues of philosophy and ethics along with selected literary, critical, and theoretical texts. Readings in English.
class-description: This class inquiries into how notions of time and subjectivity figure in different writing genres, literary traditions, and historical periods. In reading a diverse body of pre-modern and modern texts, we explore how time is constructed and articulated and how it is structured by narrative form and psychological content. We examine how diverse and competing temporalities underlie religious and secular worldviews and how they impact imaginaries of self and of society. We reflect on how articulations of temporality and historicity intersect with ideas of fate and free will, tradition and change, memory and imagination, and existential affect and collective reality. We pay close attention to how literary texts comprise multiple time horizons and we think through their relation with character development, the interplay of events and processes, and the mediation of experiences by cultural symbology.

title: Introduction to Comparative Literature
course-description: An introduction to problems of the comparative study of literature and culture. Emphasis on principles of comparative methods and analysis with focus on selected literary, critical, and theoretical texts from antiquity to the present. Readings in English.
class-description: This introduction to the discipline of comparative literature focuses on contemporary hybrid texts that work with and between literary genres and forms. While conventions of genre—such as those that define the novel, memoir, or lyric poetry—organize readerly expectation, hybrid texts deliberately push and unsettle generic boundaries. They often include an investment in poetics, autobiographic accounts, procedural narratives, and their own process of research in order to render new approaches to their concerns and objects of study. In concert with formal resourcefulness, the hybrid text requires recourse to a wide range of source materials—images, maps, ephemeral documents, historical and archival records—to animate poetic accounts and multi-perspective narratives.

title: Introduction to Comparative Literature
course-description: An introduction to problems of the comparative study of literature and culture. Emphasis on principles of comparative methods and analysis with focus on selected literary, critical, and theoretical texts from antiquity to the present. Readings in English.
class-description: In this course we will self-reflexively explore the genre of the academic or campus novel in its historical development and contemporary permutations.  How have campus novels evolved and what can they tell us about our own anxieties and desires for academic experience?   What would it mean to imagine our own lives as part of a fictitious universe?  We will read novels that focus on the experience of students and/or teachers on American college or university campuses, with detours into texts that deal with student life in Ireland, Russia and France.  This should be a rewarding and enjoyable endeavor in its own right, but we will also use this focus as an occasion for an introduction to literary theory, particularly to notions of literary genre.  Students will complete four writing assignments, including an outline for an imaginary academic novel, two analytical papers, and one mix of analysis and creative autobiography (the Batuman project).

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description:
Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

Course may be repeated for credit.

title: Discrete Mathematics and Probability Theory
course-description: Logic, infinity, and induction; applications include undecidability and stable marriage problem. Modular arithmetic and GCDs; applications include primality testing and cryptography. Polynomials; examples include error correcting codes and interpolation. Probability including sample spaces, independence, random variables, law of large numbers; examples include load balancing, existence arguments, Bayesian inference.

Modular arithmetic and GCDs; applications include primality testing and cryptography. Polynomials; examples include error correcting codes and interpolation. Probability including sample spaces, independence, random variables, law of large numbers; examples include load balancing, existence arguments, Bayesian inference.

Probability including sample spaces, independence, random variables, law of large numbers; examples include load balancing, existence arguments, Bayesian inference.

Probability including sample spaces, independence, random variables, law of large numbers; examples include load balancing, existence arguments, Bayesian inference.

Modular arithmetic and GCDs; applications include primality testing and cryptography. Polynomials; examples include error correcting codes and interpolation. Probability including sample spaces, independence, random variables, law of large numbers; examples include load balancing, existence arguments, Bayesian inference.

title: Great Ideas of Computer Architecture (Machine Structures)
course-description: The internal organization and operation of digital computers. Machine architecture, support for high-level languages (logic, arithmetic, instruction sequencing) and operating systems (I/O, interrupts, memory management, process switching). Elements of computer logic design. Tradeoffs involved in fundamental architectural design decisions.

title: Data Structures
course-description: Fundamental dynamic data structures, including linear lists, queues, trees, and other linked structures; arrays strings, and hash tables. Storage management. Elementary principles of software engineering. Abstract data types. Algorithms for sorting and searching. Introduction to the Java programming language.

title: The Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs
course-description: An introduction to programming and computer science focused on abstraction techniques as means to manage program complexity. Techniques include procedural abstraction; control abstraction using recursion, higher-order functions, generators, and streams; data abstraction using interfaces, objects, classes, and generic operators; and language abstraction using interpreters and macros. The course exposes students to programming paradigms, including functional, object-oriented, and declarative approaches. It includes an introduction to asymptotic analysis of algorithms. There are several significant programming projects.

title: Completion of Work in Computer Science 61C
course-description: MIPS instruction set simulation. The assembly and linking process. Caches and virtual memory. Pipelined computer organization. Students with sufficient partial credit in 61C may, with consent of instructor, complete the credit in this self-paced course.

title: Completion of Work in Computer Science 61B
course-description: Iterators. Hashing, applied to strings and multi-dimensional structures. Heaps. Storage management. Design and implementation of a program containing hundreds of lines of code. Students who have completed a portion of the subject matter of COMPSCI 61B may, with consent of instructor, complete COMPSCI 61B in this self-paced course.  Please note that students in the College of Engineering are required to receive additional permission from the College as well as the EECS department for the course to count in place of COMPSCI 61B.

title: Completion of Work in Computer Science 61A
course-description: Implementation of generic operations. Streams and iterators. Implementation techniques for supporting functional, object-oriented, and constraint-based programming in the Scheme programming language. Together with 9D, 47A constitutes an abbreviated, self-paced version of 61A for students who have already taken a course equivalent to 61B.

title: Freshman/Sophomore Seminar
course-description: Freshman and sophomore seminars offer lower division students the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member and a group of peers in a small-seminar setting. These seminars are offered in all campus departments; topics vary from department to department and from semester to semester. Enrollment limits are set by the faculty, but the suggested limit is 25.
class-description: This course will focus on in-depth discussions of a set of 3-4 books at the intersection of society, data, and software: social media, language models, automation, and more. We will discuss ways that these computing technologies perpetuate inequity and bias under the guise of presumed-neutral solutions. We will critique how we ourselves participate in engineering—both here at UC Berkeley and in any future roles. Students will keep a reading journal and do a final oral presentation.

title: The Beauty and Joy of Computing
course-description: An introductory course for students with minimal prior exposure to computer science. Prepares students for future computer science courses and empowers them to utilize programming to solve problems in their field of study. Presents an overview of the history, great principles, and transformative applications of computer science, as well as a comprehensive introduction to programming. Topics include abstraction, recursion, algorithmic complexity, higher-order functions, concurrency, social implications of computing (privacy, education, algorithmic bias), and engaging research areas (data science, AI, HCI). Students will program in Snap! (a friendly graphical language) and Python, and will design and implement two projects of their choice.

title: Comparative Biochemistry Seminar
course-description: The objective of this course is to provide an overview of the research activities conducted by faculty members of the Graduate Group in Comparative Biochemistry. The lectures will cover a wide range of interdisciplinary research topics reflecting the breadth of the Group. An important goal of this course is to enhance intellectual and collaborative interactions between students and faculty of the Graduate Group by increasing awareness of the range of research projects. The course will be conducted in a seminar format and is required for students new to the Graduate Group. It is also recommended for advanced students currently in the Group.

title: Gender, Sexuality, and Culture
course-description: Comparative investigation of a topic related to the study of gender and/or sexuality in literature and culture.
class-description: What makes a book pleasurable to read? What makes a book desirable or undesirable for the state? Is there such a thing as a black erotic literary tradition? This course will explore African and Black diasporic literature that has contributed to political and aesthetic debates on pleasure. The readings will be drawn from a range of genres including novels, poetry, ethnographies, and manifestoes. We will begin by interrogating the intersection of race, desire, and colonialism with writers such as Hortense Spillers, Franz Fanon, and Dambudzo Marechera. Though the readings, we will also trace additional concepts such as the “sexual commons,” the “queer customary,” and the “African carnivalesque novel.” Most importantly, the course will be an ongoing meditation on materiality and sensuality, on the book itself as a thing to hold on to or to lose.

title: The Craft of Critical Writing
special: Turn your seminar paper into an article!
course-description: The course will proceed chiefly through exercises in writing reviews and critical essays, with class discussion of the work that will be done by members of the seminar. Some analytic attention will also be devoted to existing models of critical prose. The class will deal with the minute details that make for lucidity and felicity of style and will also consider larger issues of organization, critical focus, and audience.
class-description: In this class we will use the semester’s 14 weeks to develop strategies for turning a seminar paper into an article of publishable quality. The class will have a workshop like structure.

title: Special Topics
course-description: Topics will vary semester to semester. See the Computer Science Division announcements.

title: Special Topics
course-description: Topics will vary semester to semester. See the Computer Science Division announcements.
class-description: We live in a world of networks: from our physical social network, to online networks and the WWW, to the biological networks describing, e.g, pathways in cancer cells, to name three examples. The goal of this class is to learn how these networks work.

title: Introduction to Machine Learning
course-description: Theoretical foundations, algorithms, methodologies, and applications for machine learning. Topics may include supervised methods for regression and classication (linear models, trees, neural networks, ensemble methods, instance-based methods); generative and discriminative probabilistic models; Bayesian parametric learning; density estimation and clustering; Bayesian networks; time series models; dimensionality reduction; programming projects covering a variety of real-world applications.

title: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
course-description: Ideas and techniques underlying the design of intelligent computer systems. Topics include search, game playing, knowledge representation, inference, planning, reasoning under uncertainty, machine learning, robotics, perception, and language understanding.

title: Introduction to Database Systems
course-description: Access methods and file systems to facilitate data access. Hierarchical, network, relational, and object-oriented data models. Query languages for models. Embedding query languages in programming languages. Database services including protection, integrity control, and alternative views of data. High-level interfaces including application generators, browsers, and report writers. Introduction to transaction processing. Database system implementation to be done as term project.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning, Decision Making, and Control
course-description: This course will cover the intersection of control, reinforcement learning, and deep learning. This course will provide an advanced treatment of the reinforcement learning formalism, the most critical model-free reinforcement learning algorithms (policy gradients, value function and Q-function learning, and actor-critic), a discussion of model-based reinforcement learning algorithms, an overview of imitation learning, and a range of advanced topics, including exploration, model-based learning with video prediction, transfer learning, multi-task learning, and meta-learning. Homework assignments will cover imitation learning, policy gradients, Q-learning, and model-based reinforcement learning, as well as a final project.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning, Decision Making, and Control
course-description: This course will cover the intersection of control, reinforcement learning, and deep learning. This course will provide an advanced treatment of the reinforcement learning formalism, the most critical model-free reinforcement learning algorithms (policy gradients, value function and Q-function learning, and actor-critic), a discussion of model-based reinforcement learning algorithms, an overview of imitation learning, and a range of advanced topics, including exploration, model-based learning with video prediction, transfer learning, multi-task learning, and meta-learning. Homework assignments will cover imitation learning, policy gradients, Q-learning, and model-based reinforcement learning, as well as a final project.

title: Foundations of Computer Graphics
course-description: Techniques of modeling objects for the purpose of computer rendering: boundary representations, constructive solids geometry, hierarchical scene descriptions. Mathematical techniques for curve and surface representation. Basic elements of a computer graphics rendering pipeline; architecture of modern graphics display devices. Geometrical transformations such as rotation, scaling, translation, and their matrix representations. Homogeneous coordinates, projective and perspective transformations. Algorithms for clipping, hidden surface removal, rasterization, and anti-aliasing. Scan-line based and ray-based rendering algorithms. Lighting models for reflection, refraction, transparency.

title: Algorithms for Computational Biology
course-description: This course will provide familiarity with algorithms and probabilistic models that arise in various computational biology applications, such as suffix trees, suffix arrays, pattern matching, repeat finding, sequence alignment, phylogenetics, hidden Markov models, gene finding, motif finding, linear/logistic regression, random forests, convolutional neural networks, genome-wide association studies, pathogenicity prediction, and sequence-to-epigenome prediction.

title: Efficient Algorithms and Intractable Problems
course-description: Concept and basic techniques in the design and analysis of algorithms; models of computation; lower bounds; algorithms for optimum search trees, balanced trees and UNION-FIND algorithms; numerical and algebraic algorithms; combinatorial algorithms. Turing machines, how to count steps, deterministic and nondeterministic Turing machines, NP-completeness. Unsolvable and intractable problems.

title: Software Engineering Team Project
course-description: Open-ended design project enhancing or creating software for real customers in an agile team setting. Teamwork coordination, effective customer meetings, pre- and post-iteration team meetings, running scrums and standups, technical communication. Contributing as a team to an open-source project; tools and workflows associated with open source collaboration, including fork-and-pull, rebase, upstream merge, continuous deployment & integration.

title: Introduction to the Internet: Architecture and Protocols
course-description: This course is an introduction to the Internet architecture. We will focus on the concepts and fundamental design principles that have contributed to the Internet's scalability and robustness and survey the various protocols and algorithms used within this architecture. Topics include layering, addressing, intradomain routing, interdomain routing, reliable delivery, congestion control, and the core protocols (e.g., TCP, UDP, IP, DNS, and HTTP) and network technologies (e.g., Ethernet, wireless).

title: Programming Languages and Compilers
course-description: Survey of programming languages. The design of modern programming languages. Principles and techniques of scanning, parsing, semantic analysis, and code generation. Implementation of compilers, interpreters, and assemblers. Overview of run-time organization and error handling.

title: Operating Systems and System Programming
course-description: Basic concepts of operating systems and system programming. Utility programs, subsystems, multiple-program systems. Processes, interprocess communication, and synchronization. Memory allocation, segmentation, paging. Loading and linking, libraries. Resource allocation, scheduling, performance evaluation. File systems, storage devices, I/O systems. Protection, security, and privacy.

title: Computer Security
course-description: Introduction to computer security. Cryptography, including encryption, authentication, hash functions, cryptographic protocols, and applications. Operating system security, access control. Network security, firewalls, viruses, and worms. Software security, defensive programming, and language-based security. Case studies from real-world systems.

title: Computer Architecture and Engineering
course-description: Instruction set architecture, microcoding, pipelining (simple and complex). Memory hierarchies and virtual memory. Processor parallelism: VLIW, vectors, multithreading. Multiprocessors.

title: Special Topics
course-description: Topics will vary from semester to semester. See Computer Science Division announcements.
class-description: This graduate seminar is an interdisciplinary introduction to the individual, social, economic, and political effects of AI-driven media, with particular emphasis on design approaches that grapple with these issues. Social media is an important application, but we are also concerned with LLMs and systems like news recommenders, online shopping, job listings, and “trending” algorithms.

special: Proving TCS and Math Theorems in Lean
course-description: Topics will vary from semester to semester. See Computer Science Division announcements.

title: Special Topics
