title: Challenge Lab: Building Bridges between Democracy and Technology for a Better Society
special: Challenge Lab: Democracy^Tech: Democracy raised to the Power of Tech
course-description: This experiential course prepares technical, business-minded, and policy-oriented students to build and plan the implementation of a product, startup, or policy innovation from scratch. This course is meant for students who seek a challenging, interactive, team-based, and hands-on learning experience in entrepreneurship and technology.   Students can expect to work in an interdisciplinary team to develop novel products and solutions to address existing problems in the realm of democracy and technology.
class-description: This experiential course prepares technical, business-minded, and policy-oriented students to build and plan the implementation of a product, startup, or policy innovation from scratch. Students work in an interdisciplinary team to develop novel products and solutions to address existing problems in the realm of democracy and technology. For example, engineering students may leverage technical skills to help translate ideas into products, while political science students may leverage their policy knowledge and social science skills to identify problem areas and generate plausible solutions. Students from any discipline may bring unique perspectives, domain expertise, and comparative advantages to their team. This cross-listed course utilizes the Challenge Lab entrepreneurial course foundation, offered by the College of Engineering Sutardja Center of Entrepreneurship and Technology, in partnership with the Political Science department to “Building Bridges between Democracy and Technology for a Better Society”. People and organizations have been grappling with unceasing advancements in digital technologies and their implications for society, both good and bad, real or perceived. On the one hand, technology and data can bolster democratic functions and the empowerment of communities within a society. (As one example, dashboards and products that make political data more easily accessible and interpretable to the general public.) On the other hand, there also exist risks of technological misuse. (As one example, the proliferation of disinformation.) In this Challenge Lab, students will explore the design of policies, businesses, and/or products that can help provide such benefits and/or mitigate such risks. Each student will join a team based on their own interests and knowledge. Each team will choose an area to develop and test possible solutions, build prototypes, and develop a new business, product, or policy innovation. The following are proposals for areas that teams may choose to work on: ● Misinformation (e.g. ability to distinguish between factual and non-factual political content) ● Democratic discourse (e.g. ability of citizens to engage in productive exchange with each other and their political representatives) ● Civic/political participation and empowerment (e.g. ability and motivation of members from different communities to participate in core political processes) ● Political knowledge and citizen awareness (e.g. accessibility and interpretability political data) ● Democratic representation and accountability (e.g. maintaining and revealing the accountability of political representatives) ● Transparency and trust in institutions (e.g. the conditions for the public to have faith in systems of governance) ● Data-driven policy (e.g. the use of data and AI to aid decision-making in policy processes) ● Collection and control/freedom of information (e.g. questions regarding who has access to and can use different types of digital information) This class is open to anyone who wants to examine how technology could be leveraged to democratic processes. Students from all majors, both undergraduate and graduate, are welcome. Preference will be given to masters-level students, seniors, and juniors with experience or demonstrated interest in public management, policy-making, technology businesses, and startups.

class-description: Today, we feel the effects of inflation acutely—in the grocery store, in the ballot box, and on the open market. The economic machine has been contracting for myriad reasons, and governments and central banks have responded invariably by adding grease to the wheels through measures such as printing money, buying assets, deregulating, remilitarizing, etc. This course asks how this profound and omnipresent economic phenomenon alters our perception of ourselves. How does the value of money affect our values and our modes of expression? This seminar is designed for students, new to the humanities, who wish to enrich their scholarship with concepts from a wide range of disciplines, from economic and political theory to literature and film studies. Our course will thus address inflation as a methodological problem as well, one that has deepened the divide between the humanities, social sciences, and STEM research in the American university.
requirements: the Reading and Composition A requirement

class-description: The formula of the slasher movie is a staple of modern horror: its (often virginal) “final girl” acts as heroine, sometimes a passive one, who watches her friends fall off one by one. Typically, death results as a punishment for acting on sexual desires or deviating from social norms. But questions of gender, sexuality, and taboo begin much earlier than than the slasher. Authors have used the horror to explore, condemn, and celebrate the queer and the non-normative even in the earliest examples of the genre.
requirements: the Reading and Composition A requirement

title: Reading and Composition
course-description: Training in writing expository prose.  Instruction in expository writing in conjunction with reading literature. Satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: “Life, friends, is boring,” John Berryman writes in “Dream Song 14,” yet “We must not say so.” Why do we get bored, and why can’t we talk about it? What makes one thing boring and another thing interesting? Is boredom ever good for anything? This course picks up on these questions in works that consider boredom as well as works often considered boring: “Dream Song 14,” Robinson Crusoe (Daniel Defoe), Waiting for Godot (Samuel Beckett), and Zen for Film (Nam June Paik), to name a few. We’ll look, too, at philosophy and criticism by thinkers like Søren Kierkegaard, William James, and Georg Lukács. Through these texts and objects, we’ll consider a few explanations for how boredom arises and what our encounters with boredom might mean. And we will reflect, in turn, on how we engage in the work of engaging readers as we write, on what makes a piece of writing interesting (or not), and on the experience of writing itself, an activity that can be, by turns, excruciatingly boring and thrillingly transformative.
requirements: the Reading and Composition A requirement

title: Reading and Composition

class-description: In this course, we will read and write about novels that take revolution as their theme. Special attention will be given to the way in which novels portray revolutionary transformations, which can be rather difficult to comprehend. Writing in exile between the two Russian revolutions in February and October of 1917, the Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin declared, “There are no miracles in nature or history, but every abrupt turn in history, and this applies to every revolution, presents such a wealth of content, unfolds such unexpected and specific combinations of forms of struggle […], that to the lay mind there is much that must appear miraculous.” Taking this perspective, which describes revolutions as contradictory and complex processes, as our starting point, we will ask how novelists understand and narrate such events, either those they themselves have lived through or have written about from afar (spatially and/or temporally). What forms, literary devices, and narrative techniques have novelists developed in order to represent that which “to the lay mind must appear miraculous”?

title: Reading and Composition
course-description: Training in writing expository prose.  Instruction in expository writing in conjunction with reading literature. Satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: What did it mean to be a child? What sense did we make of life before we learned what sense was? Before life became graspable through ideas, morals, and prescriptions given to us by adults? As Louise Glück writes in "Nostos," "We look at the world once, in childhood. / The rest is memory." This course explores literary texts which grapple with this paradox, the paradox that we cannot directly re-experience our first experiences of the world—we can only reconstruct them with the knowledge we have now. Throughout the semester, we will encounter works of various genres (including poetry, memoir, fiction, child psychology, literary criticism, and children's books) that attempt to recreate the world of children's experience in spite of its seeming impossibility. As we read, we will probe how racial, class, and gender hierarchies shape children's social worlds, how ideas like 'innocence' and 'agency' limit who gets to enjoy the full privileges of childhood, and how the language of childhood requires us to reconceptualize the relationship between reason, identity, and the senses. And although we begin the course with an acknowledgement of our profound distance from childhood, we will also consider the equally undeniable truth that even as we appear to age 'away' from that early period of our lives, the children we were/are have not simply vanished. Both alien and intimate, they still speak to, for, and through us.

class-description: "Everyday life' both names the felt substance of social life and suggests its abiding and disruptive strangeness. It is in everyday life and in its attendant rhythms and institutions that we register decisive movements of politics and economy, as well of course as their transformation in various kinds of cultural practice. But it is in everyday life too that such movements can at the same time seem displaced, absent, even obscured. Everyday life, then, is everything, it is nothing, it is at once a mere equivalent and somehow in excess of life itself.

title: Reading and Composition
special: English Odysseys: Homer in Various Translations
course-description: Training in writing expository prose.  Instruction in expository writing in conjunction with reading literature. Satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: Describing the impossibility of preserving the blending of sound and sense that defined his reading of Homer’s epics, Ezra Pound claimed the much of the epics’ spirits were “untranslated and untranslatable.” Nevertheless, countless authors, poets, and scholars have made the attempt, and in this course, we’ll be attempting to make sense of those various attempts. As such, we’ll read through Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, but for each segment of our reading, we’ll read the work of different translators (and we will read only in translation; no knowledge of Greek is expected or required). From Alexander Pope’s heroic couplets in his 1710s-1720s translations to Emily Wilson's blank verse versions of the last decade to non-verse renderings of Homer entire, we’ll consider the particular virtues and vices of different approaches in organizing and communicating the same tale, and we’ll also glean how slight differences in translation decisions radically transform the effects and affects of certain themes and motifs. And while Homeric translation will dominate the majority of the course, Virgil’s Aeneid will be given the same treatment for the course’s coda to test this approach against a distinct if adjacent tradition.

class-description: In this class, we’ll be thinking about the role that the history of science and its “epistemic virtues” have had on U.S. experimental literature in the 20th century. Do experiments in literature require writers to incorporate the same practices and principles as that of scientists? What does it mean to “make it new” in language? What makes writing “experimental?” What is a theory of the sentence and what is the method to find it? Poets and writers we’ll be reading may include: Gertrude Stein, William Carlos Williams, Amiri Baraka, Lyn Hejinian, Ron Silliman, Tan Lin, Natalia Cecire, Sylvia Wynter, Lorraine Daston, Bruno Latour, among others.

course-description: This lecture series serves as an entry point for undergraduate and graduate curriculum sequences in entrepreneurship and innovation. title: Special Topics in Technology Innovation and Entrepreneurship
course-description: This course will explore various topics around technology innovation and entrepreneurship. Topics will vary by semester.
class-description: Why do some innovators and their ventures seem successful while others fail? What is the secret to feeling fulfilled, despite challenges? While likely a combination of attributes and skills, resilience is one of the most often suggested and least researched traits enabling founders and founding teams to flourish (source: Phebe Tucker, MD, What is Resilience). We posit that resilience can be learned, a skill related to growth mindset. For this course, we define resilience as the ability to bounce back; explore options; take action and learn from mistakes while experiencing tension. Lack of resilience presents itself in fear; frustration at receiving negative feedback; overwhelming guilt; regret and even depression. The course objective is to provide new awareness of the brain science behind impediments to resilience, present and apply tools to increase your resilience and test various practices to improve your ability to successfully launch yourself, your venture and your ideas. Together we will learn about and analyze experiments, literature, movies and group activities to understand: The meaning of resilience and how it applies to your situation as an individual, venture team member and/or venture team lead; Neuroscience and cognitive science, at a high level, and how it impacts your actions, feelings and ability to thrive A variety of practical tools (and evaluation relative to your needs) to help you understand what is happening in your brain that impedes your resilience, that work for you and those around you that are proven to increase resilience Alternative perspectives, so that you can choose what works for you to you push forward in your work and your leadership, through challenges and opportunities As you work through group-, partner- and individual- activities, this class is designed to help you and your current or future team. With your commitment to ongoing survey participation, you will leave a lasting legacy of best practices to build resilience in others going forward. This is a Berkeley Chagemaker course.

title: Special Topics in Technology Innovation and Entrepreneurship
special: Amazoogle: AI and the Modern Data-driven Business Model
course-description: This course will explore various topics around technology innovation and entrepreneurship. Topics will vary by semester.
class-description: AI, machine learning and Big Data are well understood technologies, yet their applications in business are dominated by a small group of uber-practitioners, as exemplified by Amazon, Google and OpenAI. What do these companies know – and practice – that others do not? The Amazoogle class is an introduction into the strategy and technology of data-driven business models in the age of AI. Beyond its application in well-known business sectors, the Amazoogle model also brings particular impacts in technology ethics and sustainability. Students in the class will learn the practices in building data-driven, AI-centric business models that strive to provide positive impact, both on the bottom line and in society.

title: Special Topics in Technology Innovation and Entrepreneurship
special: Future of Technology: How Innovators Critically Examine Game Changing and Time Wasting Technologies
course-description: This course will explore various topics around technology innovation and entrepreneurship. Topics will vary by semester.
class-description: Why did Altavista fail, and Google succeed? Same for Myspace and Facebook? Was it technology, marketing, people, luck, execution, or something else? It is trivial to discern good ideas and profound technological shifts after the fact. But how could you become your own futurist and learn to analyze emerging trends and foretell the outcome? We will study and analyze both failures and successes in virtual reality, blockchain, artificial intelligence, healthtech, and other technologies. Students will conduct literature reviews, netnographic analysis, and case studies in order to identify patterns that they could later apply to their own research, career decisions, or entrepreneurial ventures. The format of the class will include lectures, guest speakers from distinguished entrepreneurs and innovators, peer-reviewed presentations, quantitative and qualitative data gathering, and group exercises. Students will produce a technical report highlighting the barriers for adoption of emerging technologies. The report has the potential to be published and added to your professional portfolio. Critical thinking and the ability to question everything are the only prerequisites for this analytical survey course.

class-description: Is poetry a luxury? Do you, too, dislike it? The proposition that gives this course its title, from Gertrude Stein’s Lectures in America (1935), implies an unconventional view of the matter. For Stein, poetry is not—or at some point, was not—merely one literary genre among many. Against this rarified conception, she evokes a poetry that “includes everything,” encompassing a far greater range of creative and productive practices through which worlds are made.

course-description: Training in writing expository prose.  Further instruction in expository writing in conjunction with reading literature. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: Caliban, the part-man, part-monster "creature" who lives on an island alongside the sorcerer Prospero and his daughter Miranda in William Shakespeare's play The Tempest, has had a long literary, performance, and cinematic afterlife. From his first appearance onstage in Jacobean England in 1609 to his Civil War-era reincarnation as "Gator Man" in the American Deep South, to his alienation in Cold War-era science fiction films, to his recreation in revolutionary Latin American and Global South conversations about race, Otherness, and freedom--Caliban has remained a figment of our creaturely imagination, a mainstay in a globalized and fraught conversation about what it is to be human, and what it is to be free. In this class, we will work from Shakespeare's play outward, from plays and films to art installations and novels. Like the music of the island Caliban alone hears and appreciates, we will work to hear resonances, echoes, and "strange music" between each new Caliban we encounter and our own embodied cultural moment, and write what we see, hear, and sense.

class-description: This course examines how ideas of waste, renewal, and sustainability emerged within the context of colonialism and slavery. Centered on the British Caribbean, we will trace how composting—a seemingly mundane agricultural practice—became a powerful metaphor for an imperial economy imagined as endlessly productive. Planters and writers celebrated the Caribbean environment’s prodigious fertility, even as colonial agriculture depended on the disposability of enslaved lives and the degradation of land. Through historical, literary, and theoretical texts, students will explore how metaphors of recycling and fertility helped naturalize extractive economies, while also laying conceptual foundations for modern environmental thought.

class-description: Do poems take up truths? Can a novel be a way of thinking about something? What can you learn—about others, about the world, about yourself—from a film? This course considers the ways literature and art not only engage our creative imaginations but also offer powerful insights into what is actual. We will occupy ourselves with the diverse ways that literature and art help us “think” about our world. We will become interested in how fictional and imaginative works come to touch what is worldbound, and we will ask how they participate in realms of thought and ideas. Our ultimate interest will be in reading philosophically—that is, attuned to the claim literature makes to helping us understand the world around us. Our texts will include poetry (William Blake, William Wordsworth, Emily Dickinson, Langston Hughes, Wallace Stevens), fiction (Jane Austen, James Baldwin), drama (Henrik Ibsen, Samuel Beckett), film (Alfred Hitchcock, Terrence Malick), and philosophy (Plato, Nietzsche).

title: Reading and Composition
special: Pauline Hopkins: Black Feminism, Political Action, and Untimely Fiction
course-description: Training in writing expository prose.  Further instruction in expository writing in conjunction with reading literature. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: How does an author become representative—of a time and place in history, of an identity category, or of a political movement? In this class we will read a selection of novels, short stories, and essays by Pauline Hopkins (1859–1930), tracking the political stakes of her fiction about black life at the threshold of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. In this respect, we will pay special attention to two of her four novels: Contending Forces (1900) and Of One Blood (1902–1903). We will also engage with scholarship about Hopkins’s oeuvre in light of its own context of emergence. That is, we will track the development of black feminist criticism and theory, which revived Hopkins from literary obscurity in the name of a “tradition” of novels by black women that had been largely suppressed before the 1970s. How does Hopkins’s work fit into this “tradition”? How do scholars from the late twentieth century fulfill or extend the political aspirations outlined in fiction from the beginning of the twentieth century? Why and how does literature become relevant beyond its own time and place? Can a novel’s politics extend across large swaths of time? Can a novel itself be a medium of political action? In this class we will work through these thorny questions with recourse to two methods: close reading and analytical writing. Both methods rely on focusing our attention on something specific that we believe to be representative of something greater than itself. We will establish stakes and extend the reach of our own writing by asking questions. In short, we will write in order to learn something we could not have possibly known before engaging in the writing process.

class-description: Moments of confusion force us to seek understanding that explains horrors currently beyond comprehension, systems of government beyond recognition, others beyond their social labels, sensations and feelings without names. In this class we will ask ‘What is it?’ in each moment of confusion to identify the nature of things as they appear to characters, to artists, and to ourselves. We will start with moments of self-recognition in Milton’s Paradise Lost and in fairy tales before considering human judgments about similarity and difference when people are introduced. In reading Octavia Butler’s Kindred , we will explore the construction and representation of identity across the boundaries of race, gender, class, age, and even centuries.

class-description: What is it for a work of literature to evade translation, and what happens when we translate it anyway? Both the process of original literary composition and our understanding of reference and world-hood have been heavily inflected by these concerns. This course will track both theoretical and practical approaches to translation and translatability, paying special attention to the development of these concepts in the early twentieth century, and the mark they have left on modernist poetics and philosophy. Readings will include Borges’, Benjamin’s, and Weinberger’s more general speculation, alongside modernist translations of poetry from Provencal, classical Chinese, classical antiquity, and the modern languages.

course-description: Training in writing expository prose.  Instruction in expository writing in conjunction with reading literature. Satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: 300 years after Daniel Defoe wrote Robinson Crusoe—the story of a man who finds himself cast away alone on a desert island—the figure of the castaway lives on in our culture as an archetype and a myth. Crusoe has been read as a symbol of modern individualism, an avatar of industrial capitalism, an apologist for settler-colonial conquest, and an icon of human ingenuity in the face of hardship (among other things!). In this course, we’ll consider some of these canonical interpretations while paying particular attention to Crusoe’s craft, understood both in terms of practical survival skills and in terms of the literary techniques that the narrator uses to write himself into being, such as reflecting on his past; keeping a journal; engaging in dialogue with his “servant,” Friday. How do survival and storytelling intersect in Crusoe’s narrative? How does the craft of writing help him establish the borders of the self, just as physical crafts of building, weaving, and sowing help him establish the borders of his island home? How does Crusoe write other people—especially the indigenous and black individuals he encounters in his travels—into or out of his narrative?  We will extend our consideration of these questions by looking at postcolonial responses to the text (J.M. Coetzee’s 1986 adaptation, Foe) and considering contemporary reworkings of the archetype in fiction and in film. We’ll consider how and why castaway stories continue to speak to our present moment, resonating with modern-day concerns like global inequality and impending ecological crisis. Throughout, short essays will offer opportunities to practice the craft of academic writing, from brainstorming to drafting, revising, and editing.

Course may be repeated for credit.

class-description: How do you tell a story in the absence of verifiable history? How do you construct a memoir, a poem, or a novel when the archive is fragmented, when families are silent, and state histories are withheld from you? In this seminar, we will investigate how Asian American writers navigate erasure, displacement, and the unreliability of memory in genres that range from memoir, poetry, and film. We will read across literature, history, and theory to examine how both narrative and the lyric can become sites that contest and reconstruct what has been erased from personal and institutional memory. We will look at the works of Maxine Hong Kingston, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha, Bhanu Kapil, and Viet Thanh Nguyen. This course will combine critical inquiry with creative practice, asking students to write both critical and personal essays.

title: Practices of Literary Study
course-description: This course is a small, faculty-led seminar on the practice and discipline of literary analysis.  It is meant for all students who seek an introductory literature course and would like to improve their ability to read and write critically, including those who may wish to major in English.  Focusing on the close study of a few works, rather than a survey of many, the seminar will help students develop college-level skills for interpreting literature, while gaining awareness of different strategies and approaches for making sense of literary language, genres, forms, and contexts. The seminar also will develop students’ ability to write about literature and to communicate meaningfully the stakes of their analysis to an audience.
class-description: In this course, we'll read the poetry of William Butler Yeats, from his early work to his last poems. We'll also take a look at some of his prose and other writings. Our hope is to use the oeuvre of Yeats as a lens with which to view the history and politics of the first part of the twentieth century, particularly in the English-speaking world. We'll touch on the work of Yeats’s contemporaries, writers and thinkers in the Anglophone world such as Robert Frost, H.D., T.S. Eliot, and W.H. Auden, and we'll understand the poetry in terms of form, lyric, political violence, spiritual philosophy, Ireland and England, the natural world, childhood, music, folklore, artistic ambition, and more, all as made manifest in Yeats’s work. Requirements include two four-page essays and one six-page essay, as well as regular attendance and participation in discussion.

class-description: Aliens and sentient robots, time loops and parallel universes—Ted Chiang’s fiction has all the out-of-this-world trappings of traditional science fiction. At the same time, each of his 18 short stories—a notably slim output for a writer who has been publishing for more than 34 years—is meticulously crafted, polished to the exquisite sheen of a well-wrought urn. His fiction elegantly combines the “hard science” of STEM fields with the social analysis and emotional impact of the “softer” sciences and humanities. It reveals the entanglement of such seemingly contradictory perspectives as physics and philosophy, free will and determinism, memory and speculation, and cognition and feeling.

class-description: Ecopoetry – nature poetry that is environmental and environmentalist – is an international twenty-first century movement.  But in the nature poetry and poetics of the United States ecopoetry has deep and wide-spread roots.  This seminar will explore this movement in U.S. nature and environmental(ist) poetry and poetics from the nineteenth century into the present.  We’ll read the romantics and post-romantics (including Bryant, , Emerson Thoreau, Whitman, and Dickinson), the modernists (including Frost, Stevens, Jeffers, Moore, Eliot, H.D., and Sterling Brown), the post-modernists (including Bishop, Merwin, Snyder, and Berry), and our contemporaries (including Sze, Graham, Hass, Baker, Gander, Dungy, Diaz, Perez, and Hirshfield).  We’ll read relevant theories of nature and of animals, and of their representation in poetry, including essays by poets and critics about the natures and uses of ecopoetry.  While our exploration will be primarily historical, our focus will also be theoretical, involving a number of recurrent topics, including anthropocentrism (and ecocentrism), anthropomorphism (personification and the pathetic fallacy), animals and things; place, disaster, and pollution; and species extinction, environmental justice, and climate change; and climate emotions, including denial, despair, courage, and hope.  You will learn how to hear a poem’s rhythms and to trace its figures.  You will also learn how to read a poem responsively and ecocritically.  You will be asked to write three (five-page) essays, one each on a poem by a (post-)romantic, a modern, and a post-modern poet.  At least the first of these essays will be written out by hand in class.  I welcome students from English and from other majors.  This seminar is multi-centered and open-ended.  It will be shaped by your own local experiences and expertise.  I will learn from you as much as I teach you.

class-description: A great deal of fiction is oriented around protagonists who are "growing up wrong" — out of step with the expectations of adults and their peers, and deeply conflicted about the shape of their own desires and aspirations (at the very moment that they are trying to define those desires and aspirations for themselves). These characters may rebel or sabotage themselves, search for a new home or a new friend or a new lover—all while struggling to see and feel the world as it truly is or might be. If their present is in crisis, it's often because their future is in question too. In this seminar, we'll explore a wide variety of short stories and novels about growing up — diverse in their narrative strategies and tone as well as in the stories they tell — from authors ranging from Tillie Olsen and Toni Morrison to Hanif Kureishi  and Ocean Vuong.

title: Literature in English: The Late-17th through the Mid-19th Century
course-description: Historical survey of literature in English: The late-17th through the mid-19th century.
class-description: Readings in prose fiction, poetry, and autobiography from the British Isles and the Atlantic world from c.1680 through c.1850: a century and a half that sees the formation of a new, multinational British state, with the political incorporation of Scotland and then Ireland, the global expansion of a maritime commercial and colonial empire, the revolt of the North American settler colonies, and the expansion and abolition of the British Atlantic slave trade. Our readings explore the relations between home and the world in writings preoccupied with journeys outward and inward, real and imaginary, voluntary and forced …

title: Literature in English: Through Milton
course-description: Historical survey of literature in English: Beginnings through Milton.

title: Freshman Seminars
course-description: The Berkeley Seminar Program has been designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small-seminar setting. Berkeley Seminars are offered in all campus departments, and topics vary from department to department and semester to semester.
class-description: Students in this course will watch, analyze, and discuss influential examples of Hollywood cinema such as City Lights, Frankenstein, The Public Enemy, Bringing Up Baby, Stagecoach, The Wizard of Oz, Citizen Kane, Casablanca, It's a Wonderful Life, Double Indemnity, Mildred Pierce, Singin’ in the Rain, Rear Window, Rebel Without a Cause, and Imitation of Life.

title: The Seminar on Criticism
course-description: This seminar is designed to provide English majors with intensive and closely supervised work in critical reading and writing. Although sections of the course may address any literary question, period, or genre, they all provide an introduction to critical and methodological problems in literary studies.
class-description: This course will consider how literature helps us see and make sense of the self as a discursively constructed entity. How do we narrate a self, which is to ask, how do we organize a self? And how does this organization necessarily demand and depend upon a certain fragmentation? What makes the novel form particularly well suited for narrating the processes of historical subject formation? To begin exploring these questions the course will read a single novel – Doris Lessing’s The Golden Notebook (1962). We will then towards some of the vast critical scholarship produced about the novel as way of familiarizing ourselves with some of the methodological and theoretical problems in literary studies, including feminist, postcolonial, psychoanalytic, and historicist modes of reading. In reading the novel alongside the scholarship we will examine how literary texts anticipate, resist, and court their desired critical engagements and how criticism, in turn, deconstructs and frustrates those expectations.

title: Medieval Literature
course-description: Development of literary form and idiom throughout the Christian West from the first to the fifteenth century.

title: Short Fiction
course-description: A seminar in writing short stories.

title: Short Fiction
course-description: A seminar in writing short stories.
class-description: The aim of this course is to explore the genre of short fiction—to discuss the elements that make up the short story, to talk critically about short stories, and to become comfortable and confident with the writing of them. Students will write two short stories, a number of shorter exercises, weekly critiques of their peers’ work, and a final writer's reflection. The course will be organized as a workshop and attendance is mandatory. All student stories will be edited and critiqued by the instructor and by other students in the class.

title: Modes of Writing (Exposition, Fiction, Verse, Etc.)
course-description: Lectures and discussion on the crafts and/or processes of writing in various genres including fiction, poetry, creative nonfiction, etc. Topics for reading and writing assignments vary semester to semester.
class-description: "This course will introduce students to the study of creative writing—fiction and poetry. Students will learn to talk critically about these forms and begin to feel comfortable and confident writing within these genres. Students will write a variety of exercises and more formal pieces. Class will be a combination of lecture/discussion and small in-class workshops where student work will be edited and critiqued by other students in the class.

title: Topics in Chicana/o Literature and Culture
course-description: Topics in Chicana/o literature and culture.
class-description: Latino/a/x poets comprise a significant part of the contemporary poetry field; they write in fixed forms and free verse; they influence the trajectory of digital aesthetics and spoken-word performance; they have built an impressive number of institutions and journals dedicated to their craft; and they pay homage to a genealogy that extends back to the nineteenth century in multiple languages. Yet Latino/a/x poetry remains a relatively small presence in scholarship on contemporary poetry and poetics. This course will offer a general introduction to the field and a guided exploration of four major themes: history, language, movement, and form.

title: Topics in American Studies
course-description: A course on the intellectual, cultural, historical, and social backgrounds to American literature. Topics will vary from semester to semester.
class-description: This course will consider a series of fascinating and influential Hollywood films released between 1930 and 1960. Tracking the development and breakdown of the studio system over the middle decades of the twentieth century, we will closely analyze films including City Lights (1931), Stagecoach (1938), Meet Me in St. Louis (1944), Double Indemnity (1944), Singin’ in the Rain (1952), and Imitation of Life (1959) with an eye to understanding their relationships to the historical and political contexts in which they were produced. Along the way we will be thinking about storytelling, continuity, technology, genre convention, mass production, and the representation of space and time.

title: Romantic Period
course-description: Blake, Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley, Keats, and contemporaries.
class-description: As revolutions rocked the Atlantic world at the turn to the 19th Century, writers witnessed the social and political order that structured their reality break open. Not only did the American, French, and Haitian Revolutions seem to put the world up for grabs: radical new ways of investigating nature that had been set in motion during the Scientific Revolution contributed to a breathless sense of technological acceleration, even as the human and ecological ravages of the Industrial Revolution made themselves felt. Such transformations unleashed the fury of artistic experimentation known as “Romanticism”: an attempted “revolution in taste” that might seize and shape – or receive and refine – the changing experience of historical time, the felt crisis between human and nonhuman nature, and the potential for social, sexual, and racial liberation. This class will survey a diverse array of boundary-pushing Romantic writing, tracking the entwined themes of “experience” and “experiment” to unfold the gorgeously experimental means by which Romantic poets, novelists, memoirists, and philosophers grappled with their revolutionary age.

title: Shakespeare and Film
course-description: Close study of the texts and films based on 8 to 10 plays. Lectures will emphasize the critical implications of transposing plays to film. The goal of the course is the critical understanding of Shakespeare, and the course satisfies the departmental requirement of a course on Shakespeare in the major.
class-description: Hamlet and His Problems

title: The English Renaissance
course-description: Literature of the 17th century.
class-description: In a now-famous note added to the second edition of Paradise Lost in 1674, Milton characterized the poem as an example of “ancient liberty recover’d to heroic Poem from the troublesom and modern bondage of Rimeing.” Written in the aftermath of the radical social and political experiments of the 1640s and 1650s, the note appears to suggest that literary form is an impediment to freedom. But Paradise Lost isn’t written in free verse, and as the note explains, what is at stake in Milton’s claim is to distinguish rhyme, which he characterizes as “vexation, hindrance, and constraint” from the “true Ornament(s)” of verse. What, then, is a “true ornament,” and how is it different from an untrue one? When do forms constrain freedom, and when do they license creation? Does free speech have a form peculiar to it? These are some of the questions we’ll discuss in the context of works by Mary Sidney, William Shakespeare, John Donne, Ben Jonson, Aemilia Lanyer, George Herbert, Katherine Phillips, Robert Herrick, John Milton, Andrew Marvell, and others.

class-description: Ursula LeGuin has described writers of science fiction and fantasy as “realists of a larger reality.” In this course we will explore the relationship between science fiction and the realist novel, first by reading theory and criticism about science fiction, and second by reading important science fiction novels from the last fifty years. The goal of this course will be to get students to think critically about literary texts and literary criticism and theory. We will also spend some portion of our time learning how to write about and engage the arguments of other scholars. Students will write two papers, one shorter and one longer, and keep a journal of their annotations. They will also give presentations on the course readings.

title: The Seminar on Criticism
special: Edith Wharton, Henry James, and Amerian Realism
course-description: This seminar is designed to provide English majors with intensive and closely supervised work in critical reading and writing. Although sections of the course may address any literary question, period, or genre, they all provide an introduction to critical and methodological problems in literary studies.
class-description: Our readings will focus on two major writers of the late-nineteenth and early-twentieth century whose works helped to define the literary mode of realism in the United States. Focusing mainly on James and Wharton as novelists, we will see how their works adapt the literary conventions novels of manners and marriage to explore a modernizing world. We will be asking questions about how literature responds to new ways of representing the world that emerge with technologies such as photography and the phonograph that challenge what it means to capture and document “reality” itself. We will also investigate how writers understood the social and political mission of literary expression at a time of rapid change in the years after the Civil War. Critical readings will explore the formal elements that distinguished realism (and naturalism) from other styles of American writing, and also look at some of the dominant themes--from economic anxiety and evolutionary decline to sexual exploitation and criminal violence—that have long defined these genres for readers and critics.

class-description: This seminar takes up the old problem of literary character. Why are we so attached to characters, and what does it mean for us to identify with one, or feel like another is a close friend? How has the idea of what constitutes a character changed over time? What are the literary techniques through which the illusion of a thinking, feeling person is created? In this class we’ll read criticism drawn from narrative theory, history of the novel, psychoanalysis, and queer theory. We’ll also read a few novels spanning the 19th century to 21st centuries as test cases for thinking about issues of (dis)identification, relatability, subjectivity, and personhood. Sample authors may include Jane Austen, George Eliot, Ralph Ellison, Zadie Smith, and Susan Choi.

title: The Seminar on Criticism

Although sections of the course may address any literary question, period, or genre, they all provide an introduction to critical and methodological problems in literary studies.
class-description: Focusing on the Victorian novel, this course will examine why it emerged as the dominant expressive mode in nineteenth-century Britain. What made the novel so popular, and in what ways did the novel shape—and was shaped in turn—by the prevailing social, political, and aesthetic concerns of the time? What accounts for the Victorian novel’s abiding hold on us even now? In addressing these questions, we will read various genres of the Victorian novel, such as  the bildungsroman, the historical novel, and the fin de siècle gothic, among others. In so doing, we will consider the development of formal characteristics of the Victorian novel as well as its thematic and material concerns.  The (tentative) list of novels includes: Charlotte Bronte, Jane Eyre; Charles Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities; George Eliot, Silas Marner; Bram Stoker, Dracula.

title: The Seminar on Criticism
course-description: This seminar is designed to provide English majors with intensive and closely supervised work in critical reading and writing. class-description: The historiographer Hayden White characterized the archive as an unruly repository of the history’s materials; while the chronicle presents a first order attempt to organize archival material chronologically, the archive itself presents an ever expanding and contracting collection of details, documents and accounts of past events. Yet, as unimaginably expansive and as intricately detailed archival material may be, history, the narrative presentation of our past, is astonishingly narrow. Frequently entire constituencies are missing –the working classes, migratory peoples, the peasantry, the enslaved, women. Or events once instrumental to an age fade into the background. This course examines the relationship between the archive and literature. How does literature, the novel and poetry work with and against historical material. The assigned novels and poetry address the question of how literature experiments with the archives dizzying plenitude and puzzling scarcity. This course will also introduce students to formalist writings on historiography, the historical novel, and theories of the archive itself.

title: The Seminar on Criticism
special: Czesław Miłosz in English: Poetry and the Twentieth Century
course-description: This seminar is designed to provide English majors with intensive and closely supervised work in critical reading and writing. Although sections of the course may address any literary question, period, or genre, they all provide an introduction to critical and methodological problems in literary studies.
class-description: Czesław Miłosz was one of the great poets of the twentieth century, and though he wrote in Polish, his work was carried masterfully and comprehensively into English by a cadre of the finest translators, including the American poet Robert Hass. Miłosz and Hass, who were at Berkeley for decades, created with others a body of Miłosz’s work in English establishing the poet as a transnational writer and a writer with claims on the traditions of English literature. In this course, we'll read all of the poetry by Czesław Miłosz that’s been translated, from his early work to his last poems. To this body of work we'll bring a variety of critical sources and texts, reflecting on Miłosz, English-language literature in the twentieth-century, and modes of reading. Our hope is to use Miłosz’s oeuvre as a lens with which to view the literature, history, critical conversation, and politics of the twentieth century, particularly in the English-speaking world. We'll touch on the work of Miłosz’s contemporaries, writers and thinkers like Robert Hayden, W.H. Auden, Elizabeth Bishop, and others, and we'll understand the poetry in terms of form, lyric, political violence, authoritarianism, spiritual philosophy, the United States, Europe, the natural world, childhood, philosophy, artistic ambition, and more, all as made manifest in his work. Requirements include two four-page essays and one six-page essay, as well as regular attendance and participation in discussion.

class-description: In its original published form, The Waste Land is slightly more than four-hundred lines long. When it was republished as a slim volume, T. S. Eliot added a few pages of notes, seeking to augment a poem that had proven “inconveniently short.”

class-description: This seminar will introduce students to “law and literature” studies, focusing on the way literature imagines the relation between law and justice. We’ll begin with literature of the Romantic period, concentrating on novels, poems, and dramas structured around  trials and confessions. What does it mean to speak “before the law”? How might we understand understand the “word crimes” of perjury and sedition; how do words like "infanticide" and "tyrannicide" affect ideas of guilt and innocence?  We’ll also examine the relation of aesthetic judgment to justice and the law. Does the experience of beauty correct or corrupt legal judgment? What is "poetic" justice? Can justice repair injury?

class-description: Los Angeles has been described, variously, as a "circus without a tent" (Carey McWilliams), "seventy-two suburbs in search of a city" (Dorothy Parker), "the capital of the Third World" (David Rieff), and "the city of angels and constant danger" (Tupac Shakur). This class will investigate these and other ways that Los Angeles has been understood over the last century — as a city-in-a-garden, a dream factory, a noirish labyrinth, a homeowner's paradise, a zone of libidinal liberation, and a powder keg of ethnic and racial violence, to name but a few. We will trace the history of Los Angeles from its complicated and contested origins to its rise as the sprawling megacity that has often been taken as a prototype of postmodern urban development. And we will do so primarily by looking at the fiction, film, drama, and music that the city has produced in the postwar era.

course-description: Research-oriented and designed for upper-division English majors. Intensive examination of critical approaches, literary theory, or a special topic in literary and cultural studies. Topics vary from semester to semester. class-description: In this course we’ll review the U.S. poetry of the present, reading representative poems from the last 25 years or so in relation to a number of formal concerns, poetic subjects, and debates within the social field (and its media), including: the advent of the Internet and its ongoing effect on writing and reading practice, dissemination, and national conversations about race, gender, class, and community; the emergence of “ecopoetics”; the waning and reinvention of traditional forms; prose poetry; Conceptual poetry; movement poetry (Occupy-era and antiracist work). All readings will be drawn from a digital Course Reader and may include Kevin Davies, Juliana Spahr, Claudia Rankine, Ben Lerner, Jennifer Moxley, Graham Foust, Ariana Reines, Douglas Kearney, Fred Moten, Lisa Robertson, Cathy Park Hong, Brenda Hillman, Javier Huerta, Monica Youn, and many others.

class-description: The late Lyn Hejinian left behind a corpus of immense scale and enormous intricacy: testing and casting across more modes, styles, genres, discursive practices, media, and arts; involving more collaborators (and other conspirators); launching more conceptual experiments than one might easily number, each tracking and twisting and reinterrogating the whole possibility that writing might be ‘experimental’ in the first place.

Intensive examination of critical approaches, literary theory, or a special topic in literary and cultural studies. Topics vary from semester to semester. Students should consult the department's "Announcement of Classes" for offerings well before the beginning of the semester.
class-description: The Harlem Renaissance was a cultural movement of black artists and writers in the 1920s and 1930s. Centered in New York, the movement extended outward through international collaboration. We will be reading together works by writers like Claude McKay, Langston Hughes, Alain Locke, Nella Larsen, and Zora Neale Hurston as well as manifestos on the nature and function of black art. Course themes include migration and metropolitan living, primitivism and the avant garde, diaspora and exile, passing and identity, sexuality and secrecy, and the relationship between modern art and vernacular tradition.

course-description: Research-oriented and designed for upper-division English majors. Intensive examination of critical approaches, literary theory, or a special topic in literary and cultural studies. Topics vary from semester to semester. class-description: In this seminar, we will read our way slowly into the forbidding and exciting “fourfold” poetic environments of the visionary artist William Blake: graphic works of “Illuminated Printing” in which a city like London, or “Golgonooza,” is also a level of consciousness, a bodily organ, a phase of fallen history, and grotesque fun with g’s and o’s. With the aid of intertexts ranging from the Book of Revelations to colonial travel literature, Romantic political philosophy, and contemporary literary theory, we will trace Blake’s mythic characters’ attempts to form artistic, erotic, and political community while enmeshed in what the poet called “the Web of Urizen”: the internalized system of moral “virtues” that shored up the national defense, wage-labor exploitation, and colonial slavery in Blake’s era of revolution and reaction.

class-description: This seminar will provide you with a sustained reading course in the poetry of Emily Dickinson.  We’ll begin with her early poetry, and trace her evolution into the singular poet we read today, with particular attention to her hymn forms and her poetic figures.  We’ll also consider how her poems might be read in relation to history and her biography.  Since Dickinson wrote most of her poetry in the span of a few years, we’ll group and read her poems largely by topics.  Our topics will include gender and sexuality, definition and riddle, poetics, nature, religion, death and dying; suspense, horror, and loneliness; despair and hope; the self in society and by itself, abolition and war.  We’ll also delve into her manuscripts of individual poems, packets of poems (fascicles), and her letters.  Especially with her later poems, the distinctions between verses, poems, drafts, and letters become hazy.  To guage Dickinson’s singularity and commonness, we will also read poems and essays by her contemporaries (e.g., Lydia Sigourney, Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Edgar Allan Poe, and Helen Hunt Jackson).  Your first essay is diagnostic and will be a responsive reading, without secondary sources, of a single poem.  This essay will be written by hand in class.  In the second half of the term, you will be choosing your research topic from my list and discussing it with me.  I will also help you choose and respond to Dickinson criticism.  Your research paper will gather a collection poems on your topic in conversation with recent criticism.  You will also be expected to read assignments, poetry and prose, before class.  I will guage your preparation by class discussion, and by occasional quizzes.  By the end of the seminar, you should be reading and writing on Dickinson with confidence, pleasure, and satisfaction.

title: Science Fiction
course-description: Study of speculative fiction (or science fiction) as a genre. Topics may vary from semester to semester. Focus may be historical or thematic.
class-description: “Not real can tell us about real.” This is one of the fundamental lessons learned by a new race of genetically engineered trans-humans in Margaret Atwood’s 2003 novel, *Oryx and Crake*. It is also one of the underlying principles of science fiction. In this course, we will explore some of the landmarks and lesser known way stations along the history of this diverse genre, attending to the cultural and political implications of its brave new worlds and the creatures in them. We will attend in particular to the ways that science fiction pushes at the limits of human knowledge: What is our place in the universe? What makes us different from machines or animals? What can the future tell us about the present day or the historical past? In reading stories about aliens, robots, androids, clones, and zombies, we will ask ourselves: what does it mean to be human?

title: Tragedy
course-description: Study of representative tragic forms, techniques, and points of view.
class-description: Since the beginning of Western drama, tragedy has been the most celebrated dramatic genre, and, indeed, Aristotle argues that tragedy is the greatest of all forms of literary art. In this class, we will keep many general questions about tragedy—why are philosophers so drawn to tragedy?; how do tragedies reflect and shape political values?; what kind of pleasure do audiences find in tragic representation?; and so on—percolating as we engage three particular moments in the history of tragedy: the origins of tragedy in Ancient Athens; the flourishing of tragedy in Shakespeare’s London; and Wole Soyinka’s and Suzan-Lori Parks’ recent and remarkable reinventions of tragedy.

title: Literature and Philosophy
course-description: Studies in the relationship of literature in English to philosophy.
class-description: Why read the first volume of Capital more than 150 years after its initial publication in 1867?  The world around us is in crisis. Coming to grips with that crisis requires understanding how it got that way. Marx’s Capital continues to be an illuminating guide in that project. Marx wrote Capital in the mid-nineteenth century, as the set of relations he called “capitalism” was just falling into place. Having lived in this system all our lives, it is harder for us to see its particular configuration than it was for someone to whom it was all new. Hence, we turn to Marx, and to Capital, as a lens through which to understand the present. Not only is Marx being seriously and widely read again since the financial crisis of 2008, but it is his mature critique of political economy that is of interest. Reading Capital today, we’ll see why 20th and 21st century radical thinkers on questions of racism, gendering, colonialism, environmental destruction, imperial war and financial predation have sought to build on its concepts and methods or, even in moving past them, feel that they must first be confronted and critiqued anew. As we make our way through the book, we’ll be turning to some of these contemporary thinkers as a way of gaining an introduction to Marx’s continuing critical relevance to explanations for the radical inequalities and social violence of our times. To be clear, most of the course will be devoted to understanding Capital Vol 1. So if you have long wished to study and work through this book in a structured manner, this is your chance.

title: Literature and Philosophy
course-description: Studies in the relationship of literature in English to philosophy.
class-description: This course will examine key texts from the history of moral philosophy and philosophy of mind and juxtapose them with a set of novels that share similar concerns. Our aim will be to arrive at clear, precise understandings of the philosophical concepts at hand as well as the ways these concepts can change, or must change, as they become part of a fictional world. Writers discussed will include James Baldwin, Samuel Beckett, Ford Madox Ford, Iris Murdoch, Mary Shelley, and Virginia Woolf. Philosophical readings will include extracts from Aristotle, Chalmers, Descartes, Hobbes Hume, Kant, Locke, Mackie, Mill, Mills, Plato, Nietzsche, Russell, Scanlon, Strawson, Walton, and Williams.

title: Special Topics in American Cultures
special: Race and Revision in Early American
course-description: In this course, students investigate the way literature and other art forms have both represented the diversity of the United States and shaped conceptions of diversity. English 166AC provides students with an opportunity to deepen and complicate their appreciation of the way fictions make meaning, shape our understanding and experience of the world, and transform society. Topics vary from term to term and might focus on a form (e.g. "Race and Ethnicity in American Cinema"), a literary historical period (e.g. "Race and Revision in Early America"), or a concept (e.g. nationhood in "Literatures of the Asian Diaspora in America").
class-description: In this course, we will read both historical and literary texts to explore how racial categories came into being in New World cultures and how these categories were tested, inhabited, and re-imagined by the human actors they sought to define.  Our study will be organized around four early American sites:  Landfall in the North Atlantic, Pocahontas at Jamestown, Witchcraft at Salem, and Jefferson’s Virginia. In each of these places Native, European, and African ways of making meaning collided, and concepts of racial difference were formed. These sites will function as interpretive nodes.  For each, we will read a selection of primary documents and then explore how racial constructions forged at each site have been re-imagined and revised throughout American cultural history to the present day.

class-description: This lecture course explores the intersection of poetry and political action, focusing on developments over the last century, particularly in the writings of Black, Asian, and Arab diasporas. Beginning with key historical and theoretical contexts, the course moves into contemporary controversies dedicating class time to current developments in our literary landscapes. Guest poets will join us for readings and conversation. Students will write a combination of creative and critical work throughout the semester.

title: Special Topics
course-description: Immersive study of an author, genre, form, or literary historical issue. Topics vary from term to term.
class-description: Anton Chekhov said that the writer’s task is not to answer questions, but to pose questions correctly. In this course, we will consider the many questions that Chekhov—one of the most influential dramatists and short story writers in world literature—poses in his stories and plays. These are questions about: love, death, time, the environment, prisons, mental asylums, medicine, the body, pain, the self and the other, the comic, the tragic. We will examine his thematic and formal innovations; discuss the connections between his narrative and dramatic texts; and consider his understated, elusive vision of human experience. We will explore his texts in the historical context of late 19th-century Russia, as well as several theater productions and film adaptations of Chekhov in a contemporary global context. The use of AI is prohibited in this course.

title: Research Seminars
course-description: Required of all Ph.D. students. Advanced study in various fields, leading to a substantial piece of writing. Offerings vary from semester to semester. Students should consult the department's "Announcement of Classes" for offerings well before the beginning of the semester.
class-description: This course will consider poetics and theories of poetry, especially lyric poetry, since the early 19th century. We will watch as conceptualizations of poetry, lyric, and verse torque throughout the 19th and 20th centuries, beginning, roughly, with Wordsworth’s “Preface” to Lyrical Ballads and making our way into our own critical moment. We’ll look at a number of key nineteenth- and twentieth-century statements on poetry and lyric as we reconsider the projects of the New Critics alongside of other types of formalist scholarship, the place of poetry within structuralism and poststructuralism, and the importance of poetry in several varieties of Marxist criticism and psychoanalytic theory. As we come to more recent writings, we’ll investigate poetry in relation to matters of perception, cognition, technology, politics, identity, ecology, and history. We will pay close attention to the shapes and textures of a small handful of poems, many of which will be dictated by our theoretical and critical readings, but some of which we’ll choose as a class at the start of the semester. My hope is that the class is able to follow three interweaving tracks over the course of the semester: 1) the longer tradition of thinking about poetics since the start of the nineteenth century; 2) the course of scholarship on lyric and poetry over the past several decades; and 3) the routes taken by contemporary poets as they refashion notions of lyric within their own practice. All enrolled students will have the option of writing two conference-length papers (8-10 pages) or one article-length essay (20-25 pages). All readings will be available in a course reader and on bCourses.

title: Renaissance: Seventeenth century through Milton
class-description: Seventeenth-century English literature is haunted by the afterlife of the monastery. Dissolved in the Reformation and remembered largely through polemic, the monastery was recast as a space of unnatural enclosure—an image of idleness, corruption, or confinement that shaped Protestant cultural memory. Yet writers continued to reimagine this figure of the cloister, sometimes reproducing its pathology, sometimes exploring how monastic habits of discipline, devotion, and community might be reinvented. This course examines how literary forms—lyric, sermon, drama, and epic—engage the legacy of monasticism, treating enclosure not only as a site of claustrophobia but also as a resource for imagining freedom. Readings include Shakespeare’s Henry VIII, Aemilia Lanyer’s Salve Deus, Donne’s and Herbert’s devotional works, Milton’s Paradise Regained, Herrick’s Hesperides, and Marvell’s lyrics, alongside key scholarship on poetics, devotion, and cultural memory.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop
course-description: A writing workshop in poetry for graduate students.
class-description: Studies in contemporary poetic cases will focus our discussions of each other's poems.

title: Poetry Writing Workshop
course-description: A writing workshop in poetry for graduate students.
class-description: This course is a generative poetry workshop that focuses on “play” as a pathway into the hidden reservoirs of the imagination. While we will primarily devote class time to the critical discussion of our poems, we will also discuss assigned readings and do in-class prompts that inspire improvisation and disobedience.

title: Old English
class-description: Surviving in a single manuscript copy written around the year 1000, Beowulf is the longest extant poem in Old English, and a work of many dimensions and extraordinary subtlety. In this class, we will read the whole poem in the original language, attending closely to its verbal texture, intricate syntax, and challenges of linguistic and literary interpretation. Our work will be supplemented by readings in medieval analogues and critical scholarship, to help orient us in the poem’s cultural world and understand cruxes in its modern reception. Students will translate 250-300 lines of Old English each week, and work towards a final research paper.

title: Graduate Readings
course-description: Graduate lecture courses surveying broad areas and periods of literary history, and directing students in wide reading. Offerings vary from semester to semester. Students should consult the department's "Announcement of Classes" for offerings well before the beginning of the semester.
class-description: This course will have two parts: in the first, we will read across the range of Henry James’s career, from its American beginnings to the achievements of his major phase; in the second, we will discuss a series of figures directly or indirectly influenced by James’s signature aesthetic and stylistic innovations. We will be especially interested in the development of James’s “realism,” and how it provides, for himself and others, a language for examining the shape of modern life from the late-nineteenth century through the mid-twentieth century. This is a course about the “Jamesian” in James and beyond, and about the particular feelings, psychologies, and narrative structures that pattern the models of authorship and authority he practiced, and that other writers and artists have inherited, knowingly or not.

class-description: If the last part of this course’s title surprises, it will be helpful to remember that the term “aesthetic,” when first coined in 1735, described the “science of sensuous cognition” and that in 1800 William Wordsworth called poetry the “science of feelings.”

title: Graduate Readings
special: Studies in Pastoral: The Question of the Seasonal or Temporal Commons
course-description: Graduate lecture courses surveying broad areas and periods of literary history, and directing students in wide reading. Offerings vary from semester to semester. Students should consult the department's "Announcement of Classes" for offerings well before the beginning of the semester.
class-description: What are the seasonal or temporal commons? And what is literature’s role in articulating the relation between seasonal time, rhythmic time and common time or everyday time?

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate. Course may be repeated for credit.
