course-description: Bi-weekly lectures on methodology, grading and testing in French 2. Demonstration class with required attendance five times per week; laboratory observations; supervised classroom practice. Additional seminars and discussion sections on methodology. Required for all Graduate Student Instructors teaching French 2 for the first time.
class-description: The goals of this course are to discuss pedagogical concerns related to the content of French 2, presented in Chez Nous as well as broader issues relevant to language education, to provide a forum for discussing teaching-related questions and problems, to deepen a theoretical understanding of language learning processes, particularly those related to literacy and multiliteracies, and to offer participants practical experience in creating and adapting materials for instruction.

title: Dissertation Writing Seminar
course-description: Students having completed doctoral qualifying examinations and now working on a dissertation or prospectus will undertake a structured process leading to the completion of a finished piece of work, in most cases a dissertation chapter. Each week, students will discuss one or more works in progress, and will have an opportunity both to learn from other students’ process and research, and to receive feedback from a diverse group on your own writing. Alongside the work of participants, students will read relevant theoretical texts and discuss research methods, questions of genre, tools for moving through blocks, and avenues for publication.

title: Traditions of Critical Thought: French Theory
course-description: This course will introduce students to canonical texts and central issues in French theory and to the philosophical texts they presuppose. The goal is to give students the conceptual tools they need to read a range of theoretical texts and to contextualize major works in French theory from the 1960s and 1970s.
class-description: The literary genre can often be considered from an anthropological point of view, whereas anthroplogical texts can very well be perceived through their literary mode of writing. In this seminar, we will seek to understand the blurring of distinctions between these two fields. This seminar is divided into two parts. In a first moment, we will devote our analysis to twentieth-century France, by exploring the dialog between anthropological knowledge and literary writing. This dialog is best exemplified in the works of Michel Leiris, Georges Bataille and Levy-Strauss. We will consider the meaning of notions such as sacrifice, religion, ritual and community, through an analysis of these author’s main body of work. In the second part of the seminar, we will analyze the relationship between literature and anthropology in post-colonial studies. Taking as a point of departure works by Achille Mbembé, we will analyze in depth conceptual terms such as exoticism, orientalism and otherness when they relate to the understanding of colonial and post-colonial societies. The material for this seminar is in French and the discussion can be held in both English and French.

title: Comparative Studies in Romance Literatures and Cultures
course-description: Topics will vary. Comparative studies in literary, cultural, or historical issues that cut across the literatures of the Romance languages.

title: History of the French Language
course-description: A history of the French language from its Latin origins through the modern period. Emphasis on "external history" (development of the language in relation to other social and cultural phenomena) with some historical grammar (phonology, morphology, syntax, orthography) introduced through textual readings from the various historical periods. Sociolinguistic emphasis, focusing on the emergence of a standard language and its relationship to other varieties of French.
class-description: This course covers the history of the French language from its Latin roots through to contemporary usage. Both internal and external history will be considered so that students acquire a firm grounding in the linguistic evolution of the language, coupled with an understanding of its development in relation to a range of social and cultural phenomena. The course will be structured around our analysis of the wide range of texts from different genres presented by Ayres-Bennett (1996) and which date from 842 CE to the present day. We will use the relatively new historical sociolinguistic approach to try to capture what Anthony Lodge (2009) has called “une image multidimensionnelle de la langue du passé”.

title: Advanced Proseminar
course-description: This course gives first-year graduate students a general introduction to reading, analyzing, and writing about French texts.
class-description: This course gives first-year graduate students a general introduction to reading, analyzing, and writing about French texts.

title: Configurations of Crisis
special: Le problème de l’immigration dans la France contemporaine
course-description: A study of the pressures on artistic, political, and economic structures at moments of crisis in French history. Problems of continuity and discontinuity in esthetic and social history.
class-description: Ce cours est une introduction à la question de l’immigration maghrébine en France des années quarante jusqu’au présent contemporain. Nous étudierons d’abord la première vague d’immigration des années quarante, puis nous analyserons les différences profondes qui existent entre les différentes générations d’immigrés. Nous analyserons dans un second temps la question de l’immigration en relation avec la question de l’identité nationale française. Nous montrerons comment cette question est un enjeu de société capital, et nous analyserons son utilisation politique. Nous utiliserons une variété de matériel: des oeuvres littéraires, des essais, des documentaires et des films.

title: A Concept in French Cultural History
special: The French Court under Louis XIV: Myths, Realities, Representations
course-description: An examination of certain large cultural concepts, such as "the Baroque" or "Romanticism," in French cultural history. Topics vary from year to year.
class-description: "The Court, the Court, the Court! In this word lies all evil.” So spoke, in the 18th century, an influential courtier named the marquis d’Argenson. Today, popular culture sometimes fantasizes about court etiquette, the splendor of court festivities, and the amorous intrigues that unfolded at Versailles in the 17th century. The reign of Louis XIV, during which the court was codified into a system of government, is also frequently regarded as the political and cultural high point of the Ancien Régime. Yet, like d’Argenson, many of the Sun King’s contemporaries — while flocking to this place where aristocratic fortunes were made and unmade — saw the Court as an unstable and dangerous environment, which corrupted their morals, and threatened, in the long run, both their freedoms and the welfare of the kingdom. This course explores this tension by systematically comparing a series of literary and historical primary sources with the most recent historiographical works on the French court. We also investigate current representations of the court in three cinematic productions, one of them being a historical reconstruction of a 17th century performance. The analysis has a twofold aim: to understand the social, political, religious, and aesthetic practices that shaped Louis XIV’s court, and to examine how this phenomenon continues to shape France’s relationship to its past, as well as its understanding of its present. All coursework is done in French.

title: Translation Methodology and Practice
course-description: In-depth knowledge of the French language and accuracy in its use are the goals of this course. A textbook and systematic exercises will be used to assist in the demanding task of translating, both from English to French and from French to English.
class-description: This upper-division course introduces students to the practice of translation between French and English. It draws on developments in the relatively recent discipline of ‘translation studies’ to develop students’ skills as translators. We will learn about methodologies of translation and have the chance to put them into practice as we translate both from French into English and from English into French. We will pay particular attention to the linguistic and cultural differences which typically pose problems for practicing translators. As we carry out the translation work, we will explore a range of methodological questions. For example, we will explore how the practice of translation varies according to the type of text being translated and the purpose of the translation. We will also explore how to make use of different tools and resources from dictionaries and databases to Generative AI. Students will come away from the course with a better understanding of what translation is and how to practice it but they will also find that it improves their French.

title: French Literature in English Translation
special: Films of the French New Wave
course-description: Major texts of modern French literature. Readings and writing assignments in English for non-majors; in French for French majors and minors. Class discussions in English.
class-description: This class will introduce students to a number of classic films of the French New Wave, perhaps the most important and emblematic moment in modern cinema, and a still a point of reference for filmmakers ranging from Quentin Tarantino and Martin Scorsese to Alfonso Cuarón and Wong Kar-Wai. Along the way, we will look at the theoretical and cultural factors that help explain this extraordinary flowering of filmmaking talent in the late 1950s and early 1960s; we will also be reading some important short essays from the period that will help bring the films’ originality into focus, as well as more recent scholarship. General points to be explored include: France and American popular culture; post-war economic transformations and consumerism; changing norms of sex and gender; the documentary image; the subversion and pastiche of genre; the ideology of form. All films available for streaming, with subtitles. No knowledge of French is necessary.

title: French for Professions
special: French for Politics, Economics, and Business
course-description: Introduction to the French vocabulary and syntax specific to fields (i.e., economics, politics, and business) and industries. Oral and written comprehension, written compositions (including correspondence), translations, training in oral expression. Conducted entirely in French.
class-description: This class will consist in a solid introduction to French-speaking political and economic cultures to help you:

title: Senior Seminar
special: Senior Seminar: Rabelais and the Renaissance
class-description: François Rabelais is the greatest writer of the French Renaissance, one of the inventors of the novel, an innovator of the French language and one of the most influential writers in the Western literary tradition. In this course we will read carefully through his hilarious fables of giants and monsters, place him in dialogue with the intellectual and political forces shaping the emergence of modern France. Among the topics to be covered; Rabelais’s relationship to humanism, his invention of a modern French prose style, his use of the grotesque and the exorbitant. We will be especially interested in his work as a creator of the genre that comes to be known as the novel, and we will look at his influence on such later writers as Shakespeare, Diderot, Sterne, and

title: Literary Themes, Genres, and Structures
course-description: Topics vary from year to year. Past topics have included "litterature fantastique," science fiction, autobiography, French lyric poetry.

title: Eighteenth-Century Literature
course-description: A study of authors of the second half of the 18th century stressing the importance of the "Movement Philosophique" and the development of libertine values as well as the emergence of the pre-Romantic aesthetics.
class-description: Eighteenth-century thinkers wrote about “others” with remarkable frequency.  Sometimes they represented those “others” as abject and subaltern; sometimes they represented them as sublime.  Many impulses, many forms of intellectual inquiry and of curiosity propelled the creation of these texts. Writers grappled with the astonishing diversity of customs, institutions, and social practices as they sought to understand, and sometimes reform, the culture, political structures, religion, and economy that structured their own societies.

title: Language and Culture
special: "Garden Tour": the representation of the garden in French and Francophone literature from the Middle Ages to the 20th century
class-description: This course will explore the space of the garden as it appears and functions in literary texts from the medieval period to the 20th century.  We will investigate how this space—saturated with meaning since its Judeo-Christian origins—is constructed and cultivated in a wide variety of texts and genres.  Along the way, we will encounter the walled medieval garden, the formal “jardin à la française”, and the pleasures of the garden, whether as an escape, a space of production, or a return to the maternal.  The garden also fosters reflections on colonization, as we will see in several 19th and 20th-century works. This tour will allow us to read stories, poetry, essays and novels, as well as discover the history of the garden in its concrete forms, for example, the gardens of Versailles or the Tuileries.  We will also enhance our experience of the garden by dipping in to other arts, such as Rococo and Impressionist painting.  Finally, we will address the philosophical dimension of the garden, especially how it allows us to think about the place of the human in relation to nature.

title: Teaching French in College: Second Year
course-description: Lectures and discussion on the methodologies used in teaching second-year French, grading and testing; occasional attendance at demonstration classes; supervised classroom teaching. Required of all instructors teaching French 3 or 4.
class-description: French 375C provides readings and a forum for discussing topics in language pedagogy related to the intermediate level (study of grammar in review; continued study of culture; work on the writing process in L2) and experience in creating and adapting instructional materials for use in the UC Berkeley French discovery-centered language classroom. Also provides training in the development of a teaching portfolio in preparation for the job market. Seminar meets weekly for a two-hour session.

title: Decolonial Border Geographies
course-description: This course examines how today’s bounded geographies were shaped by racialized and regionalized discourse and practice, setting the foundation for contemporary struggles over political, economic and social identities along and across Latin America. Specifically, the course incorporates the study of the United States’ historical relationship with Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean in order to understand how these histories map onto the productions of borders, regimes of migration and citizenship, and movements that increasingly articulate a decolonial turn in intellectual thought and within political and social action.

title: Racial and Ethnic Geographies of Latin America
course-description: This course offers a geographic survey of race and ethnicity across Latin America, including Californiam, Mesoamerica, Brazil, the Andes, and the Caribbean. The course draws from academic scholarship, creative non-fiction, podcasts, and film in order to weave together critical voices from across the region that speak to racial and ethnic identities. Students will come away with a stronger knowledge of the region’s history and geography, as well as key debates on political, economic and cultural topics concerning Latin American peoples and intellectual movements.

title: Rethinking Latin American Geographies Through Social Mapping
course-description: Maps are important tools for our daily activities and spatial imaginaries; however, the ways in which official and dominant Western maps organized the information about the world occludes other ways of knowing territories. How are these “other” geographies represented? How are maps re-designed and appropriated to visualize different spatialities? In this course, students will be introduced to key themes and design practices in social cartography in Latin America. These reflect on collective or individual mapping practices to represent and increase the visibility of social issues and ways of knowing and being in this region. Previous knowledge of maps not required.

title: Physical Landscapes: Process and Form
course-description: Understanding the physical characteristics of the Earth's surface, and the processes active on it, is essential for maintaining the long-term health of the environment, and for appreciating the unique, defining qualities of geographic regions. In this course, we build an understanding of global tectonics, rivers, hillslopes, and coastlines and discover how these act in concert with the underlying geologic framework to produce the magnificent landscapes of our planet. Through our review of formative processes, we learn how physical landscapes change and are susceptible to human modifications, which are often unintentional.

title: Food and the Environment
course-description: How do human populations organize and alter natural resources and ecosystems to produce food? The role of agriculture in the world economy, national development, and environmental degradation in the Global North and the Global South. The origins of scarcity and abundance, population growth, hunger and obesity, and poverty.

title: Geographic Film Production
course-description: What makes a film geographical? How can we explore humans’ relationships to their environment through sound and image? How might we make nonfiction films which foreground place and give it actual agency and voice? How can we use documentary film practices to depict place, culture, society, gesture, movement, rhythm and ﬂow in new and exciting ways? This is a production workshop where each student will conceptualize, shoot, and edit one short documentary film project that centralizes some aspect/s of geographic thought. This course is geared towards first time filmmakers. All film projects must fit the theme designated by the instructor, per term.

title: Sonic Geographies
course-description: This is a practice-based course in which students will record, edit, and produce audio works that document and interpret the built environment and people in public places throughout Oakland and Berkeley. Through the process of making location recordings, analyzing those recordings, composing them into autonomous works, and critiquing them along the way, this course will engage with questions of how sound can help us understand the people we encounter and the spaces we move through everyday.

title: Audio Narratives of the Bay Area
course-description: This hands-on course trains students in the art and craft of journalistic podcasting, covering research, interviewing, scriptwriting, scoring, and audio editing. Students will examine podcasts from the Bay Area and then create their own stories. Students will conceptualize, pitch, and produce audio stories, explore different podcast formats, prepare pre-production materials, and develop technical skills in recording and mixing. The semester culminates in the public release of a pilot episode focused on the Bay Area.

title: Storytelling in Place
course-description: This course examines how places shape stories and how stories influence places. Drawing from the fields of geography, journalism, and creative writing, students will investigate the ways in which storytelling intersects with notions of place and identity. Through a combination of readings, short films, and audio, students will create their own place-based stories.

title: Reclaiming Jerusalem: Critical Readings in the  Historical Geography of a Contested City
course-description: This course explores the contested history of Jerusalem, examining how its geography evolved through competing religious and political claims. From its origins as a Canaanite city to its status as Israel's capital, Jerusalem’s landscape was formed through diverse influences, including the Israelites, Byzantines, Crusaders, Ottomans, and British. We will analyze sacred sites, urban plans, films and maps and understand how each power visualized the city to reflect their own political and cultural agendas. The course offers students a deeper understanding of Jerusalem's complex, multifaceted history and design. Ideal for students in history, geography, and urban studies and those interested in Jewish, Israeli and Middle Eastern studies.

title: Global Development: Theory, History, Geography
course-description: This course examines whether the convergence between the ‘new Right’ and the ‘new Left’ has successfully addressed the central challenge of contemporary global development studies. It asks students to assess the multiple, nonlinear, and interconnected paths of change in Africa, Asia, Latin America, and the Middle East that are now taking place. It explores the context of intensified global integration and capitalist development. Students will consider what changes in this context mean for larger social change, especially given ongoing global economic crises and rapidly evolving relations.

title: Critical Economic Geographies
course-description: This course examines the fundamentally geographic nature of our current, historically unique system of material reproduction—capitalism—and how capitalist logics have shaped places and forms of life over the course of the system’s growth and change. We will explore how capitalist processes shape the rise (and inevitable fall) of places, techniques, social worlds, and divisions of labor, and pay close attention to the power relations and spatial organization that accompany them. The course provides a grounding in critical perspectives such as the Marxian, Black radical, and feminist traditions to equip students with theoretical tools to understand and interpret the spatiality of contemporary capitalism.

title: Virtual worlds: games, play and geography
course-description: Through the critical study of games, play, and virtual worlds, this course examines the importance of geographical concepts to historical and current gaming contexts. Our media consumption practices are part of an increasingly ‘ludic’ culture centred on play, digital gaming, and interactive media. As video games become increasingly mainstream, how can we best contextualize the significance of play in relation geographical concepts like landscape, power, space and place, and environment and ecology? How can the geographical study of cities, architecture, worlding and identity – through games and play – help students understand more about their own digital experiences, and the centrality of geography to everyday digital life?

title: The Bay Area
course-description: This course examines the distinct but ill-defined San Francisco Bay Area. Our approach will be neither to simply learn about the individual places that compose the Bay Area nor to study a succession of detached periods of development. Instead, we will think critically about the creations, contestations, and transformations of Bay Area spaces—landscapes, communities, neighborhoods, cities, suburbs, and the metropolitan region.  Topics include indigenous geographies, colonialism, industrialization and economic geography, cities and suburbs, gentrification and displacement, regional racial formation and place-based identities, and resistance and rebellion.

title: Introduction to Global Studies
course-description: This course is designed as an introduction to Global Studies. Using a social science approach, the course prepares students to think critically about issues of international development, conflict, and peace in a variety of societies around the world. As such, it provides students with a basic theoretical introduction to the impact of global interaction as well as an opportunity to explore such interaction in a variety of case studies.

title: Freshman Seminar
course-description: The Freshman Seminar Program has been designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. Freshman seminars are offered in all campus departments, and topics vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to 15 freshmen.
class-description: This weekly seminar introduces GETH students to a range of environmental work done on campus as well as opportunities for courses, volunteer work, extra-curricular activities and research through a series of guest speakers and group projects. Enrollment is limited to students who are part of the GETH residential hall program.

title: Reading and Composition
course-description: This course offers a survey of modern German literary, cultural, and intellectual currents, as well as an introduction to argumentation and analysis. Students will examine numerous issues and questions central to defining the complexity of modern German culture. R5A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R5B satisfies the second half.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

Students will examine numerous issues and questions central to defining the complexity of modern German culture. R5A satisfies the first half of the Reading and Composition requirement, and R5B satisfies the second half.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement
