title: Undergraduate Seminar: Problems in Research and Interpretation: Ancient
special: Undergraduate Seminar: The Etruscans: Pasts, Presents & Futures
course-description: Concentration on specific problems or works in a particular area of art history. Assigned readings, discussion, and a substantial paper. For specific topics and enrollment, see listings outside 416 Doe Library.
class-description: This seminar will explore the material culture and art of the Etruscans through the lens of indigeneity  (both ancient and modern) with a special emphasis on reception studies (how have the Etruscans been understood/misunderstood throughout the ages). We will approach this subject from a variety of perspectives, including, but not limited to an introduction to Etruscan art; “rediscovery”, collecting and display. The seminar will discuss aspects of decolonizing and question the various historicities crafted throughout the centuries regarding Etruscan art and culture. We will address a series of important questions, such as, how have the Etruscans been branded, packaged and presented throughout the centuries and why? And finally, how does the study of Etruscan art and culture deepen our understanding of the ancient Mediterranean as a whole? In addition to this, students this year will be studying a special Etruscan exhibit in the Doe Library (opening in early 2026).

title: Undergraduate Seminar: Problems in Research and Interpretation: Asian
special: Undergraduate Seminar: Sacred Sites as Palimpsests
course-description: Concentration on specific problems or works in a particular area of art history. Assigned readings, discussion, and a substantial paper. For specific topics and enrollment, see listings outside 416 Doe Library.
class-description: This course is an introduction to the art on the trade routes across Eurasia often known collectively as the Silk Road. We will organize our discussions around two important East Asian sites found along these routes: Dunhuang, a large Buddhist cave complex outside an oasis town in western China that served as the gateway for cultural exchange and trade between China and Central Asia; the Shōsō-in, a Japanese imperial collection in Nara, first assembled in the mid-eighth century, which encompasses artifacts that were created, traded, and (in some cases) made to order along the Silk Road and found their ways to Japan through mechanisms of trade and diplomacy. This seminar will explore this rich material in relation to topics such as the spread of Buddhism and its material culture, the role of these sites in the history of royal patronage, how artifacts were enacted in rituals and ceremonies, as well as how these two sites were mobilized in modern writing of national histories of art in East Asia.

class-description: What does revolutionary art look like? What is the role of the artist in building a new society? This course explores a wide variety of artistic forms and experiments undertaken over the history of the Soviet Union, from 1917 to 1991, including those of the early avant-garde, socialist realism, and underground art. Looking at projects in diverse mediums, from easel painting to performance art to film and architecture, this course will think about the questions posed by explicitly political art and the efforts to revolutionize life at every level. We will consider work created in the Republics of the Soviet Union as well as in the nations of the so-called Eastern Bloc, and examine Soviet culture in an internationalist frame. Some topics considered include: the relationship between abstract art and propaganda; documentary film and photography; monumental art; and the built environment of socialism, constructed and imagined.

title: Reading and Composition in History
special: Illicit Republics: A History of Smuggling in the United States
instructor: Carlotta Wright de la Cal, Carla Hesse
course-description: Reading and composition courses based upon primary historical documents and secondary historical scholarship. These courses provide an introduction to core issues in the interpretation of historical texts and introduce students to the distinctive ways of reading primary and secondary sources. Courses focus on specific historical topics but address general issues of how historians read and write. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: What does illicit trade reveal about law, empire, borders, and state power? Students will examine how informal economies have shaped U.S. state formation and national identity. Which markets have been deemed legitimate, patriotic, and profitable, and which condemned as “black markets,” un-American, or morally corrupting to the citizenry? Why have people engaged in the smuggling of goods, ideas, and raw materials, as well as illegal immigration networks—and how has the law changed to restrict or accommodate them? This seminar explores these questions by tracing the long and murky history of smuggling in North America. Taking as broad a view of “smuggling” as possible, we will cover topics ranging from the eighteenth-century world of piracy and privateering through to California Indian horse raiding and the Atlantic slave trade after abolition, from Prohibition-era rum running to modern drug and human trafficking. By reading court records, customs documents, newspaper accounts, as well as secondary literature in weekly workshops, students will investigate the shifting moral and legal boundaries of trade.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Special Topics in the History of the United States
special: Foodways: An Edible History of the Modern World
course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may also explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the complex political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors and subject will vary.
class-description: We’ve all got to eat—but there, the consensus ends. Long before celebrity chefs, food TV, and trade-marked diets competed for our attention, the production and consumption of food and the meanings attached to it were the subjects of great controversy. Poets and painters, philosophers and bureaucrats, merchants and prophets explored why we eat what we eat and how we define, acquire, and consume food. Ways of preparing and consuming food affirmed—and still affirm—bonds of kinship and community but also distinguish “us” from “them,” whether along national, religious, gendered, ethno-racial, or other lines. As an object of cultural exchange, global trade, and profit, food also played a major role in the conquest and colonization of the Americas and the rise of industrial capitalism. This course offers a history of foodways organized around two basic questions: How and why have food production, what people eat, dining customs, and ideas about the moral, scientific, and medical value of food itself changed since 1492? What role have foodways (networks of food production, procurement, preservation, preparation, consumption, nutrition, and culinary culture in any given society) and foodscapes (the spaces in which food is raised, procured, distributed, and consumed) played in the making of the modern world—and the remaking of the planet?

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

title: Earth on Fire: Global Environmental History since 1492
course-description: The past five hundred years have witnessed the rapid transformation of the earth’s biosphere, resulting in biodiversity loss, species extinction, deforestation, land-use change, and the concentration of greenhouse gas emissions impacting the stability of the earth system. This class examines the origins of these environmental crises by studying global transformations of environment and society since the fifteenth century, emphasizing the intensifying resource demands of imperial globalization, industrial capitalism, commodity frontiers, unfree labor, food systems, and postwar economic development. By ending in the late twentieth century, the course also situates the ideas and politics that have emerged to imagine new environmental futures.
class-description: What is happening to the planet? Over the last several decades there has been a new awareness that human societies have changed the natural world with alarming intensity. While environmental problems like pollution, climate change, and species extinction are often presented as areas of relatively recent concern, the processes that gave rise to them have much longer histories. This course explores their origins by tracking transformations of the global environment from the fifteenth century to the present. It documents how intensifying resource demands have remade human-nature relations across time, why environmental ideas intersect with issues of global connection and inequality, and the ways in which modern societies have become dependent on the technological control and stewardship of resource ecologies distributed across the planet.

title: Freshman Seminar
special: The Uses and Abuses of History
course-description: The Freshman Seminar Program has been designed to provide new students with the opportunity to explore an intellectual topic with a faculty member in a small seminar setting. Freshman seminars are offered in all campus departments and topics vary from department to department and semester to semester. Enrollment limited to fifteen freshmen.
class-description: This discussion-based, interactive seminar explores the nature of history. Though frequently perceived as dead and buried, the past—as cancel and woke cultures demonstrate—is very much alive and kicking, shaping and reshaping present and future. Our discussion probes key questions: What is an historical fact? Can we trust the evidence of social media, documentaries, memoirs, biographies and official records? How and why does history become weaponized? Does it offer ‘lessons’? How do historians approach the past?

course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. class-description: This course examines how dinosaurs have shaped and reflected culture from their scientific recognition in the nineteenth century to their global prominence in popular media today. From Gertie the Dinosaur and Sunoco to Calvin and Hobbes and Jurassic Park, dinosaurs have variously served as symbols of modernity and lassitude, of empire and extinction. We will examine dinosaurs as scientific objects and cultural symbols to trace the reciprocal influence of science and culture, and how their conception has changed over time. By evaluating scholarship in the history and philosophy of science and environmental thought, along with the inimitable visual culture of paleontology in popular culture, we will examine how diverse and contradictory depictions of dinosaurs reflect broader questions of scientific authority, capitalism and modernity, national identity, and ecological consciousness. We will consider how and why dinosaurs mediate anxieties about extinction, technology, and humanity’s place in nature.

title: Special Topics in Comparative History
course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may also explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the complex political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. class-description: Given recent trade union organization-drives in the gig and service economies, the conflict between capital and labor has come to the forefront again. This course will take a historical perspective and explore the relationship between capital and labor in the last 200 years. After some theoretical considerations, we will look at the nature of work in precapitalist Europe, before we deal with the Industrial Revolution and its impact on work organization and working conditions. The Industrial Revolution spurred the development of trade unions, first in Britain and then in other parts of Europe and the world. Trade unions were formed against the opposition of employers and were often banned by governments. We will look at how trade unions changed with the spread of mass production and how after a series of mass strikes a compromise was found in many countries after the Second World War. This compromise crumbled in the 1980s with a new employer attack against trade unions in the capitalist centers and beyond. We will end the course with a discussion of current challenges such as working in a digital and global economy and the relationship between organized labor and the environment.

title: Special Topics in African History
course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. class-description: This course is an introduction to major themes in the economic history in Africa. We will take a long view of these issues, examining a series of approaches that have animated Africanist scholarship over time. In many respects, the focus on economic history was central to the emergence of the discipline of African history in the 1960s. Economic historical methods proved appealing to historians interested in recovering African experiences under European domination and in explaining the high levels of poverty across much of Africa. Since the 1990s, these questions have become less central to the discipline of African history, although there is still significant work being done on questions of gender, ‘informal’ economic activity, youth, and the broader push to ‘end poverty’ as part of the UN millennium goals.

title: Special Topics in Asian History
special: History of Chinese Socialism: Laws, Rights, State
course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may also explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the complex political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors and subject will vary.
class-description: This course examines the relationship between socialism and law in the history of the People's Republic of China. Marxists offered a radical critique of the rule of law—what they called "bourgeois law”—and made the case that humankind would be better off without the state and its legal apparatus. Yet, upon taking power, the Chinese Communist Party didn't stop at abolishing the old order; it immediately began constructing a new legal system with distinctly socialist characteristics.

title: Special Topics in Latin American History
course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may also explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the complex political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors and subject will vary.
class-description: This course will cover the topic of authoritarianism as a form of government, theory of power, and a way of life in Latin America. It will be taught in several phases. The first will quickly cover the political history of the region, naming and explaining authoritarian leaders and movements so students have a timeline to follow. After that we will transition to thematic sections covering resistance to authoritarianism, race and gender under authoritarian regimes, the differences between left and right-wing authoritarianism, and other topics. The course will conclude with deep-dive lectures into the stories of particular movements and individuals that illustrate these topics.

title: Special Topics in the History of the United States
special: Survey of LGBTQ History in America
course-description: This course is designed to engage students in conversations about particular perspectives on the history of a selected nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon as specified by the respective instructor. By taking this course, students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for, some combination of: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may also explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the complex political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors and subject will vary.
class-description: We have arrived at a unique historical moment for LGBTQ rights, visibility and inclusion in U.S. society and beyond. What led to such (still evolving) empowerment and activism? Who were some of the bold change makers of the past, and in what ways did different communities negotiate and confront homophobia? How and when did language shift from sodomite to invert to pansy to homosexual, and then to today’s queer or nonbinary? This survey course in American history offers an exciting overview of how, when and where LGBTQ history was made. Beginning with an introduction on origins from the ancient world, the course will focus on religious, cultural, social and political responses to LGBTQ love and desire from early America to the present, with emphasis on the history of identity and activism. We will also examine the rise of psychology, the medicalization of the body, and shifting gender roles in the workplace, the arts, and in wartime. The founding of modern political activism and affinity groups and mainstream media censorship will also receive scrutiny, leading to comparisons of separatist movements and more recent media representation.

title: Introduction to the Civilizations and Cultures of South Asia
course-description: South Asia is often imagined as exceptional and timeless. Home of many religions, over thousands of years it has seen dozens of dynasties ruling diverse peoples speaking scores of languages and worshiping both many gods and the One. This course offers a rapid jaunt through South Asia’s historical contradictions: from the sublime peaks of its myriad philosophies to its brutal postcolonial realities; from its depleted jungles to its teeming cities; from its ageless epics and arts to its obsession with Bollywood and cricket today. Our inquiries are driven by a single question of universal relevance. How do we reconcile this varied land’s millennia of civilization with its fractured present?
class-description: In this course we will study South Asia through a thematic lens, beginning with sport, and moving to the themes of the Partition of 1947, the creation of colonial knowledge, Indian religions, the workings of caste and power in society, the historical evolution of Indian cuisines, agriculture and cities; and a sustained focus on politics and culture—cinema, art, and music—in the period after 1947. Regular collaborative readings of a range of primary sources will be supplemented by movie viewings and discussion sections, with an in-class mid-term and a final examination.

title: Latin American History: Modern Latin America
course-description: This introductory course surveys the history of modern Latin America from independence to the present, with a strong emphasis on the twentieth century. Our focus will be on broad transfomations in politics, place, identity, and work.
class-description: This course covers approximately the last 150 years of Latin American history, starting in the 1860s and 70s and going to the 2020s. Focusing on the experiences of everyday people as well as leaders and elites, it will weave together stories of religious, political, racial, economic, social, and cultural transformation. Lectures will be interactive, inviting student participation and questions, and readings will range from films and photos to government memos to journals and diaries to academic texts.

title: Introduction to the History of the United States: The United States from Civil War to Present
course-description: What does it mean to be American? Whatever your answer is to this question, chances are it is deeply connected to the themes and events we will discuss in this class. Here we will track America's rise to global power, the fate of freedom in a post-Emancipation political setting, and the changing boundaries of nation, citizenship, and community. We will use landmark events to sharpen our themes, but we will also take care to analyze the equally important (and shifting) patterns of where and how Americans lived, worked, and played.
class-description: This course presents a history of the United States since the Civil War. We will pay particular attention to three, often interrelated, themes that weave throughout these 150+ years and go by the mnemonic “The 3 P’s”: (1) pluralism, (2) political economy, and (3) projection of power. Pluralism refers to the nation’s extraordinary social diversity and the struggles to expand the boundaries of just who is included in the “We” of the Constitution’s “We the People.” Political economy refers to the interaction between politics/policy and economics, in particular, how 19th century populism, early 20th century progressivism, mid-20th century New Deal liberalism, and late 20th century and early 21st century neoliberalism offered different political and policy responses to the nation’s shifting economic base from agriculture to industry to post-industry/service, striking different balances between how much faith and responsibility to vest in the public sector (government) vs. the private sector (the free market). Projection of power refers to the engagement of the United States with the world beyond its boundaries (initially across the continent, later beyond the continental United States), from “hard power” military force to “soft power” economic and cultural influence.

title: Introduction to Chinese History: From the Mongols to Post-Mao China
course-description: This is an introduction to Chinese history from the 13th through the 20th centuries -- from the Mongols and Khubilai Khan's conquest of southern China to the amazing turnaround following the death of Mao Zedong in 1976 and the opening of the era of reform that has led to China's emergence as a major economic and strategic power today. The course assumes no prior knowledge of Chinese history.
class-description: This course offers an introduction to Chinese history from the Mongol conquest in the thirteenth century to the People's Republic's emergence as a major global power in the twenty-first century. We will examine forces for political unification and economic integration under the imperial dynasties of the Yuan, the Ming, and the Qing, the transformation of China from a continental empire to a nation-state integrated into a global capitalist economy, the formation of a socialist alternative under the Chinese Communist Party, and the origins and limits of systemwide reforms following Mao Zedong's death in 1976. Students will be expected to attend lectures, take part in discussion sections, and read a variety of assigned materials, with a strong emphasis on primary sources in English. The course assumes no prior knowledge of Chinese history or Chinese language.

title: Origins of Western Civilization: Medieval Europe
course-description: This course surveys medieval European history from Constantine's conversion to Christianity in 310 to 1400, emphasizing the creativity of the new peoples populating Europe in adapting the heritage of the Roman world and the role of economic change in transforming European societies after the millennium. Topics include the development of kingship and states, courtly literary and material cultures, economic change, the environment, and religious movements. Discussion sections will explore medieval sources—heroic epics, biographies of kings and saints, letters and chronicles, documents, social satires, and material artifacts—while lectures narrate the changes transforming Europe over the Middle Ages in conversation with our contemporary world.
class-description: This course offers a survey of medieval history via twice-weekly lectures and a weekly discussion section. Students will complete a midterm exam, a final exam, and two essays based on assigned readings. Attendance and participation in weekly discussion sections will also be considered as part of the overall grade for the course.

title: Reading and Composition in History
special: “Blues People”: Black Political Thought and Action in the United States, from the Middle Passage to the Present
course-description: Reading and composition courses based upon primary historical documents and secondary historical scholarship. These courses provide an introduction to core issues in the interpretation of historical texts and introduce students to the distinctive ways of reading primary and secondary sources. Courses focus on specific historical topics but address general issues of how historians read and write. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: What does it mean to be free? How have Black thinkers and activists responded to this question over the last 400 years in the U.S.? How did race, class, and gender influence this thinking? Why has the Black radical tradition continuously been viewed as one of the most significant threats to white supremacy, patriarchy, and the global capitalist order? This course examines the ideas, forms of expression, and political aspirations articulated by those living in a society in which “enlightened” promises of freedom and liberty were never meant to apply equally to them. From the infamous 1857 Dred Scott decision that affirmed Black people “had no rights that the white man was obligated to respect,” to late 1960s-1970s Black Power and the bi-partisan “punishment bureaucracy” that came in its wake, we will trace the evolution of Black political thought and praxis in the United States from the era of enslavement to its afterlives.
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Reading and Composition in History
special: From Keystone Kops to Demolition Man: A History of American Policing through Film in the 20th Century

These courses provide an introduction to core issues in the interpretation of historical texts and introduce students to the distinctive ways of reading primary and secondary sources. Courses focus on specific historical topics but address general issues of how historians read and write. Satisfies the second half of the Reading and Composition requirement.
class-description: From Keystone Kops to Demolition Man: A History of American Policing through Film in the 20th Century
requirements: the Reading and Composition B requirement

title: Seminar in Historical Research and Writing for History Majors
course-description: Individual research projects carried out in seminar sections in various historical fields resulting in a lengthy paper, with readings and discussions on general problems of historical inquiry. In addition to regular class meetings, individual consultations with the instructor, research, and preparation totaling ten to twelve hours per week are required.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: United States
special: Love, Sex, and Marriage in the United States
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: Though shaped by human biology and universal evolutionary impulses, human sexual and romantic relations have varied widely among and within different societies and have changed dramatically over time. This course explores some dimensions of that diversity and change in the social, cultural, and legal history of the United States since the American Revolution. Of particular interest will be the complex and overlapping histories of the three distinct phenomena featured in the course title: cultural ideals of romantic emotional attachment; erotic norms, practices, and ideals; and most especially, the social and legal institutions that regulate and legitimate particular sexual and conjugal relationships.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Europe
special: Thinking in Crisis. Hannah Arendt’s Origins of Totalitarianism
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: In this seminar we will closely read Origins of Totalitarianism (1951) and other writings by the German-Jewish émigré and political theorist Hannah Arendt. Additional readings include works inspired by Arendt such as Charlotte Beradt’s The Third Reich of Dreams. Reflecting on Arendt’s thinking about the crises of the 1930s and 40s and their historical roots in European racism and imperialism, we will consider its insights for our present moment.

title: The Craft of History
course-description: The principal aim of this course is to prepare students to write a capstone/thesis in history (in either the History 102 or 101A/101B seminars). To that end, its goals are (i) to introduce students to the methods and craft of history; (ii) to model approaches to the discipline of history and provide exposure to methods in lecture; and (iii) to provide ample opportunity in discussion sections to practice and hone these methods. The course is offered in fall and spring semesters, and is designed to precede the required 103 and 101/102 seminars.
class-description: How is history created? This course is designed to welcome students into the History major and prepare them to research and write a capstone/thesis in history (in either the History 102 or 101A/101B seminars). To that end its goals are (i) to introduce students to the methods and practices of history and historians; (ii) to explore a variety of approaches to the discipline and discuss them in lecture; and (iii) to provide opportunities in section to practice and hone historical methods and techniques. You will learn both how to think like historians and how to “do” history—by which we mean how to ask historical questions and go about answering them. More than other history courses you have taken at UC Berkeley, or will take, this course is focused on active learning and skill acquisition. The syllabus is structured according to the historian’s process, beginning with how to ask historical questions, moving through how to locate primary sources, how to analyze them, and how to write new histories for either public or academic audiences. Lectures and sections will familiarize you with different approaches and methods, and will give you the tools to construct your own historical research projects.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Comparative History
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: Marxism has been one of the most enduring, impactful, and contested intellectual traditions in the modern world. Organized around Martin Jay’s classic 1984 text, Marxism and Totality, this class will survey key primary texts by the thinkers identified with the tradition of "Western Marxism," including Georg Lukacs, Antonio Gramsci, Theodor W. Adorno, Herbert Marcuse, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, and Louis Althusser. We will also engage with historiographical debates over the meaning and scope of the category of “Western Marxism,” situating Marxism and Totality in its moment and engaging more recent efforts by historians and theorists to reconstruct, deconstruct, and critique the category and the tradition it names.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Comparative History
special: Environmental Equity in China and Beyond
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: This seminar, co-taught with Thomas Hahn (Ph.D. Heidelberg), aims to introduce students to a selection of sources that will equip them to better engage others in their community on the set of existential questions arising from climate change and the state of an “altered earth” which is entering our consciousness on an almost daily basis now.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Middle East
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: This advanced undergraduate seminar explores the evolution of American involvement in the Middle East from missionary origins in the early nineteenth century to superpower hegemony in the early twenty-first century. Rather than only examining the perspective of U.S. policymakers and media representations about the Middle East, this seminar will focus as well on how people in the region have variously understood America and how they have reacted to U.S. policies that have affected the geopolitics, cultures, and political economy of the region. Students will read a range of primary and secondary sources, including declassified government documents, and major works like Orientalism, in order to prepare them to make their own, original contributions in the form of a substantial research paper.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Middle East
special: World War I in the Middle East
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: The Middle East is the forgotten front in World War I, but the importance of the region in the broader war, and the importance of World War I in the making of the Modern Middle East cannot be overstated. We will be considering the lead-up to the war in the Ottoman Empire, the history of European involvement in the Empire which determined the Ottoman role in it, the key battles that took place, the many internal conflicts that came to a head within the Empire due to the global conflagration, and the ways the secret wartime treaties as well as the post-war treaties created the conditions for the Modern Middle East.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Asia
special: The Early Chinese Historians, with nods to the Western
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: In a world hyper-focused on transitory impressions, this seminar introduces participants to two antique historians (Sima Qian and Ban Gu) whose writings in classical Chinese (available in English translation) invite us to consider what motivates human beings to act to intervene, for better or worse, in predictable situations, and what are the likely long-term consequences of the decisions we make to pursue power, riches, reputation, longevity, or other goals. These historians, in addition, ask readers if it possible to live a good life, absent legitimate government, comparative peace, and communities founded on personal trust and a fair division of labor and capital. While several excellent studies in the last twenty years have focused on Sima Qian’s distinctive voice, Ban Gu’s compelling narratives in the History of Han (Hanshu) have elicited far less interest recently, perhaps because Ban’s rhetoric is more concerned with the political. This course seeks to rectify the imbalance by comparing and contrasting the two historians’ projects, which students will analyze partly through the lens of Michael Nylan’s own book project (now in draft).

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: United States
special: Race and Politics in Modern America
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: The politics of race is a defining hallmark of U.S. history that has structured policymaking and electoral campaigns for well over a century. From local power struggles to presidential elections, race is a constant factor in the development of political strategy. This seminar explores the predominant role of race and ethnicity in the political history of the twentieth-century United States through a series of key questions. What does it mean to be part of a voting bloc or swing vote? Why do political coalitions shift over time? How are the dividing lines of race and ethnicity formed, changed, and reinforced in the political sphere? Who is included and who is excluded in mainstream party politics?  Major themes in this investigation include identity politics, partisan realignment, representation, and racial formation.

title: Proseminar: Problems in Interpretation in the Several Fields of History: Europe
special: The Rise of Global Empires and Imperial Culture in Early Modern Europe, 1400-1800
course-description: This seminar is an introduction to some dimension of the history of a nation, region, people, culture, institution, or historical phenomenon selected by the respective instructor. Students will come to understand, and develop an appreciation for: the origins and evolution of the people, cultures, and/or political, economic, and/or social institutions of a particular region(s) of the world. They may explore how human encounters shaped individual and collective identities and the political, economic, and social orders of the region/nation/communities under study. Instructors prioritize critical reading, engaged participation, and focused writing assignments.
class-description: This course will focus on the history of the first global empires that arose in early modern Europe. Spain, Portugal, France and Britain all strove with varying measures of success to build global empires in this period that marked the beginnings of imperial contest that has shaped the modern world. Among our themes will be the Renaissance ideas at the roots of this imperialism, the political practices and institutions of empire, and the art and architecture that comprised the cultural foundations of European empire. Requirements include weekly participation in the seminar, some short written assignments and a final paper of roughly 15-20 pages.

title: The Life Sciences since 1750
course-description: This course will survey the development of the sciences of living nature from the mid-18th to the late-20th century. Topics include scientific and popular natural history, exploration and discovery, Darwin and evolution, cell theory, the organizational transformation of science, physiology and experimentalism, classical and molecular genetics, and the biomedical-industrial complex. Emphasis is on the formation of fundamental concepts and methods, long-term trends toward specialization, institutionalization, professionalization, and industrialization, and the place of the life sciences in modern societies. Many lectures are illustrated by slides.
class-description: This course provides an account of the origins and development of modern biology from a jointly social and conceptual perspective. Significant developments in the human knowledge of life on earth will thus be presented as both an intellectual process—the advocation and contestation of key ideas and theories through time—and as the result of the entanglement of those ideas with the cultural, political, economic, and institutional contexts in which they are produced. Students will come away from the course with an understanding of both the major problems, puzzles, and solutions that biologists wrestled with in their collective attempts to understand the phenomenon of life over the past three centuries, and the deep connections between those efforts and the unique historical environments in which they were pursued.

title: Armenia and Armenians from 1500s to the Present
course-description: In the early modern era, cultural, literary, social, economic, and political transformations occurred among Armenians of the Ottoman Empire, Safavid Iran, and later the Russian Empire. Armenians engaged in global trade and cultural processes from India to Venice and beyond. We will particularly focus on the different iterations of Armenian identity in various imperial settings, diasporan communities as well as in relation to the Armenian genocide and the Soviet and contemporary Republic of Armenia. We will examine the changing meanings and roles of Armenian identity across space and time.
class-description: At its premise, Armenian history assumes the existence of an Armenian identity. But what does it mean to be Armenian? How does the identity of a 17th-century Armenian merchant from Iran correspond to that of an Armenian in contemporary Paris?

title: Jews in the Modern World
course-description: This course will examine the impact of modern intellectual, political, cultural, and social forces on the Jewish people since the eighteenth century. It is our aim to come to an understanding of how the Jews interpreted these forces and how and in what ways they adapted and utilized them to suit the Jewish experience.  In other words, we will trace the way Jews became modern.  Some of the topics to be covered include Emancipation, the Jewish Enlightenment, new Jewish religious movements, Jewish politics and culture, immigration, antisemitism, the Holocaust, and the state of Israel.

title: Modern Germany: Germany 1914 to the Present
course-description: This course will survey the political, economic, social, and cultural development of Germany since 1914. Special attention will be paid to the impact of World War I; problems of democratization under the impact of defeat, inflation, and depression; National Socialist racism and imperialism; the evolution of the German Federal Republic and the German Democratic Republic; unification and its problems; and modern Germany's role in Europe.
class-description: By covering German history since 1914 with an eye towards political, social, cultural, and economic developments, you will also learn how to approach and evaluate historical sources and reflect upon them to discuss the matter at hand. Together with the weekly reading, you will become informed thinkers and critical readers so that you can contribute to discussions in class. In this way, the sessions should amount to collaborative enterprises, a fact which will help you to critically reflect upon the past and to effectively write a historical research paper yourself, employing the insights gained and skills trained throughout this class.

title: The Power of Ideas: The History of Economic and Social Thought
course-description: This course looks at the history of economic and social thought from the 18th to the 21st century. It does so by presenting major thinkers and schools of thought and discussing the relevance of their theories for current economic, social, and ecological challenges. Among the thinkers that are covered are classical economists such as Smith, Malthus, and Ricardo, along with Marx, utilitarian and marginalist economists, as well as a number of undogmatic and radical thinkers. The course will, furthermore, discuss the work of Keynes and the theories of his neoliberal critics. Finally, the course also looks at more recent developments such as feminist and environmental economics and economics of race and discrimination.

title: History of Democracy: Europe 1620-present
course-description: What causes some democracies to succeed, others to fail? Using modern Europe as a laboratory we survey numerous societies over 400 years of history, to seek answers, from the unlikely beginnings in consensual practices of monarchies and Christian churches; to the rise of parliamentarism, the revolutionary theories of liberalism, and the rise of mass politics and modern ideologies of nationalism and socialism, fascism and populism. Why have hopeful democratic experiments, especially in Germany and Eastern Europe, given way to the most vile forms of dictatorship known to history? Why does democracy never seem consolidated, but always under attack from unpredictable but "popular" forces of left and right?

title: The Multiracial History of Slavery & Servitude in America
course-description: This course introduces students to the entwined, overlapping, multiracial histories of involuntary servitude and slavery in British North America/the United States. We will cover topics such as Native American systems of bondage, European enslavement of Indigenous men, women, and children, the often-forcible transport to and compulsory servitude of European migrants, the captivity and enslavement of African-descended people, and the coerced servitude of Asian migrants in the 19th century. The class concludes by considering the development of the post-Civil War penal state and the rise of mass incarceration. Students will leave the class with a more expansive understanding of American systems of captivity from settlement to the present.
class-description: Throughout the semester, the readings and lecture material will also be attentive to the laws that sanctioned slavery and other systems of captivity, captive people’s ongoing resistance to enslavement, and the ways that age, religion, gender, and sexuality shaped experiences of captivity. The class concludes by considering the development of the post-Civil War penal state, the widespread criminalization of formerly enslaved African Americans and their descendants, the concurrent emergence of convict leasing and debt peonage, and mass incarceration. Students will leave the class with a rich, more expansive, multicultural understanding of American systems of captivity from settlement to the present.

title: United States Legal and Constitutional History since 1850
course-description: This course explores some of the major questions and problems of United States legal history since 1850. The course weaves together historical and legal approaches and materials. Themes include federalism and the evolving nature of constitutional authority; citizenship and rights; law and economic change; law and social movements; and popular understandings of ‘the law.’ We will look to the “high” sphere of constitutional jurisprudence and to other legal and extra-legal arenas where law was applied, argued over, and worked out. By the end of this course, you should be able to analyze different kinds of legal texts; understand key legal concepts and doctrines; and make evidence-based arguments about core themes in legal history.

title: Latinx Histories
course-description: Latinx peoples are the largest U.S. minority group. How and why did so many different peoples come to be seen as like one another and as not “American”? Although often perceived as “aliens” or foreigners, Latinx peoples have lived in North America since before the nation existed. In the words of historian Vicki Ruiz, “Our America is American history.” As we move across Nuestra América from precolonial times to the present, we will examine diverse cultural practices, social movements, processes of community formation, intellectual trajectories, and responses to U.S. empire and white supremacy. We will also consider how race, class, gender, sexuality, and indigeneity have shaped belonging and inclusion within Latinx communities.
class-description: Latinx/e peoples are the largest U.S. minority group. Although often perceived as foreigners, they have lived in North America since before the U.S. nation existed. How have they come to be seen as like one another but not as “American”? Our course will move across the continent from precolonial times (pre-1492) to the present, and examine Latinx/e community formation, cultural practices, social movements, politics, and responses to empire and exploitation. We will pay particular attention to how race, class, gender, sexuality, indigeneity, and language have shaped belonging and inclusion in Latinx communities as well as the United States more broadly.

title: Antebellum America: The Advent of Mass Society
course-description: This course examines half a century of life in the United States (roughly from the War of 1812 until the secession of the Southern states), focusing on race relations, westward expansion, class formation, immigration, religion, sexuality, popular culture, and everyday life. Assigned readings will consist largely of first-person narratives in which women and men of a range of ethnic and cultural backgrounds construct distinctive visions of life in the new nation.
class-description: The Civil War is commonly regarded as the second American Revolution—the grand rupture after which a new modern nation came into being. But many of the institutions, ideologies, and practices that make up modern society and culture in the United States emerged more gradually during the period that preceded the war. To understand the origins of such contemporary phenomena as the mass media, corporate capitalism, wage labor, the two-party system, family values, and racism, we need to trace their evolution in the nineteenth century. This course examines a little over half a century of life in the United States (roughly from 1800 until the secession of the South), focusing on everyday life, popular culture, race relations, democratic politics, westward expansion, urbanization, immigration, class formation, religious experience, gender roles, sexuality, print communication, and competing claims to wealth, power, and the good life. Assigned readings will consist largely of first-person narratives in which women and men of varied descent, backgrounds and cultural identities tried to make sense of their own experiences against the backdrop of major social change. Lectures will explore both the narratives and the social changes. Course requirements include two short (300-400 word) analyses of assigned primary sources, two midterm exams, and a cumulative exam during finals week.

title: The Atlantic World
course-description: This course explores the history of the four continents on the Atlantic rim—Europe, Africa, North and South America—and their increasing interconnectedness in the wake of Columbus’s voyage in 1492. It takes the Atlantic Ocean and its peripheries as a common zone of interaction, where peoples, cultures, ideas, goods, foodstuffs, and pathogens came into contact from diverse regions. The course begins with a portrait of Amerindian, African, and European civilizations c. 1400 and ends with an overview of the protracted struggles for decolonization and emancipation from slavery in the 19th-century Americas. Throughout these five centuries of profound transformation, we will study conflict and encounter between the region’s many diverse peoples.
class-description: This course explores the history of the four continents on the Atlantic rim—Europe, Africa, North America, and South America—and their increasing interconnectedness in the wake of Columbus’s voyage in 1492. It takes the Atlantic Ocean and its peripheries as a common zone of interaction, where peoples, cultures, ideas, goods, foodstuffs, and pathogens came into violent contact. The course begins with a portrait of Amerindian, African, and European civilizations c. 1400 and ends with an overview of the protracted struggles for decolonization and emancipation from slavery in the nineteenth-century Americas. Throughout these five centuries of profound transformation, we will study conflict and encounter between the region’s many diverse peoples. Topics include Indigenous survival amid the violent reconfiguration of their worlds; the rise of African slavery, the transatlantic slave trade, and African diaspora in the Americas; the origins of ideas of race and racialization; European imperialism, coercive labor practices, the rise of racial capitalism, and the consolidation of an increasingly integrated Atlantic economic system; as well as the strategies of resistance, accommodation, and insurgency employed by men, women, and children in each of these groups. Unfamiliar perspectives will be offered on familiar stories, and students will frequently be asked to think comparatively about parallel processes at work in different regions, as well as the many connections between them. Throughout the semester we will link these processes to their ongoing impacts and afterlives for us in the present day.

title: The Twentieth Century in Japan
course-description: This course addresses a twofold question: what did the 20th century mean for Japan? And what did Japan mean for the 20th century? In search of answers, we will trace Japan's emergence as a “world-shaper” in its two phases, military and economic, focusing on the institutional, social, and cultural transformations that were attendant to each phase and continue to define Japan’s presence in the contemporary world.
class-description: This course addresses a twofold question: what did the 20th century mean for Japan?  And what did Japan mean for the 20th century?  In search of answers, we will trace Japan's emergence as a “world-shaper” in its two phases, military and economic, focusing on the institutional, social, and cultural transformations that marked each phase and continue to define Japan’s presence in the contemporary world.

title: China: Twentieth-Century China
course-description: Chinese history from the decline of the Qing empire to the reforms under the Chinese Communist Party in the late 20th century.
class-description: This course is an overview of Chinese history from the final decades of the Qing empire (1644-1911) to the present. China will be our vantage point as we explore some responses to one of the central questions of the twentieth century: What kind of order is right for industrial society? We will approach this issue from multiple vantage points. Topics include the position of women in society, the cultivation of citizens and rehabilitation of criminals, national self-determination and anti-colonial struggle, the peasant economy, the governing of border regions, economic development and socialist transformation. We will pay particular attention to how law gained importance in these domain and others, why this development was celebrated by some and criticized by others, and how Chinese leaders defined and restricted the scope of legal regulation in the twentieth century.

title: Colonialism and Nationalism in Africa
course-description: This course examines the nature and effects of European colonization of Africa, and African responses to the colonial encounter. Broad themes include colonial conquest and practices of administration, African responses to the imposition of colonial rule, colonial economies, labor migration, introduction and impact of Christianity and Western education; women and the colonial state, urbanization, social change, the apartheid system, liberation struggles, decolonization, and the colonial legacy.
class-description: The conquest and colonization of the bulk of Africa started in the last decades of the nineteenth century. This course will examine the process and impact of European colonization of Africans. As well as examining the diverse ways Africans negotiated the colonial encounter, the course will also focus on nationalist movements, decolonization, and the attainment of independence. Rather than dwell on the minutiae of the period, the course will focus on broad themes and case studies to explore: colonial conquest and practices of administration; African responses to the imposition of colonial rule; colonial economies; labor migration; women and the colonial state; social change; urbanization, leisure, and social mobility; Africans and the Two World Wars; post-1945 politics and nationalism; case studies of guerrilla liberation movements; women in liberation movements; the colonial legacy. Documentaries will be shown in class.

title: Vietnam at War
course-description: This course explores the history of the wars that engulfed Vietnam during the post-WWII era. While focusing on the Second Indochina War (1954-1975), it also examines the history of the First Indochina War (1946-1954) and the Third Indochina War (1978-1980). It will address military, political, and social dynamics of the conflict as well as representatives of the war in film, fiction, and memoirs.
class-description: This course examines the history of the wars that engulfed Vietnam during the post-WWII era. It introduces two interpretive approaches to the history of these conflicts known as the “Orthodox” school and the “Revisionist” school.  It also discusses a new framework for studying the war known as the “Vietnam-centric” school that foregrounds Vietnamese actors and institutions and places twentieth-century developments within the broader context of Vietnamese history. While focusing on the Second Indochina War (1954-1975), this course also examines the rise of Vietnamese regionalism, nationalism, and communism prior to WWII as well as the history of the First Indochina War (1946-1954) and selected issues in postwar Vietnamese history. Major topics addressed include the precolonial and colonial origins of the war, the rise of rival communist and nationalist movements during the interwar era, the impact on Vietnam of Japanese Occupation during WWII, the armed struggle over decolonization between 1946 and 1954, the growth of Chinese communist influence in Vietnam after 1949, the battle of Điện Biên Phủ and the Geneva Accords in 1954, the establishment of northern and southern Vietnamese states during the late 1950s and early 1960s, the growth of a southern communist insurgency,  the dynamics of the American intervention and military escalation, the Tết Offensive, Vietnamization, the impact of the War on neighboring Cambodia and Laos, the Paris Accords of 1973, the American withdrawal, the fall of Sài Gòn and the unification of the country after 1975. We also discuss enduring legacies of the conflict in the postwar era.  In addition to history books and articles we will read first-person accounts of the War from the Vietnamese communist, anti-communist and American sides.

title: The Middle East From the 18th Century to the Present
course-description: The breaking of pre-modern empires and the formation of national states in the Arab world, Turkey, and Iran; Islam and nationalism.
class-description: This course explores the history and politics of the modern Middle East as they have developed from 1798 to the present. From Napoleon’s invasion of Ottoman Egypt at the end of the eighteenth century to the Gaza genocide in the twenty-first century, the Middle East has been at the heart of debates about colonialism, knowledge production, resource extraction, and resistance. Themes covered are how and why Western colonial powers have shaped the contemporary map and meaning of the Middle East, how they affected a prior history of coexistence, why the question of Palestine emerged as a burning ethical and political cause that traversed regional and religious divides, and how people in the region have adapted, accepted, defied, and resisted foreign and domestic tyrannies.

title: Research Seminars: United States
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: This research workshop guides graduate students through the process of framing, researching, and writing an original, chapter-or-article-length paper on race, ethnicity, and/or indigeneity in North American history.  We will begin with readings that demonstrate the geographical, temporal, and methodological dynamism of recent and classic works on race and colonialism. We will then consider how historians craft questions, work with sources, and situate their interventions within the historiography. We will meet regularly at the start of the semester, before breaking for independent work on an archival-based papers. We will then reconvene mid-semester for peer-review and writing workshops. All students should develop a feasible topic and locate relevant archival collections and primary sources before our first class.

title: Research Seminars: Europe
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: This seminar is designed to introduce students to an intensive examination of the major themes and issues concerning the history of the Jews in Germany from the eighteenth through the twentieth centuries. Among the topics to be explored are the debates over Jewish emancipation, the German-Jewish struggle with Jewishness, Wissenschaft des Judentums, religious innovation, integration into and separation from the mainstream, German antisemitism and Jewish responses, economic and family life, and Jewish culture in the Kaiserreich and Weimar Republic.

title: Research Seminars: Europe
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: This seminar surveys English-language scholarly literature on Soviet history, covering the period from the 1917 Revolution to the 1991 dissolution of the USSR. Each week, we will read a selection of influential studies and recent publications on a key theme in Soviet history. The goal of this seminar is to deepen understanding of the history and historiography of the USSR, as a basis for further work in Soviet history or for connected work in other fields and disciplines.

title: Advanced Studies: Sources/General Literature of the Several Fields: Africa
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: This course focuses on new scholarship on post-World War II histories of decolonization and state formation in Africa. We will pay particular attention to the immediate post-colonial period when now independent regimes were established across the continent beginning in the 1950s.  Much exciting new work has sought to revise our understanding of the economic and political ‘failures’ of the period right after independence by seeking to better evaluate the local and global context of newly independent African governments, and some of their achievements and lasting legacies. One focus in this area is the relationship between Africa and different forms of socialism, projects of Pan Africanism, the politics of continuing white minority rule in southern Africa, and the fraught project of development.

title: Advanced Studies: Sources/General Literature of the Several Fields: Asia
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: In this course, students will read and discuss important works in Vietnamese history with a special focus on the history of communism and labor.  Students taking the course as a 280 will write weekly response papers. Students taking the course as a 285 will research and write a long paper due at the end of the term, addressing a topic chosen in consultation with the instructor.

title: Advanced Studies: Sources/General Literature of the Several Fields: Latin America
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: This seminar offers a selective introduction to literature on Atlantic history, c. 1400-1888. We will explore the linked histories among the various “Atlantic worlds” scholars have identified as operating in this vast region, ranging from West and West Central Africa to western Europe, North and South America, the Caribbean, and the seas in between. Our emphasis will be on influential and innovative methodological approaches, particularly those that seek to center the experiences of Indigenous Peoples, Africans, people of African descent, and other marginalized actors; the circulation of objects, commodities, animals, ideas, and disease; and the maritime world—all topics that are often sidelined in more traditional colony-, empire-, or nation-centered approaches. Atlantic history provides an excellent opportunity for scholars to grapple with the challenge of scale, or how to write on both a “macro” and “micro” level and toggle in between the two. In addition to covering major topics in the field and their afterlives—from European invasion of the Americas to the Atlantic slave trade and the Haitian Revolution—this seminar will also provide an opportunity to collectively imagine what the next generation of Atlantic histories might look like.

title: Advanced Studies: Sources/General Literature of the Several Fields: United States
course-description: For precise schedule of offerings see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.
class-description: This course provides graduate students with an introduction to historical scholarship on U.S. immigration from the colonial period to the present. The central part of this course is classroom discussion based on intensive reading of scholarly articles and books. Through the discussion of classic and more recent studies, students will familiarize themselves with major theories, concepts, methodologies, and scholarly debates in the field of U.S. immigration history. Topics to be discussed in the course include community, identity, politics, labor, gender and sexuality, citizenship and belonging, transnationalism, colonialism, race, xenophobia and nativism, immigration law and policy, and borders.

title: Core Courses in the Literature of the Several Fields of History: Yearlong, 2-unit
course-description: To provide a broad survey of the literature and historiographical problems of the different fields in history.
class-description: This year-long course (4 units total, 2 units per semester) explores recent scholarship across a broad range of periods, themes, and methodologies in the study of the history of North America. Through these assigned readings, seminar discussions every two weeks, and regular lecture attendance in the History 7A/7B undergraduate sequence, the course aims to lay a foundation for PhD field examinations in North American history from antiquity to the present.

title: Core Courses in the Literature of the Several Fields of History: Europe
special: Introduction to Late Modern European History, 1789-present: "Democracy: Promise and Catastrophe"
course-description: To provide a broad survey of the literature and historiographical problems of the different fields in history.
class-description: This course aims to stimulate thought and conversation on the history of Late Modern Europe, with a particular attention toward the uneven development of liberal democracy. Emphasized are readability and new questions, rather than panoramic view or systematic geographic and thematic coverage. Requirements include attendance and participation; brief reviews of weekly readings (2-3 pgs.); and introducing at least one week's readings to the class, with a set of organizing questions sent to the class five days before our meeting.

title: Science and Technology Studies Research Seminar
course-description: This course will cover methods and approaches for students considering professionalizing in the field of STS, including a chance for students to workshop written work.
class-description: This interdisciplinary seminar is aimed at graduate students in fields related to science and technology studies who are undertaking significant writing projects, such as dissertation chapters, journal articles, or conference papers. This seminar will serve two functions. First, it will act as a writing lab in which students will share their projects for discussion and critique from the perspective of science and technology studies. Second, it will help develop students’ professional skills, particularly the ability to speak across academic disciplines about one’s areas of expertise. Above all, the seminar will be grounded in a collaborative learning community where students will share their knowledge and ideas with each other in a highly interdisciplinary, constructive environment.

title: Berkeley Connect
course-description: Berkeley Connect is a mentoring program, offered through various academic departments, that helps students build intellectual community. Over the course of a semester, enrolled students participate in regular small-group discussions facilitated by a graduate student mentor (following a faculty-directed curriculum), meet with their graduate student mentor for one-on-one academic advising, attend lectures and panel discussions featuring department faculty and alumni, and go on field trips to campus resources. Students are not required to be declared majors in order to participate.

title: History of Christianity: History of Christianity from 1250
course-description: This course follows 185A as the 2nd of two semesters on the History of Christianity. It treats the history of (principally Western) Christianity between the High Middle Ages and the present in Europe and in the rest of the world. The course's main theme is Christianity and the encounter of cultures. Its core readings range from Thomas a Kempis, Martin Luther, and St. Teresa of Avila to Simone Weil and Dietrich Bonhoeffer. The lectures will treat social, cultural, and intellectual topics, such as ecclesiastical authority institutions, forms of piety, revivalism, evangelization, theological speculation, Biblical scholarship, and philosophical arguments for and against religion.

title: Historical Colloquium
course-description: Colloquium on topics of current research. For precise schedule of offerings, see department catalog during pre-enrollment week each semester.

class-description: This seminar meets regularly to advance the development of individually proposed research projects on themes concerning the frontiers and the metropoles in late imperial and modern China. The objective of the course is a research paper that may contribute to a dissertation project.
